item.title: Chinese tech giant Huawei found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

China’s Huawei found guilty of trade secrets conspiracy, fraud in US trial

But jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced of engaging in criminal racketeering conspiracy.

A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.

However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.

The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.

Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.

US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.

The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.

Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.

The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.

Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.

Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.

Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.

“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.

It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.

Founder’s daughter detained

The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.

Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.

She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.

The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.

Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.

During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.

Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.

Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.

Banks knew

The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.

Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.

He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.

Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-24 21:43 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/11/24/chinese-tech-giant-huawei-found-guilty-of-conspiracy-to-steal-trade-secrets?traffic_source=rss

item.title: Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Dell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that topped Wall Street expectations for earnings and sales, and provided a strong guide for the fourth quarter.

Dell shares rose in extended trading.

Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:

- EPS: $9.45, adjusted, versus $6.59 expected

- Revenue: $54.94 billion, versus $49.32 billion expected

Dell said that it expected earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion in revenue.

The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.

The company's largest line is its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, which makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD.

ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion. Of that, $22 billion was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue.

"We are now a different company, with Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth," said Jeff Clarke, Dell's vice chairman and COO, in a statement. He said that Dell has 7,500 customers buying AI servers.

In prepared remarks, Clarke said that Dell has a competitive advantage over other computer equipment makers because it allows customers to get their computers working within hours of delivery.

"That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably," Clarke said in the prepared remarks published by Dell.

The company also raised its forecast for AI-servers in the coming fiscal year to $78 billion, versus $74 billion expected. The company says it has a backlog of $132.3 billion in AI server orders it is working through.

"Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power," Clarke said on an earnings call with analysts.

The company also sells laptops and PCs, in a group it calls CSG, or client services group. It reported $12.89 billion in sales, which was below LSEG expectations of $14.33 billion.

The overall PC market has been getting whacked of late, with some estimates calling the lull the worst ever, as memory prices have led to higher device prices and consumers are choosing to hang on to their old laptops longer.

Dell said that it had authorized $25 billion in share repurchases, and that it had spent $4.9 billion in the third quarter on share repurchases and dividends.

Dell shares are up over 135% so far in 2026.

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-24 22:04 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/24/dell-earnings-report-q3-2027.html

item.title: Colombian president blames ex-FARC rebels for car bomb blast
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Colombian president blames ex-FARC rebels for car bomb blast

Colombian President says Villavicencio bomb attack came in retaliation of government offensives.

Car bomb strikes governor’s office in Meta, Colombia

Bogota, Colombia – Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has blamed ex-FARC rebels for a car bomb attack last night targeting a state government building, which injured at least 23 people.

On a visit to Villavicencio on Tuesday, where the attack took place, the president accused Antonio Medina, a commander of the Central General Staff (EMC) rebel group, of plotting the bombing in retaliation for government offensives in the province.

“The bandit Antonio Medina from the [FARC] dissidents is to blame, and we’re going to go after him and make him pay with blood,” de la Espriella told reporters.

Last night’s attack rocked the seat of government in Meta, a province bordering the capital, Bogota, to the southeast. Videos show extensive damage to the building in Villavicencio, which houses the governor’s office, as well as surrounding businesses and vehicles.

The Head of National Police Operations, Ricardo Alarcon, told local media that initial tests indicate the car was laden with between 80 and 100kg (176-220 pounds) of pentolite, a high explosive used in military warheads, as well as civilian mining.

Meta was a historical heartland for the FARC, which officially demobilised following a historic peace deal in 2016. In the years since, dissident rebels who refused to lay down their arms or returned to war have expanded their control in the province, a key access point to the coca plantations, gold mining and drug smuggling routes of the Amazon River Basin.

The most powerful group is the EMC, headed by alias Ivan Mordisco, one of Colombia’s most wanted men. The government earlier this year announced a bounty of 5 billion pesos (roughly $1.4m) for his capture or killing.

In recent months, the government has increased pressure on the EMC, bombing its camps and targeting senior members. Just yesterday, the president confirmed the killing of alias El Churco, an EMC commander.

The campaign is part of the new far-right government’s security pivot, which aims to tackle criminal organisations through military force and has suspended the negotiations initiated under the previous government.

De la Espriella has suggested that last night’s bombing in Villavicencio was likely a retaliation against ramped-up state pressure on armed groups.

“The narco-terrorists are running wild, launching desperate attacks, because they know we are defeating them and that their end is near,” the president wrote on X this morning.

The attack, which happened on the eve of the 10-year anniversary of the 2016 peace deal, highlights the growing risks to civilians under de la Espriella’s heavy-handed security strategy, say experts.

“As the government increases pressure, armed and criminal groups are trying to raise the cost of doing that for the government by exerting pain, instilling fear and causing direct harm against communities and against the civilian population,” said Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at the International Crisis Group.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-24 21:45 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/24/colombian-president-blames-ex-farc-rebels-for-car-bomb-blast?traffic_source=rss

item.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering

Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which also included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.

Following the verdict, Huawei said the five trade secret-related charges "were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades".

"No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation," the company said.

"We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests."

Source: BBC World | Published: 2026-11-24 21:32 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy49ngydqzpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: Saudi national charged in OpenAI bugging to be released on $1 million bond
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.

Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk.

"We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse.

Tse's ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."

The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia."

Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote.

Alfozan, who was arrested Oct. 9, is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.

Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "including

dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets."

Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.

Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of that nation's ruling royal family, as a fellow partner.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Alfozan's planned release.

— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

This is developing news. Check back for updates.

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-24 22:03 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/24/openai-bugging-aflozan-release-saudi.html

item.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback sends AI videos into overdrive
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback sends AI videos into overdrive

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Issued on:

Just 11 days after resigning as Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang’s return has unleashed a fresh wave of AI-generated videos. But the internet has changed its tune: while last week’s memes mocked Huang, many now celebrate his comeback. One viral video purportedly showing him dancing is actually AI-manipulated footage of a basketball coach from 2016. From humiliation to hero worship, the technology Nvidia helped popularise is rewriting the narrative surrounding its own CEO, as Vedika Bahl explains.

Just 11 days after stepping down as Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang returned to the helm of the world's leading AI chipmaker on Monday, unleashing a fresh wave of AI-generated videos. But the internet appears to have changed its tune: while last week's memes mocked Huang following his resignation, many are now celebrating his comeback.

Nvidia's board announced on Monday that it had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as CEO, following his resignation amid a scandal involving alleged extramarital affairs and espionage allegations. The reversal came despite the board previously saying it had no plans to reinstate him, and after US President Donald Trump said he had personally intervened.

Huang received a warm welcome from employees upon his return to Nvidia's headquarters, with genuine footage showing him being greeted with applause and hugs. But within hours of the announcement, AI-generated videos purporting to show his celebrations began circulating on social media.

Viral dancing video is AI-manipulated

One video, which has racked up millions of views across TikTok, X and Instagram, appears to show Huang dancing his way into a room before being surrounded by a cheering crowd. Many users shared the footage alongside captions declaring that "the king is back".

However, the video has nothing to do with Nvidia. The original footage is a well known internet clip, and was published on YouTube in March 2016 by the University of North Carolina's basketball team, the Tar Heels. It shows players celebrating in a locker room after defeating their rivals, Duke University.

The man dancing at the centre of the celebrations is the team's then-head coach, Roy Williams. A side-by-side comparison reveals that the surroundings, people and movements are practically identical. The footage has been manipulated using artificial intelligence to replace Williams with Huang, repurposing a decade-old viral clip to capitalise on a major news event.

While many users shared the video humorously, comments on social media suggest that some believed the footage was genuine.

From humiliation to heroism, powered by AI

The dancing video is far from the only fabricated footage circulating in the wake of Huang's comeback.

Elon Musk, who was a vocal supporter of Huang's reinstatement, has inspired a series of AI-generated videos depicting the two tech billionaires celebrating together. Other viral memes show Huang returning from the dead or appearing as a character in the video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

What is particularly striking is how quickly the online narrative surrounding Nvidia's CEO has shifted.

Following his resignation, social media users flooded platforms with AI-generated videos ridiculing Huang, depicting him in embarrassing scenarios relating to his alleged affairs and departure from the company. Now, those same tools are being used to portray him as a triumphant, almost heroic figure.

While many of these videos are intended as satire rather than deliberate misinformation, there's a striking irony in the fact that one of the key architects of the AI revolution has become such a prolific subject of AI-generated content himself.

Source: France24 English | Published: 2026-11-24 21:28 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/truth-or-fake/20261124-jensen-huang-s-nvidia-comeback-sends-ai-videos-into-overdrive

item.title: How to get your paycheck up to 2 days early: 14 banks with early direct deposit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information, but not as in-depth

When it comes to getting paid, every day counts — especially when you're facing mounting bills or even potential overdrafts. According to CNBC and SurveyMonkey's Quarterly Money Survey from July 2026, 63% of Americans said they were living paycheck to paycheck.

Some banks, credit unions and online institutions offer early direct deposit, allowing your paycheck to clear a few days before your scheduled payday. Early direct deposit is also often available for pensions, military pay and government benefits, like Social Security benefits.

In addition to giving you access to your cash sooner, setting up direct deposit can help you avoid monthly service fees and unlock other account perks.

Find out what early direct deposit is, how it works and which banks offer the service.

What is early direct deposit?

Early direct deposits provide access to paychecks and other eligible eletronic deposits one to two days before they would normally clear. If you typically get paid on a Friday, for example, you could potentially see the money in your account as early as Wednesday.

Early direct deposit is usually free and automatic if you've enroll in direct deposit. It's not a loan, though, and it's not available at every bank. Features vary depending on the financial institution and your employer's payroll process.

New direct deposits often take one to two pay cycles to start arriving early, and weekends and holidays can also shift when funds post.

How does early direct deposit work?

Employers generally submit payroll information to banks through the Automated Clearing House (ACH) network a few days before the funds actually arrive. Because they know the funds are en route, some banks will credit your account once they receive that information, rather than waiting for the traditional clearing period.

While the process is typically free and automatic, early access is not guaranteed. Check with your bank about its early deposit policy.

To set up direct deposit, you'll need to provide your bank account and routing number to your employer or fill out a direct deposit form with your bank.

Banks that offer early direct deposit

While early paycheck access is increasingly commonplace — PNC Bank just began offering it in fall 2026 — it's by no means standard. Check with your bank or credit union to see if it offers early direct deposit and if you're eligible.

Alliant Credit Union

You can qualify for Alliant Credit Union's High Rate Checking's Early Payday feature just by setting up direct deposit. The account also comes with no monthly service fees, no overdraft fees and a 0.25% APY.

Alliant is a digital-only credit union, but members have access to 80,000+ ATMs and receive up to $20 per month in out-of-network ATM fee reimbursements.

- Earns 0.25% APY.

- 80,000 fee-free ATMs, plus up to $20 per month in out-of-network ATM fee reimbursements.

- No overdraft fees or minimum balance requirement.

- Membership is open to anyone and Alliant will cover $5 fee.

- You must opt into paperless statements and make at least one electronic deposit per month to earn interest.

- No physical branches.

Ally Bank

The Ally Bank Spending Account offers early direct deposit automatically and your paycheck can be available up to two days early. You're limited to eight early direct deposits per account per statement cycle and each deposit must be $10,000 or less.

- 0.10% APY on balances under $15,000 and 0.25% on balances of $15,000+

- 75,000+ free ATMs and $10 per month in out-of-network ATM fee reimbursements.

- No monthly service fee, minimum opening deposit or balance requirements.

- Can get paycheck deposited up to two days early with direct deposit.

- No physical branches.

- Low APY on checking.

- Inconvenient to make cash deposits.

Axos

Early direct deposit is a free, automatic feature with both Axos Checking and the Axos ONE checking and savings bundle. Setting up direct deposit of at least $1 with Axos Checking also unlocks a 1.00% APY.

- Competitive APY for a checking account

- No monthly maintenance or overdraft fees.

- Unlimited domestic ATM fee reimbursements.

- You can receive your paycheck up to two days early through direct deposit.

- Must enroll in direct deposit to receive APY.

- No physical branches.

- Axos does not support Zelle for peer-to-peer transfers.

Capital One

The Capital One 360 Checking® account offers direct deposits up to two days early. New account holders who set up direct deposit may also qualify for one of Capital One's frequent cash welcome bonuses.

A traditional brick-and-mortar bank, Capital One has more than 250 branches and over 60 Capital One Cafés.

- Earns 0.10% APY on all balances

- No minimum opening deposit

- No overdraft fee or foreign transaction fee

- 300+ branches and Capital One cafés

- Direct deposits available up to two days early

- Over 72,000 fee-free ATMs via Capital One, Allpoint and MoneyPass networks

- Out-of-network ATM fees aren’t reimbursed

- Physical branches limited to nine states and Washington, D.C.

Chase

You can get early direct deposit automatically with Chase Secure Banking. Setting up at least $250 in qualifying monthly deposits will also get the $4.95 service fee waived.

The consumer banking division of JPMorgan Chase, Chase is the largest bank in the U.S., with more than 5,000 locations and 14,000 ATMs.

Chase has the largest branch network in the U.S., making its Secure Banking account a good fit if you prefer an in-person experience. We like the relatively easy-to-waive service fee and that it can function as a second-chance checking account for people rebuilding their banking history. The main drawback with Secure Banking is that it doesn't earn any interest.

- New account holders may be eligible for a cash bonus.

- No minimum opening deposit or balance requirement.

- May be able to get your paycheck up to two days early.

- Free money orders and cashier's checks.

- Over 5,000 branches and 15,000 ATMs nationwide..…

item.title: A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, technical detail

A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster

Why are some groups of molecules remarkably stable while others readily break apart? Researchers at Bar-Ilan University have discovered a surprising explanation for why clusters containing exactly six molecules of glycine, the simplest amino acid, are exceptionally stable—making six a "magic number." Moreover, they have uncovered the reason for this increased stability. The secret lies in a transformation that takes place when the molecules come together: they change their structure and become zwitterions, allowing them to form stronger bonds with one another.

The discovery sheds new light on how molecules interact and organize themselves, offering a new perspective on the chemistry of amino acids and the early molecular processes associated with the origins of life.

Published in the Journal of Chemical Physics, the study combines laboratory experiments with advanced computer simulations to investigate how glycine molecules (and amino acids in general) assemble into clusters.

The study was led by Michal Roth, a Ph.D. student working with Yoni Toker from the Department of Physics at Bar-Ilan University and Dan Thomas Major from the Department of Chemistry at Bar-Ilan University. Combining laboratory mass spectrometry experiments with advanced computational modeling and molecular dynamics simulations, the team investigated how glycine molecules assemble and what makes certain clusters exceptionally stable.

"Magic numbers are a well-known phenomenon that has always fascinated me," says Toker. "I was therefore very surprised when my student discovered a new source for magic numbers that has not been reported before."

Why six? The surprising chemistry behind molecular stability

Scientists have long observed that clusters containing certain numbers of molecules are much more abundant than others. These particularly stable groupings are known as "magic number" clusters. Until now, their unusual stability has generally been explained by the way molecules arrange themselves: magic numbers occur when the number of molecules in the clusters exactly corresponds to forming especially symmetrical and stable structures.

The Bar-Ilan researchers discovered a different explanation for the six-molecule glycine cluster. Glycine, like other amino acids, can exist in different electrical forms. The form usually drawn in textbooks is known as the neutral form. However, by changing the position of one proton, one can arrive at another form, known as a zwitterion. In this form, one end of the molecule is positively charged while the other is negatively charged.

While this charged arrangement is energetically unfavorable for a single glycine molecule in the gas phase, zwitterions bind more strongly to each other, and therefore it is expected that for larger clusters the molecules will change to their zwitterionic structure. The researchers found that this transition is abrupt: in clusters with five or fewer molecules, the molecules are in their neutral form, while in the hexamer, all the molecules switch to their zwitterionic form.

Computer simulations showed just how dramatic the difference is: the six-molecule cluster had a calculated dissociation temperature of approximately 1,200 kelvin, compared with approximately 450 kelvin for a cluster of five molecules and 480 kelvin for one containing seven molecules. In other words, the six-molecule cluster can withstand far higher temperatures before breaking apart.

What does this mean for understanding the origins of life?

Glycine is of particular interest to scientists studying the origins of life. It is the simplest amino acid, one of the building blocks of proteins, and has also been detected in meteorites, asteroids and comets. Indeed, in this detection, glycine had the highest abundance of all amino acids.

Understanding how amino acid molecules interact, bond and organize themselves is an important part of investigating the chemistry that preceded life. The discovery that six glycine molecules can undergo a collective electrical transformation and form an unusually stable structure provides a new example of how interactions between molecules can produce properties that individual molecules do not possess.

While the study does not directly examine the formation of proteins or peptides, its findings could help researchers better understand the molecular interactions that may have played a role in the early stages of their formation.

The researchers now hope to investigate whether other amino acids undergo similar transformations when they form molecular clusters.

item.title: Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: multisensor data, complex topic explained

Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations

Tropical cyclones frequently undergo rapid, complex structural changes within their inner cores, such as eyewall replacement and wind-field expansion, that strongly influence typhoon intensity and coastal hazards. However, capturing these multilayered transformations continuously from the ocean surface to the upper cloud tops remains a major observational challenge.

To address this challenge, a research team from the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IOCAS) reconstructed the full inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi by integrating 17 repeated spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) overpasses with geostationary infrared imagery and synthetic microwave brightness temperature fields.

Their findings were published in the Journal of Remote Sensing on Nov. 11.

Tracking the typhoon across vertical layers

To track the typhoon across multiple vertical levels simultaneously, the researchers combined near-surface ocean wind fields derived from NOAA/STAR tropical cyclone SAR products with cloud-top center positions identified from the Japan Meteorological Agency's Himawari-9 infrared observations. In addition, they generated hourly synthetic 89-GHz microwave brightness temperature fields from multispectral infrared measurements to monitor deep convection and eyewall reorganization around the typhoon's eye.

These integrated satellite observations uncovered a clear temporal sequence in how the typhoon's inner core reorganized: A secondary eyewall formed and contracted inward first, followed by a pronounced horizontal separation between the near-surface circulation center and the upper-level cloud-top center. Finally, the typhoon's strong-wind region expanded substantially during its weakening stage.

"Coordinated multisensor observations provide a rare vertical cross section of a typhoon's life cycle," said Dr. Mu Shanshan, first author of the study. By pairing repeated high-resolution SAR wind snapshots with continuous geostationary infrared and synthetic microwave tracking, the researchers can pinpoint the exact timing of eyewall replacement, vertical vortex tilt and near-surface wind broadening.

Eyewall replacement precedes growing vortex tilt

Between 00:00 UTC on July 5 and July 6, the synthetic 89-GHz imagery captured the formation, intensification and inward contraction of the outer eyewall, showing that the eyewall replacement cycle concluded around 23:00 UTC on July 6.

During the initial formation of the secondary eyewall, the horizontal offset between the near-surface circulation center and the infrared cloud-top center (defined as the SAR–IR tilt) was relatively small at roughly 5 to 10 km (3 to 6 miles). As the replacement process neared completion, this offset widened to 17.8 km (11.1 miles) and further increased to 20.8 km (12.9 miles) in observations on July 7.

Weaker winds spread over a wider area

High-resolution SAR wind retrievals further revealed that as Typhoon Bavi weakened in its later stages, its maximum near-surface wind speed declined overall while its radius of maximum wind (RMW) expanded dramatically. During the typhoon's peak intensity phase, the RMW was tightly concentrated between 15 and 26 km (9 and 16 miles). In subsequent multiscene observations, however, the RMW stretched beyond 100 km (62 miles) and exceeded 200 km (124 miles) in individual overpasses, demonstrating a marked outward broadening of the gale-force wind swath.

"Understanding when and how a typhoon's wind field expands is just as critical for disaster preparedness as forecasting peak wind speed," said Dr. Wang Chong, corresponding author of the study.

This observational case provides a valuable benchmark for studying the physical coupling between eyewall replacement cycles, cross-layer center displacement and outer wind-field growth.

More information

Shanshan Mu et al., Repeated Spaceborne SAR and Multisensor Observations of Tropical-Cyclone Inner-Core Structural Evolution, Journal of Remote Sensing (2026). DOI: 10.34133/remotesensing.1095

item.title: Earth’s Water May Have Formed in This Fiery Furnace
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original hypothesis, technical detail

It’s one of the most fundamental questions about life on Earth: How did water get here?

One possibility is that it was delivered as frozen ice by a bombardment of meteorites smashing into our planet’s surface. Another is that the chemistry of the early Earth somehow produced water from molten rock—a theory that’s the focus of a new study published in Nature Geoscience.

The researchers behind the hypothesis are calling it “pebble rain” (or “pebble accretion”). What happens is silicate rocks with iron inside, drawn toward Earth by its increasing mass and gravitational pull, react with hydrogen in the atmosphere. Given the high speeds, high pressure, and high volume of incoming rocks involved, the subsequent chemical reactions could have stripped away the oxygen from the iron in the pebble showers, releasing water vapor as a by-product.

The researchers estimate that around 200 oceans’ worth of H2O may have been released in this way, supplying the planet with the magic ingredient for life. These pebbles would have been external visitors, like meteorites, but the water would’ve been formed on Earth rather than in space.

What’s more, the same process could plausibly happen on other planets as they form too—opening up new possibilities in our search for extraterrestrial life. “Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites,” study author Zachary Sharp explained in a statement. “Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism.”

The researchers simulated the conditions of the early Earth in their lab with temperatures of up to 2,552°F, and heating silicate rocks in streams of hydrogen. Almost 80 percent of the iron oxide in the samples turned into metallic iron, producing water vapor along the way.

“Looking out over a large body of water, it’s hard to imagine that that water may have been produced four-and-a-half billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere,” Sharp said, “but it very well may have.”

Lead Image: University of New Mexico

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: historical significance, technical detail

On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Why it mattered

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds."

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

item.title: Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation

Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees

Contrary to popular belief, mindfulness training in the workplace can make some employees angrier and more likely to treat coworkers with disrespect.

According to the Harvard Business Review, more than half of large companies offer some form of mindfulness training, often promoted as a way to make employees calmer, kinder and more considerate of others.

But a new study from the University of South Florida, published in the Journal of Business Ethics, reveals a surprising catch: mindfulness training can backfire, depending on the personalities of employees who undergo it.

"Mindfulness training makes us more aware of our thoughts and feelings, but that doesn't necessarily make us better people," said Adam Kay, the study's author and assistant professor in the School of Management at USF's Muma College of Business.

What comes into focus may differ from person to person. For Machiavellian employees, who tend to be manipulative and contemptuous of others, Kay suggests that mindfulness training can heighten their awareness of negative feelings they already harbor, with troubling implications for how they treat coworkers.

To investigate, Kay recruited 600 health care workers for a monthlong field experiment, randomly assigning them to mindfulness training, breathwork or a waitlist control. Results showed that Machiavellian employees who underwent mindfulness training experienced heightened feelings of contempt, anger and disgust toward their coworkers, which they then channeled into workplace incivility.

"Workplace incivility isn't always obvious," Kay said. "It usually involves subtle acts of disrespect that are easy to dismiss or deny—but that doesn't make it harmless." Indeed, the Society for Human Resource Management estimates that workplace incivility costs U.S. employers more than $2 billion each day in lost productivity and absenteeism.

"That workplace incivility can be so damaging yet so difficult to pin on perpetrators may be precisely why it appeals to Machiavellians, who tend to be calculating and reputation-conscious," Kay said.

In line with this reasoning, the study found that Machiavellians who underwent mindfulness training engaged in more subtle forms of mistreatment—such as being rude or dismissive—but not in more blatant forms of misconduct, such as publicly embarrassing coworkers.

Kay cautioned that these findings are not a reason for organizations to abandon mindfulness training. Instead, they underscore the importance of considering how different employees respond to mindfulness programs and evaluating not only their intended benefits but also their potential costs.

"Mindfulness training can bring our darker feelings into sharper focus," Kay said. "And sometimes, it's our coworkers who pay the price."

Publication details

Adam A. Kay, The Dark Side of Mindfulness at Work: How Mindfulness Training Enlivens Machiavellian Incivility, Journal of Business Ethics (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s10551-026-06513-3

Journal information: Journal of Business Ethics

item.title: 'Blade Runner 2099' executive producers talk architectural easter eggs and franchise continuity for Prime Video's new sci-fi series (interview)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original content, clear explanation

Prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

item.title: Medieval chain mail discovered during underwater excavation of 15th-century 'floating castle' that sank off Sweden
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: historical significance, technical detail

Medieval chain mail discovered during underwater excavation of 15th-century 'floating castle' that sank off Sweden

A 15th-century shipwreck is yielding clues to the medieval tragedy that destroyed Griffin, King Hans's "floating castle."

Archaeologists have recovered high-quality chain mail armor from the 15th-century wreck of Gribshunden or Griffin, a royal warship that doubled as a "floating castle" for King Hans of Denmark. The ship exploded and sank in 1495, but maritime archaeologists have just begun exploring the area beneath the forecastle, an elevated combat platform at the front of the ship, where they discovered the armor and a unique munitions chest.

The chain mail was, "rather surprisingly, completely exposed," Rolf Warming, an archaeologist at Stockholm University and lead investigator of the Griffin project in collaboration with Södertörn University, told Live Science in an email. "It was only by chance that we came across it, and it shows just how much is still on the wreck site."

The mail armor was made of copper alloy and was found in a part of the ship that may have been used as a storage area for military gear, according to a Nov. 24 statement. "Historical sources indicate that German mercenaries, or Landsknechts, were aboard Griffin when it sank in 1495," Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, an archaeologist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who is the co-investigator on the project, said in the statement. The mercenaries may have stored their armor in the area, "although we've yet to establish a precise function for the space," Pacheco-Ruiz said.

The 15th-century warship was rediscovered in the Baltic Sea off the south coast of Sweden in the 1970s but formally identified by archaeologists as Griffin in 2013.

Griffin was the flagship of the naval fleet of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. In 1495, Hans was sailing to Kalmar in Sweden to negotiate a political alliance and force Sweden back into a union with Denmark and Norway. He had brought with him around 150 German mercenary soldiers. "It was important to demonstrate military prowess, and the German and Swiss mercenaries were the finest you could get at that time," Warming told Live Science.

During a stop at the port of Ronneby in what is now Sweden, Griffin caught fire, perhaps after being struck by lightning, and sank. Eyewitnesses who escaped reported that many men died in the tragic event. King Hans, however, was onshore when the warship sank.

The warship has been well-preserved over the centuries thanks to the low salinity of the Baltic waters and the lack of shipworms, marine mollusks also known as the "termites of the sea" because of the damage they do to wood.

The chain mail recovered in October is of exceptionally high quality, Warming said in the statement, but it was not necessarily the armor of an elite knight. "This kind of armour could remain in use for extended periods, often undergoing repairs or being reused, so these fragments may represent older military equipment that was still active," he said.

But the researchers discovered more than just the chain mail.

"This year's campaign was an unusually exciting investigation!" The team found a unique munitions chest called a "zeuglade" in German. "We have taken different samples to try to determine the contents of the chest and perhaps find traces of gunpowder," Warming said. The chest may have belonged to the German mercenaries who were aboard.

"It was in the process of documenting the chest that I unexpectedly discovered exposed mail-armour fragments in the vicinity of the chest, along other items that could indicate more chests," Warming added. "This leads us to believe this may have been a stowage area, located just beneath the forecastle."

Warming said that the research team is currently using chemical analysis to investigate the origins of the armor and the chest to learn more about medieval military matters.

"It is probable that the mail armour belongs to the mercenaries, but it could also belong to someone else," Warming said. "The chest might also belong to them, but we don't know yet.

item.title: Doctors report less burnout in practices they rate as efficient, even during long workweeks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear reporting on physician burnout and efficiency

Doctors report less burnout in practices they rate as efficient, even during long workweeks

When it comes to physician burnout, how you spend your working hours may matter more than how many hours you work.

A new study led by Stanford Medicine researchers, published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, found that physicians who perceived their clinical practices as more efficient reported less burnout, greater professional fulfillment and less intention to leave their jobs, regardless of how many hours they worked each week.

The findings suggest that improving clinical workflows, reducing administrative burdens and making better use of care teams could be important strategies for addressing physician burnout.

"This is good news if you're a clinician or a health system administrator and you're worried about productivity, but you're also worried about physician well-being," said Bryan Bohman, M.D., associate chief medical officer for Stanford Medicine's Workforce Health and Wellness and the lead author of the study.

"You may not need to 'balance' those two goals, one against the other; in fact, our data suggest that you may be able to improve both well-being and productivity by focusing on improving practice efficiency."

Not just about hours worked

The researchers analyzed survey responses from 16,649 physicians at 14 academic health systems across the United States. The survey asked them about their experiences with clinical workflows, scheduling, administrative responsibilities and other factors that could affect their ability to provide care efficiently.

Physicians who rated their practices as more efficient reported significantly less burnout and greater professional fulfillment. Physicians who perceived their practices as more efficient were also substantially less likely to report an intent to leave their employer within two years.

The relationship between efficiency and burnout remained strong even after researchers accounted for hours worked. In fact, physicians who reported low practice efficiency and worked 40 hours or fewer per week experienced more burnout than those who reported high efficiency and worked 66 hours or more.

"What we doctors want is to give high-quality care to our patients in an efficient way," said Bohman, a clinical professor of primary care and population health. "That makes us feel fulfilled, and it reduces burnout—even when we work long hours."

That doesn't mean long work hours are harmless. Previous research has consistently linked excessive work hours with physician burnout, and this study didn't establish that inefficiency causes burnout. But the findings suggest that reducing work hours isn't the only way—and alone may not be enough—to improve physicians' experience.

Inefficiency impedes good patient care

Efficiency isn't simply about how many patients a physician sees or how quickly they complete their work. It's also about whether the systems around them make it easier or harder to provide high-quality care.

Consider a surgeon whose first surgery starts late because the operating room isn't ready. Or a doctor who must track down missing imaging results, take on tasks that could be handled by other care team members or finish documentation after an already full day of appointments.

Together these problems can make the workday frustrating, unpredictable and unnecessarily demanding. They can also have an impact on personal life, further exacerbating burnout and reducing the quality of care.

"In other research, we've shown that the impact of work on personal relationships has a very high correlation with burnout—they didn't make it to the wedding, the violin recital, the soccer game because it took an hour and a half to prepare the operating room for the final surgery of the day," Bohman said.

To capture physicians' workplace experiences, the researchers asked physicians whether operational problems interfere with patient care, make it difficult to stay on schedule or prevent them from completing their work during the day. Other questions addressed the availability of patient information, appropriate delegation of tasks and whether the clinical environment feels chaotic or unpredictable.

Finding the friction points

The researchers say the questions on their survey could help health system leaders identify where operational problems may be contributing to burnout.

If physicians at one outpatient clinic, for example, report substantially lower efficiency than those at another location, administrators may be able to pinpoint the problem, with the understanding that it could be contributing to burnout and professional dissatisfaction. Bohman recommends bringing physicians together with operational and quality improvement leaders to develop solutions.

There are still unanswered questions. The study relied on physicians' perceptions rather than objective measures of efficiency or productivity. Because it captured responses at a single point in time, it also cannot determine whether improving efficiency would directly reduce burnout. Future research could examine how perceived efficiency relates to quantifiable productivity and whether changes in efficiency lead to improvements in physician well-being.

"A productive clinical day where we provide good-quality care to more patients is an important element of our professional fulfillment and helps protect us against burnout," Bohman said.

Researchers from Texas A&M University, College of Medicine; the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health; The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center; and Yale University School of Medicine contributed to the study.

Publication details

Bryan Bohman et al., Associations of Perceived Efficiency of Clinical Practice With Physician Well-Being, Mayo Clinic Proceedings (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.mayocp.2026.08.018

item.title: Novel metric accurately distinguishes metastasis from an independent primary tumor
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research on tumor differentiation

Novel metric accurately distinguishes metastasis from an independent primary tumor

Research has found that the newly developed Clonal Relatedness Index (CRI) can accurately determine whether tumors in the same patient share a common clonal origin. The findings, detailed in an article appearing in The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics, have important implications for the clinical management of complex cases of cancers of the digestive system and abdominal lining, specifically gastrointestinal, hepatopancreatobiliary and peritoneal carcinomas.

"When two tumors arise in the same patient, one of the most crucial questions is whether they are related or represent independent primaries," explains lead author Namrata Setia, M.D., Department of Anatomic Pathology, University of Chicago. "This is particularly challenging when tumors in different organs share overlapping cellular features, or when genomic complexity limits the diagnostic clarity of conventional markers. Even experienced pathologists can reach the limits of microscopic and marker-based evaluation."

The researchers of this study analyzed 60 pairs of gastrointestinal, hepatopancreatobiliary and peritoneal tumors using targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) data and developed the CRI, which is calculated as the number of shared genomic alterations divided by the average number of alterations in the two tumors. CRI outperformed conventional phenotype-based assessment in distinguishing whether a tumor has metastasized or whether it represents a new independent lesion.

First author Gertruda Evaristo, M.D., Department of Anatomic Pathology, University of Chicago, and Department of Pathology, McGill University, adds, "Unlike more complex statistical approaches that require specialized software or biostatistical expertise, we aimed to turn genomic data that laboratories already generate into a simple, quantitative measure of tumor relatedness. The CRI does exactly that: it takes a complex diagnostic question and makes it more measurable, interpretable and potentially accessible to routine molecular pathology practice."

The CRI showed particular value in diagnostically challenging cases involving hypermutability, where morphologic and immunophenotypic overlap or divergence can complicate assessments of tumor relatedness. The method held up in a validation cohort, although it failed for one ultramutated POLE-mutated pair. The researchers urge particular caution in cases with extremely high mutational burden.

Potential clinical implications of using CRI are as follows:

- Diagnosis: The CRI may be particularly useful in cases with overlapping histologic features, limited tissue or unusual growth patterns that obscure tumor origin. It may also be valuable in patients with hereditary cancer syndromes or mismatch repair deficiency, in whom phenotype-based assessment can be unreliable.

- Prognosis: Misclassification can substantially alter the perceived extent of disease and expectations regarding clinical course. Although the investigators did not directly evaluate clinical outcomes, more accurate classification of metastatic disease versus independent primary tumors could improve staging and prognostic assessment.

- Treatment: More accurate classification could help avoid inappropriate systemic treatment for an independent primary or inadequate local treatment for metastatic disease. The extent to which CRI-guided classification changes clinical management or improves patient outcomes remains to be established.

"Although further validation is needed, especially across tumor types and sequencing platforms, our approach provides an accessible quantitative adjunct when conventional pathology reaches its limits," concludes Setia. "Sequencing is often used to identify actionable alterations, but the same data can tell us something fundamental about the relationship between tumors. We see an opportunity to extract more diagnostic value from genomic information that is already available."

Publication details

Gertruda Evaristo et al., Clonal Relatedness Index, The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jmoldx.2026.09.001

Journal information: Journal of Molecular Diagnostics

item.title: Low vitamin D could be keeping you up at night
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information on vitamin D and sleep

Low vitamin D could be keeping you up at night

Tossing and turning at night? The problem might not be your mattress—it could be your vitamin D levels.

A new study suggests people with higher vitamin D levels may get more sleep and stay awake for shorter stretches during the night.

Researchers analyzed blood tests and sleep data from 460 middle-aged and older adults.

Those with the highest vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night than those with the lowest levels, they found. And participants classified as vitamin D deficient averaged about 23 minutes less sleep than those with normal levels.

"These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health," said senior author Adam Spira, a sleep researcher at Johns Hopkins University.

The connection between vitamin D and sleep appeared stronger among Black participants.

But researchers noted that the study can't prove that low vitamin D causes poor sleep—or that taking supplements will improve it.

They also couldn't tell whether participants got their vitamin D from food, sunlight or supplements.

Future studies may examine whether the connection to better sleep differs depending on the vitamin's source.

The paper is published in The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences.

More information

item.title: Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: report on mpox cases and antiviral drug trials

The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox, an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026.

Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness.

The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17, which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year.

The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23, compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022.

The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak.

In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.

In response, the Ministry of Health purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease and instructed states and municipalities to administer it intradermally – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold.

The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just failed two clinical trials.

What has changed about the virus?

Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024.

Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs.

At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, 43 of the 62 samples identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.

Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases.

Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first cases with evidence of community transmission – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026.

The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care.

In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV.

Antiviral drug failed the test

During the 2022 outbreak, the antiviral drug tecovirimat was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U.S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been eradicated from the planet since 1980. But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people.

An April 2025 trial compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant.

In February 2026, a second trial settled the question regarding clade II. The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox.

Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients.

What the vaccine does

The only vaccine for mpox is MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos, a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, observational studies conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes.

Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two, compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses.…

Source: The Conversation Health | Published: 2026-11-24 21:09 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100
