item.title: Weak and immature management putting patients at risk at failing health board, review finds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: report on health board management issues

Weak and immature management putting patients at risk at failing health board, review finds

Wales' largest health board is still failing, with "fundamental weaknesses" in governance and management, a new report says.

Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has been in special measures for nine years in total, with the latest period starting in 2023.

A review of its leadership published on Tuesday found, in some parts, targets and money "have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".

Committed staff and ability to deliver some strong local services were highlighted.

The health board apologised and said it now needed to concentrate on improving its leadership and allowing its staff to "flourish".

The review was commissioned by the Welsh government in the summer, after it gave Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board (BCUHB) a "final chance" to improve.

It concluded that senior leadership was "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.

The review did not suggest splitting up the health board, but Wales' health minister said the findings were "unacceptable" and BCUHB "does not function as a single coherent organisation".

The report said: "Many areas reported a culture where targets and financial matters have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care.

"Fear of speaking up was described often... staff did not believe that raising a concern would result in corrective action.

"Despite this, the panel witnessed many teams striving to deliver the very best care they could for patients."

The reviewers also found a "toxic" culture at the health board where staff were afraid to speak out, and worried that no-one would listen if they did.

The chair of BCUHB, Dyfed Edwards apologised for the health board's failings.

"We haven't done things as we should," he said. "We have got things wrong.

"We need to take a step back from all the firefighting that has been going on, and address key things.

"We need to allow staff to show leadership and to flourish, and for us all to get systems in place which will allow us to address key performance issues like waiting times."

The health board's chief executive, Carol Shillabeer, previously announced she would be leaving in the new year to take up an NHS role in England.

Her departure follows a string of other senior leaders who have left the organisation in recent months, including the chief operating officer and executive director of finance.

The report also said that bureaucracy and slow decision-making led to a "loss of local ownership" and staff feeling frustrated.

'Betsi spaghetti'

The reviewers wrote: "Staff and leaders described decisions moving through multiple layers of approval, authority becoming concentrated at senior levels and operational leaders lacking sufficient autonomy to act.

"A phrase used in a focus group characterised the resulting complexity as 'Betsi spaghetti'."

However, the review concluded the health board could still be improved without being broken up into smaller organisations - an option previously discussed by ministers.

It said staff were "loyal and committed", and there were "strong local services" and "significant clinical expertise across north Wales".

Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said: "these failings are utterly unacceptable".

"I also share the understandable frustrations of staff and patients alike in north Wales at the lack of progress in delivering and embedding improvements to services and standards of care," he said.

"The report identifies that the health board does not currently demonstrate the organisational conditions required to deliver and sustain reliable improvement."

But the health minister rejected calls for radical action or structural change to the NHS in north Wales.

He said he would be making an order to appoint a new deputy chief executive and an independent board governance advisor. The post of vice chair - currently vacant - would also be filled.

Professor Medwin Hughes, chair of the patients' watchdog Llais said: "There should be no more final chances â significant concerns have been expressed over many years by patients, and now is the time to really address these.

"It's not good enough just to identify the issues. We now need there to be realistic targets and outcomes that deliver for patients and that deliver for citizens."

'People are dying'

Benjamin Hodge Mckenna MS, Reform UK Wales's health spokesperson, said BCUHB had been "plagued by mismanagement, poor performance and repeated failures".

"Senior leaders and government ministers cannot continue to preside over failure without facing consequences," he said.

Darren Millar MS, leader of the Welsh Conservatives, said: "These damning findings are sadly nothing new.

"Putting the health board in special measures was supposed to improve performance, yet things have got worse and people are dying as a result."

Ken Skates, Welsh Labour spokesperson for health, said the people of north Wales "deserve clear evidence that sustained improvement will be delivered".

"Progress and accountability were disappointingly absent from today's announcement," he said.

item.description:

Why it is here: report on GP surgery appointment suspension

GP surgery suspends routine appointments due to 'tsunami' of demand

A GP surgery has suspended all routine appointments due to what it calls a "tsunami" of demand.

It is the second time in a week that Aberfoyle Medical Practice in Londonderry has told patients that it is not offering routine appointments - either in person or online.

Dr Donna Mace, who is a partner at the practice and also a member of the Northern Ireland General Practitioners' Committee, said the practice was currently dealing with unprecedented demand.

In real terms, that means their doctors are seeing around 60 patients a day, which she said was not safe.

The Department of Health (DoH) said general practices across Northern Ireland "continue to experience significant demand for services".

At times, the department said, practices may need to "to implement temporary measures to manage patient care safely and effectively".

As independent contractors GP surgeries are responsible for managing their own appointment systems, DoH said.

Prioritising of urgent appointments according to clinical need, the department added, is an "established approach within health care."

"Aberfoyle is one of the biggest practices in Derry and we are really fortunate in that we have 11 doctors, social workers, physios, mental health practitioners and counsellors but unfortunately the last few weeks have just not been manageable at all," Dr Mace told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"Every single day the appointments have been filled up, so much so, that every on-call doctor is dealing with 60 patients per day.

"In my on-call, that is dealing with emergency mental health patients, patients in palliative care and very ill children and it was just not manageable," she said.

"I am a partner at the practice and we employ four salaried doctors and there was a risk of losing those doctors If we lost them due to stress or resignation because they couldn't cope, that would mean we would lose 100 appointments so we had to manage the risk.

"They couldn't go on and there was a total crisis."

The doctor said the decision was taken due to concerns about patient safety.

"It was not manageable and it was not safe, no patient is going to appreciate if we miss something because we have less than the usual 10 minutes with them," she said.

The doctor said they could only deal with urgent appointments and apologised to all those affected.

In October, the practice saw more then 4,000 patients face-to-face, handled 1,500 telephone consultations and dealt with nearly 9,000 prescription issues.

The practice would review the situation on a "day-to-day basis" to determine when it could reopen routine appointments.

item.title: How antibody therapy reverses type 1 diabetes in mice
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explanation of antibody therapy for type 1 diabetes

How antibody therapy reverses type 1 diabetes in mice

Researchers at UC Davis Health have uncovered key mechanisms behind an experimental antibody that reverses type 1 diabetes (T1D) in mice. Findings from their study, published in the journal Diabetes, could advance efforts to develop treatments for patients with acute T1D.

Previous studies have shown that T1D can be prevented in mice. However, preventing the condition has limited clinical relevance because most patients are diagnosed only after they have developed the disease and require treatment.

T1D occurs when the body's immune system mistakenly attacks insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. As these cells are destroyed, the body loses its ability to regulate blood sugar levels, requiring lifelong insulin therapy.

Current treatments manage the disease but do not reverse the underlying autoimmune process.

"Most people are diagnosed with T1D after the disease has already developed and significant damage has occurred to the insulin-producing cells," said William Ridgway, chief of rheumatology, allergy & clinical immunology at UC Davis Health. "To help patients, we need therapies that can reverse the disease process. Our study helps explain how this experimental treatment works and identifies biological pathways that could one day be targeted in people with T1D."

A new approach to type 1 diabetes

Most experimental treatments for T1D focus on T cells, components of the adaptive immune system that attack insulin-producing beta cells. Ridgway and his colleagues instead investigated the role of the innate immune system, a less-studied branch of immune biology in type 1 diabetes.

The team utilized a mouse model of T1D and advanced single-cell sequencing to show that antibody treatment produced myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). MDSCs are specialized immune cells that help control inflammation. The antibody treatment induced the MDSCs to travel to the pancreatic islet and reduced the immune activity responsible for damaging beta cells.

The team also found that the treatment depended on the anti-inflammatory signaling molecule interleukin-10 (IL-10). Without IL-10, MDSCs failed to develop, and the therapy lost its ability to reverse diabetes.

"These findings show that innate immune cells may play a much larger role in controlling autoimmune diabetes than previously appreciated," Ridgway said.

Reduction in beta-cell stress

One of the study's most significant discoveries involved beta cells.

As T1D progresses, surviving beta cells experience increasing stress. Not only are they under attack from the immune system, but they must also work harder to produce enough insulin to meet the body's needs. Over time, this stress can contribute to beta-cell dysfunction and death.

The researchers found that shortly after treatment, biological markers of cellular stress within beta cells dropped dramatically. Specifically, the therapy reduced pathways associated with endoplasmic reticulum stress and the unfolded protein response—both of which are linked to beta-cell damage.

"One of the findings we were most excited about was the profound reduction in beta-cell stress," Ridgway said. "As far as we know, this is the first study to closely examine what happens inside the pancreas after T1D has been reversed."

Ridgway and his fellow researchers believe lowering stress on the remaining insulin-producing cells may be an important factor in restoring normal blood sugar levels and preserving beta-cell function.

Potential impact beyond type 1 diabetes

While the findings are limited to mouse models and additional research is needed before human studies can begin, the investigators believe the work could have implications beyond T1D.

"Understanding how these specialized immune cells develop and function may help us identify new treatment strategies not only for T1D, but potentially for other autoimmune diseases as well," Ridgway said.

Future studies will focus on adapting the approach for human therapeutics and determining whether similar mechanisms can be safely activated in patients.

Publication details

Nicolle K. Martin et al., Reversal of T1D and Rapid Reduction of β-Cell Stress by IL-10–Dependent MDSCs Induced by TLR4-Ab, Diabetes (2026). DOI: 10.2337/db26-0636

Journal information: Diabetes

item.title: What I learned building a real-time AI interview assistant in the browser
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear explanation

For the last few months I've been building Intervix, a browser-based assistant that listens to interview questions and suggests a short answer based on your CV and the job description.

When I started, I assumed the hard part would be the AI. It wasn't. Any decent model can answer "Tell me about a production incident you handled." The hard part is everything around the model: getting the question in time, deciding when the question is finished, and producing something a person can actually use while another person is waiting for them to talk.

Here are the lessons that changed how the product works. Most of them apply to any real-time AI assistant, not just interviews.

1. Your latency budget is a conversation, not a benchmark

In a chat UI, a 6-second answer is fine. In a live conversation, it's an awkward silence.

The natural gap after a question in a video call is roughly a couple of seconds before it starts to feel strange. You can stretch it with "That's a good question, let me think…", but not by much. So the useful budget for the first useful words on screen is small, and it is shared by several steps:

- capturing the audio of the question,

- turning speech into text,

- noticing that the question is over,

- sending text + context to the model,

- getting the first tokens back,

- the human reading them.

Two things helped more than any model tweak:

- Streaming everything. The answer starts rendering as soon as the first tokens arrive. Nobody needs the last sentence to start talking.

- Not waiting for "perfect" transcription. A question transcribed with a typo is still answerable. A perfectly transcribed question that arrives three seconds late is not.

2. "When is the question finished?" is the hardest UX decision

Interviewers don't ask clean, single-sentence questions. They say things like:

"So, tell me about… actually, let's start with your current project. What's the architecture, and — maybe also — how do you deploy it?"

If the assistant fires the moment there's a pause, it answers half a question. If it waits for a long silence, it's late. Any automatic rule (silence length, question-like endings, punctuation in the transcript) will be wrong in somebody's interview.

So the default is boring:

- Manual trigger by default. The candidate presses an Ask button or a hotkey when they want help. They know when the question is finished better than any heuristic.

- Automatic mode as an option, for people who want hands-off help and accept that it will sometimes fire early.

A side effect I like: the manual trigger also stops the assistant from answering small talk.

3. The best answer is short — and that has to be designed

Ask a model an interview question and you'll get a beautiful 400-word essay with headings. It's useless in a live call: by the time you've read paragraph two, the interviewer is wondering whether your connection dropped.

What I ended up optimizing for:

- Lead with the answer, then one supporting detail.

- Scannable: you should be able to glance at it, not read it.

- Spoken language, not documentation language. "I'd start by checking the slow query log" beats "The first step in diagnosing latency is to analyze query performance metrics."

Just asking the model to "be concise" doesn't work — models politely ignore it. What works better is a concrete budget expressed in speaking time:

- About 50–90 words by default — roughly 20–35 seconds when spoken.

- Up to about 150–200 words only when the question clearly needs it (a system design walkthrough, a multi-part question), and then as a short list you can talk through.

- Paragraphs of 1–3 sentences, so you can glance at the next line without losing your place.

The rest lives in the per-interview-type instructions and in the UI: readable text, no walls of markdown, and code blocks only when the question is actually about code.

4. Personalization is about picking one relevant example

The difference between a generic answer and a useful one is almost always a concrete example from the candidate's own experience. Compare:

Generic:

One difficult technical decision I faced involved balancing technical debt with business priorities. I evaluated the options and chose the best balance between maintainability and delivery speed.

Using the candidate's CV and the job description:

Our checkout API was built on Django and struggling under load. I chose to rewrite just the checkout endpoints in FastAPI behind a feature flag, so we could roll back instantly if anything broke in production.

The second one sounds like a person. But to get there, the assistant has to pick the right piece of the CV for this question, and stay consistent with the job you're applying for. A few things that mattered:

- The job description is as important as the CV. It tells the model which parts of your experience to emphasize (for a backend role, the API migration; for a team lead role, how you got the team to agree on it).

- Extra documents help a lot. A CV is a list of bullet points. A short "experience notes" document — a few real stories about incidents, migrations, conflicts — gives the model material to work with.

- Don't invent experience. If the CV doesn't contain anything relevant, the answer should be a solid general answer, not a fabricated project. This is a prompt-level rule and it matters for the candidate: you'll have to defend whatever you say in a follow-up question.

5. Privacy: keep the audio in the browser

People are (rightly) nervous about a tool that listens to their calls. The design choice I made early: speech recognition runs in the browser. The interview audio is never uploaded. Only the transcribed text of the question goes to the server and the model, together with the prompt and the CV/JD context.

It makes the first start slower — the browser has to prepare speech recognition — but it's a much easier conversation with users, and it removes a whole class of "where is my audio stored?" questions.…

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-24 22:01 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

- Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

- An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

- In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

- The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

With our research partner, Onava(opens in a new window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.…

item.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

Tackling Riemann

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”

The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.

item.title: Fun-VACE redraw: the control video decides what transfers, and an 8-frame loop makes it long
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Wan 2.2 Fun-VACE with an 8-frame overlap loop gives unbounded video redraw, and the controlling insight is that the control video you feed decides what transfers: pose video transfers pose, depth video transfers dynamics.

The core mechanism

Fun-VACE's redraw behaviour is determined by the control signal, not by the prompt. That is a cleaner mental model than prompt-based control:

- Feed an extracted pose video: the output follows the pose.

- Feed a depth video: the output follows the dynamics and volume.

- The reference is optional - it supplies style or identity, not motion.

Why the 8-frame overlap

Long redraw is done in windows. Overlapping eight frames between windows keeps the seam continuous, which is what makes a minute-long redraw look like one shot instead of a series of clips.

Dual control

The episode covers pose and depth control together - two control streams constraining the same generation. In practice that means a shot can hold a specific body configuration and a specific spatial structure at once.

What to check

- Pose transfer versus depth transfer on the same source - do they really produce different results, as claimed?

- The window seam at frame 8 boundaries, watched closely.

- Long runs: does the style drift, even if the pose holds?

Where this sits among the VACE episodes

Other episodes cover VACE with Lynx identity, VACE with audio, and VACE inside merges. This one is the plainest and most useful: control video in, redraw out, looped.

Honest limits

- Control quality dominates: a bad pose or depth extraction becomes a bad redraw, unfixably.

- Unbounded loops still accumulate drift.

- No workflow or weights are bundled with this article.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-24 22:02 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, clear explanation

After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.

Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”

The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff.

“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.

The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”

Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.

The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The President reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role

Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” the Wall Street Journal writes.

Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of Congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.

item.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants. But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives.

According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time. Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences.

ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them.

The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots, and Claude Duet, respectively.

In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily. That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs. Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are.

ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems. A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems.

It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task. Not only did even the highest performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency. When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time.

For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust.

Additionally, about 10% of otherwise correct attempts failed at least one safety criterion. Across the models and harnesses tested, agents failed to, for example, adequately account for a child’s school pickup 79.5% of the time. When handling laptop custody records, agents failed a requirement to identify and withhold a sensitive bank upload token in 18.6% of attempts. In another tasks, agents recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3% of the time.

The findings highlight a major issue for users adopting consumer personal AI assistants, namely that there’s always a risk that an agent can create more headaches in the course of trying to fulfill an otherwise ordinary request.

While AI benchmarks have largely focused on coding, professional work, or testing on specific tasks, ShellBench is attempting to evaluate how models perform on multi-step personal tasks within different agent harnesses — the software that controls how a model accesses information, uses tools, and takes actions.

While the researchers found model choice had a greater overall impact on performance than harness choice, among the more capable models, AI agent performance became more dependent on the harness.

For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 when operating within the Pi harness, but it performed worse when both models were tested within Claude Code.

Meta’s Muse Wonder Full scored 56% in Pi, but only 38.1% in Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder 1.0, meanwhile, averaged a success rate of 39.7% across the five harnesses tested.

Notably, while the researchers tested models from Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, they didn’t evaluate them within the native harnesses of Muse, Dots, or Claude Duet, so the results may not be representative of the experience millions of consumers are having with the product today.

TechCrunch has reached out to Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and the researchers in the study.

Source: TechCrunch | Published: 2026-11-24 21:33 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/24/even-the-best-ai-agents-struggle-with-everyday-life/

item.title: Walmart teams up with Meta to bring Black Friday deals to AI agent Muse
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear explanation

Shopping with AI is becoming less of a futuristic idea and more of something companies expect us to do. Walmart is the latest retailer making that shift, teaming up with Meta to let customers shop its Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.

The partnership, announced Tuesday, gives shoppers another way to find products, compare prices, and make purchases without browsing Walmart’s website themselves. Instead, customers can simply tell Muse what they are looking for and let the AI do the work.

The announcement highlights how differently Walmart and Amazon are approaching AI shopping. While Amazon has taken steps to stop third-party AI agents from making purchases for customers, Walmart is leaning into the idea.

To get started, users open the Muse app, sign in to their Walmart account, and return to the assistant to begin shopping. They can ask it to find specific products, compare options, or track down deals. Once a customer makes a request in Muse, the assistant sends it to Walmart, which returns relevant products and helps build a shopping cart.

Walmart says it has built privacy protections into the experience. For instance, Muse doesn’t get access to a customer’s Walmart shopping history or other personal information. Shoppers can also set spending limits, require approval before purchases, and review orders placed by the agent.

Plus, the company notes users can always delete their agent’s profile if they want to.

The experience is powered by Walmart’s Agent Gateway, a new system that allows outside AI assistants to connect directly with the retailer’s online store. This launched in October, and the company is planning to open it up to more developers and AI platforms, meaning Muse could eventually be just one of several assistants capable of shopping Walmart’s online store.

Walmart is not the only company teaming up with Meta’s Muse. Instacart also recently joined forces with the AI assistant.

Beyond Muse, Walmart has recently rolled out more AI-powered features to its own shopping assistant, Sparky.

Some of the newer additions include turning handwritten shopping lists into shopping carts, using photos and voice commands to find products, and helping customers get around their local store. Shoppers can search for an item and use a pin on the store map to see exactly which aisle it’s in. There’s also a “Flash Price Tag” button that makes the item’s shelf label light up.

item.title: Working with AI
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear explanation

Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory

How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:

- Sources of AI value. Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating existing work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.

- Impact on employment. Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.

- Bottlenecks. Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.

- Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches. Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.

- Reorganizing for AI. Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.

Introduction

The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”

An employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”

A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a new workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.

These three firms applied the same technology in the same industry but in different ways. The first firm automated a workflow, creating efficiency gains but risking job displacement for the mail clerks. For the second, bottlenecks to adoption and effective implementation prevented job displacement but also blunted productivity gains that would benefit the firm. The third reorganized work without eliminating any jobs, because effective use of the technology required redeploying employees toward new tasks. The firm redesigned roles to maintain human expertise as a complement to increasingly capable AI models.

In this article, we explore the connections between AI-driven value and work reorganization through 66 face-to-face interviews conducted across 58 companies in the US, all of which are in the midst of adopting AI. We interviewed executives, managers, and individual contributors. We talked to employees at AI-native startups and 100-year-old businesses. We interviewed people at manufacturers and tech companies. We spoke with structural engineers, dentists, and accountants;…

Source: Hacker News | Published: 2026-11-24 21:07 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Nvidia degrades U.S. national security as Chinese military snags its chips
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of a significant tech issue with clear reporting and useful context.

When Super Micro compliance auditors visited a Southeast Asian customer in August 2025 to inspect thousands of servers packed with Nvidia chips, the warehouse floor looked in order. The servers on hand were nonworking dummies staged for the audit; the real ones had already gone to China. When Commerce Department inspectors came later, conspirators set up the same fakes again, using a hair dryer to swap labels and serial stickers. Prosecutors say at least $510 million in servers went to China over a few weeks in spring 2025 alone.

Fifteen months later, the country is once again being asked to take tidy paperwork at face value. In less than two weeks, Nvidia’s leadership turmoil swung through an astonishing reversal. Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as chief executive on November 12, and five days later the company’s chairman declared that the board “does not intend to reinstate” him. Come Monday, directors brought him back anyway, citing assurances from senior U.S. officials and concluding that his return “poses no national security risk.” President Donald Trump claimed credit for talking them into it, telling CNBC, “It’s a threat to lose him.”

Official endorsements cannot wish away the serious security record piling up in the public view. Set aside, for a moment, the scrutiny swirling around Megaspeed, the firm tied to Huang’s paramour Alice Huang, as well as the question of whether she acted as a spy. Even apart from that controversy, a largely overlooked trove of documentation proves beyond dispute that restricted and banned Nvidia chips have been illegally shipped into China, where the Chinese military has openly recorded buying elite processors to bolster capabilities aimed against the United States.

Congressional investigators, state attorneys general, and the broader national security community will inevitably unravel what transpired with Megaspeed and Alice Huang. As they pursue that thread, however, they cannot lose sight of the larger pipeline operating right under Washington’s nose. Smuggled American chips are already strengthening the Chinese Communist Party’s military power and domestic repression, fueling weapons research, design, and manufacturing alongside electronic warfare and intelligence collection. Before anyone treats Huang’s return as case closed, investigators must confront the pressing, unanswered questions still hanging over Nvidia.

How is this allowed to happen in plain sight?

Consider some of the military-linked recipients already plainly visible in public records. A Reuters investigation published November 11 found that Northwestern Polytechnical University, a military-linked institution on the U.S. export blacklist since 2001 over alleged missile proliferation, recorded an October purchase of two H200 chips through a Chinese supplier. Its cybersecurity school also contracted in January for access to two servers containing eight H200s apiece.

Some advocates point out that the H200 is an older and less sensitive chip, but the administration’s January H200 licensing relaxation explicitly did not erase restrictions on blacklisted entities. Indeed, its safeguards expressly excluded military and military-intelligence users and prohibited remote access for specified restricted parties. The university’s disturbing procurement records therefore demand a detailed explanation: what authorization, if any, covered these supplies, and which intermediary checked the actual beneficiary? Did the U.S. government authorize these sales (it would be ludicrously stupid if so), or did Nvidia fail in its responsibility to monitor its own supply chain and maintain awareness of end customers?

The Harbin Institute of Technology offers another disturbing example. When Commerce blacklisted it in 2020, the department specifically cited efforts to acquire American technology for Chinese missile programs. Yet Reuters reported this March that Harbin’s July 2025 procurement notice described a Super Micro system containing eight Nvidia A100s. Beihang University, another blacklisted institution with military ties, recorded purchasing a workstation with four A100s in March 2026.

At a minimum, all of this points to persistent demand from the Chinese military and institutions linked to it — the very institutions the controls were designed to exclude and the very institutions that want to hurt U.S. national security the most. Who is dropping the ball here?

If the Chinese military has its way, more banned Nvidia chips will soon be on their way. WireScreen reviewed more than 3,800 Chinese military and government procurement records. The units seeking Nvidia hardware include the Rocket Force, which operates China’s land-based nuclear missiles, the Cyberspace Force, and the equipment arm of the Communist Party’s Central Military Commission. One Cyberspace Force tender for A100-class servers named a password-cracking tool as the workload. Georgetown researchers found a PLA lab requesting 16 H100s and another unit seeking a DeepSeek-linked cyber range for “intelligent attack.” That should scare any and every American.…

item.title: ‘We’re begging’: DOGE slashed federal workforce to its lowest in 60 years, and the Trump administration says it still can’t recruit Gen Z workers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and useful context for understanding government hiring challenges.

The Trump administration is doubling down on efforts to hire young people, but the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) campaign to cull the federal workforce may now be hampering that goal.

On Nov. 12, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor visited Texas Christian University and spoke with students. The reason? Recruiting the next generation of future government workers.

It’s a big problem: People younger than 30 make up just 7% of the civil service even though the age demographic makes up 23% of the total American workforce, according to Kupor. As of January 2026, young people made up 7.9% of federal employees, down from 8.9% in September 2024 before President Donald Trump took office, according to the Partnership for Public Service.

“I need young, smart people that are coming in, willing to serve,” Duffy said. “You can do it for a lifetime. You can make a career out of it, and that’s wonderful.

“I find it fascinating that more young people don’t want to apply,” he added. “We’re begging for people to come in.”

The administration’s recruiting push has been undercut by an overhaul of the federal workforce when Trump first took office, according to Elizabeth Linos, the Emma Bloomberg Professor of Public Policy and Management at the Harvard Kennedy School. The slashes in headcount, as well as disruptions in workflow as a result of reduced staffing, are discouraging the next generation of talent from joining the federal workforce, she argued, even if DOGE has officially been disbanded for about a year.

“The government sent a message, in particular to young people, saying these jobs are not going to be safe and they’re not going to be secure,” Linos told Fortune. “Even though there are efforts to try to bring talent into government right now, the administration is basically sending two contradictory messages about whether it wants talent in the federal government to begin with, and I think people hear that conflicting message.”

The Trump administration’s Gen Z recruitment efforts

OPM launched the Early Career Talent Network in March, a recruitment push for entry-level workers to apply for finance, human resources, engineering, project management, and procurement jobs within the federal government. The initiative follows the launch of the U.S. Tech Force last December, a hiring initiative for 1,000 engineers and specialists to work with private sector tech companies on the AI buildout within the government.

The Department of Transportation similarly launched a campaign in April targeting Gen Z gamers for air traffic controller roles with recruitment videos featuring popular titles like Fortnite. The agency hired more than 2,000 air traffic controllers, breaking the record in October for most air traffic controller trainees hired in a year. The department has more than 4,000 fewer employees total than it did before Trump took office, according to OPM data.

Gen Z in particular is struggling in today’s labor market, as the unemployment rate for recent college graduates exceeds that of overall unemployment, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. With concerns over AI displacement and fewer job opportunities, young people are prioritizing stability and work-life balance, Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found.

Under Elon Musk, DOGE gutted of federal agencies and implemented a deferred resignation program that saw the largest mass resignation in American history last September. Since DOGE’s inception in January 2025, the federal government is more than 258,000 roles smaller, according to Office of Personnel Management data. Even after DOGE was officially disbanded last November, sending its agents to continue their work as employees within the administration’s separate agencies, headcount decreased an additional 42,000 in 2026. About 2.68 million people work for the federal government, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released earlier this month, a decrease of about 1,000 workers from September, and the lowest since summer of 1965.

“By realigning roles, streamlining operations, and modernizing how agencies manage talent, we are strengthening performance and accountability across government,” Kupor said in a statement to Fortune. “This effort ensures taxpayer dollars support a workforce that delivers efficient, responsive, and high-quality services.”

How DOGE made the federal government’s recruitment job harder

An aging federal workforce has been a problem for years, and is not a result of DOGE or the Trump administration. The U.S. workforce more broadly is aging due to delayed retirement and extended life expectancies, but the government in particular.

The median age of a federal worker is 47 years old, per OPM data, compared to the national average of around 42 years old.

“We’ve got close to half of our population that’s within 10 years of retirement age,” Kupor told Fortune earlier this year. “So if you just did nothing else, you’ve got this major demographic challenge of a large number of people who will likely either retire or certainly be retirement-eligible over the near term, without us actually replenishing the pipeline of early-career people coming in.”

According to Linos, DOGE exacerbated the aging of the government workforce by firing primarily probationary employees, or those who had held their positions for a year or less in most cases, many of whom were early in their careers. Court documents show DOGE fired more than 24,000 probationary workers across 18 federal agencies in the first two months of its existence.…

item.title: Florida State fired Mike Norvell despite a $58.7 million buyout
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed look at a significant sports business issue with clear reporting and useful context.

Florida State fired Mike Norvell despite a $58.7 million buyout

Ten college football coaches carry buyouts between $49.5 million and $105.1 million. See what each price says about the school.

At the top of college football, firing a head coach has become one of the most expensive decisions a university can make. Schools have shown they will pay sums in the tens of millions of dollars to change direction. The Associated Press reports that Texas A&M owed Jimbo Fisher more than $75 million when it decided to start over. LSU also accepted a large buyout to part ways with Brian Kelly, according to CBS Sports. Both schools chose to pay that price rather than keep a coach they no longer wanted. A buyout's size alone doesn't decide whether a coach keeps his job. It sets the price a school must accept to make a change, and the wealthiest programs in the sport have shown they will accept it.

The figure attached to a coach is less settled than it looks, because it marks the most a school might owe rather than what the school ends up paying. The Associated Press reports that the amount depends largely on how many years remain on a contract. A school that waits a season before acting owes less than one that acts today. A school can also bargain. Penn State owed James Franklin $49 million when it let him go, CBS Sports reports, and the two sides settled on $9 million. That changes how to read any coach's price tag. Each figure describes a contract on one date. It says as much about what a school was willing to promise as about how secure the coach really is.

Sports Illustrated set out to identify which college football coaches would cost the most to fire, at programs ranging from Indiana and Illinois to Georgia and Florida State. Each figure is the price a school would pay to change course, not a measure of a coach's salary or skill. Some of these contracts were written to keep a winning coach in place. For those schools, a large number is a statement of how much they want to keep the man they have. Other contracts are being tested by losing seasons, and for those schools the figure is the real cost of a change they may be weighing. At least one school on the list has already made that change anyway.

Kirby Smart, Georgia

Illustration: Quartz

Georgia has made the largest commitment to its coach of any school in college football. As of Dec. 1, 2025, firing Kirby Smart would have cost the school $105.1 million, far more than any other known buyout in the sport, according to Sports Illustrated. Georgia faces a bill that large because of a promise it made, not because of a penalty clause. Bleacher Report reports that the school fully guaranteed Smart's deal if it fires him without cause through Dec. 31, 2028, and that the guarantee drops to 85% after that. Georgia's full promise therefore covers the next few seasons, and for those seasons the school has chosen to face the sport's highest price if it ever wants a change.

The contract binds Georgia far more than it binds Smart. Smart could walk away for a small part of what Georgia would owe to push him out, paying $5 million through the end of 2026, according to Bleacher Report. Smart, not the school, holds the easy way out. If another job ever tempts him, the decision is his.

Georgia has little reason to want a change, because Smart keeps winning. Under Smart, Georgia claimed back-to-back national titles in the 2021 and 2022 seasons and holds a 46-3 record over that stretch, according to Bleacher Report. That kind of winning makes the guarantee easy for the school to stand behind. Georgia wrote the largest buyout in college football to protect a coach who almost never loses. At a school with a struggling coach, a buyout is a price to weigh. At Georgia, it is mostly a statement of intent.

Georgia has promised more than any other school to keep its coach, and Smart is the one who decides whether the deal holds.

Ryan Day, Ohio State

Illustration: Quartz

Ohio State has made one of the largest promises any school has made to keep its coach. The school would owe Ryan Day $70.9 million if it fired him, the second-largest buyout in college football, according to Sports Illustrated, and his salary ranks among the top 10 in the sport. Ohio State made that commitment to a coach who had already delivered. Day won the national title in 2024, according to CBS Sports. With a promise that large, Ohio State was declaring that Day was the coach it meant to keep, more than it was buying him insurance.

A disappointing season has turned that promise into a cost Ohio State has to weigh. The Buckeyes lost four games in 2026, according to CBS Sports, a heavy total for a team that had won it all two seasons earlier. The cost of acting has also fallen since the $70.9 million figure was dated Dec. 1, 2025. A firing once the 2026 season ends would leave Ohio State with a $57.5 million bill, a figure dated Nov. 21, 2026. The drop comes from how the contract is built. Day's buyout is set as a fixed sum for each remaining year rather than a share of his remaining salary, so the total shrinks as each season passes. The longer the school waits, the less it would pay to make a change, and the less protection Day gets from his contract.

A smaller bill alone may not settle Day's future. A school should fire a coach only when it has a clearly better replacement in mind, and the market for coaches is thin right now. Day has gone 89-16 at Ohio State, according to CBS Sports, and has won the large majority of his games. For a change to pay off, Ohio State would need to find a coach who could top that record.

For Ohio State, the money is only one reason to keep Day, alongside his winning record and a short list of better options.

Kalen DeBoer, Alabama

item.title: 8 of the biggest MLB contracts for Japanese players, from $700 million to $34 million
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Informative article on a sports business topic with clear reporting and useful context.

8 of the biggest MLB contracts for Japanese players, from $700 million to $34 million

Major league teams now compete to sign the best players from Nippon Professional Baseball, Japan's top league, and fans tend to judge each of those signings by the total written on the contract. That total leaves out a second payment, because a team that signs a posted Japanese star pays the player and also pays the Japanese club that let him go. MLB.com reports that the Yankees paid Masahiro Tanaka's Japanese club a posting fee separate from his contract. The Blue Jays owed the same kind of fee to Kazuma Okamoto's club under MLB's agreement with NPB, with that money kept outside his contract, according to CBC. The second bill is a standing part of the price of Japanese talent. It keeps rising on deals past $50 million, with the Japanese club taking 15% of any value above that mark, according to CBS Sports. None of that money appears in the headline figure, so the total fans quote covers only part of what a team spends.

Deadlines also shape the price, and they favor the team most willing to spend. Once his club posts him, a Japanese player has 45 days to negotiate with MLB teams, according to MLB.com. Every interested team has to make its best offer within the same few weeks. The final number reflects how many teams wanted the player and how badly they needed him, as much as his record in Japan. The years and dollars on paper can also differ from what a team actually pays and how long the player stays. Money deferred for years costs a team less than money paid now, and an opt-out can end a deal well before its last season. Fans who compare totals learn less than it seems about who is the better player, and the smallest deal can turn out to be the best one.

ESPN set out to rank the largest MLB deals that Japanese players have signed, including the Yankees' 2014 contract for Masahiro Tanaka, the Cubs' deal for Teruaki Sato and the White Sox's deal for Munetaka Murakami. Each of those totals is the money a team promised, and it is best read as a starting point. Behind a total can sit a fee owed to a club in Japan, pay that arrives years later, an exit the player controls or a team in a hurry to fill a hole. Read that way, the order of these deals says more about what each team promised than about what each player turned out to be worth.

Shohei Ohtani

Illustration: Quartz

Shohei Ohtani signed the richest contract a Japanese player has ever received, and the Dodgers paid it for a star they had already watched in the majors. Los Angeles committed $700 million over 10 years to a player who had spent six seasons across town with the Angels, according to ESPN. Nobody had to guess whether his game would carry over from Japan, so the hard question about the deal is how the Dodgers built it. The Associated Press reports that 97% of the money was deferred without interest when he signed in 2023. Almost all of the record total is a promise to pay later, and the question that matters is when the Dodgers actually hand the money over.

The Dodgers will pay most of Ohtani's money long after he signed, and they will spread it across a decade. The deferred payments arrive each July 1 from 2034 through 2043, according to The Associated Press. A dollar paid that far in the future, with no interest added, is worth less than a dollar paid today, and the Dodgers' real cost is below $700 million. Nobody needs to settle on an exact figure for that gap to matter. Ohtani's total can't be compared directly with a contract that pays a player during the seasons he plays.

The 10 years are also less certain than they look, because Ohtani can leave for reasons that have nothing to do with how he plays. The Associated Press reports that the 2023 contract lets him opt out if Mark Walter stops being the controlling owner or if Andrew Friedman leaves as president of baseball operations. A change in the front office, rather than a slump, could end the decade early.

The record contract puts off most of its payments for a decade and leaves its length in the hands of the team's owner and its top baseball executive.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto

Illustration: Quartz

The Dodgers committed more money to Yoshinobu Yamamoto than any team had committed to a player moving straight from Japan to the majors, and they did it before he had thrown a major league pitch. His $325 million contract is the largest for a player arriving directly from Japan, according to ESPN. The Los Angeles Times reports that he was 25 when he signed in 2023, and that before bidding opened, he was expected to command at least $200 million. Clubs judged him on his pitching in Japan, where he won the Pacific League's MVP award in three consecutive seasons. Teams kept raising their offers well past that early estimate, and his final price measures how hard clubs competed for him as much as how good he was.

The Dodgers bid the highest because signing Yamamoto served a plan built around Shohei Ohtani. Ohtani helped recruit him, taking part with teammates Betts and Freeman in the meeting the Dodgers held with Yamamoto at their ballpark, according to the Los Angeles Times. "It was important to Shohei that this wasn't the one move we were gonna make, and I think anyone who has watched us operate over the years, we're trying to add really good players at every turn," Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers' president of baseball operations, told the Los Angeles Times in 2023. A team that had made that promise to its biggest star had little reason to stop bidding at the early estimate. When several teams compete for one player, the team with the most pressing plan usually decides the final price.…

item.title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear explanation of a government policy with useful context for understanding energy payments.

Will I get the Â£100 energy payment and when will I receive it?

Up to 20 million households in England will get a Â£100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.

Here's what you need to know about the payment.

How much is it?

For many people, the Â£100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.

A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by Â£443 a year from January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight.

Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.

Will I get the payment? And how can I check?

Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.

As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in, external. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.

If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.

Will I get it if I live in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland?

The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.

The Scottish and Welsh governments have confirmed they will use the funding to introduce equivalent or similar payment schemes.

The Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the Â£100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.

- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

Will I get it if I'm a student or don't pay council tax?

If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into your bank account.

Those who don't pay by direct debit will be contacted by their council and given the choice to receive the Â£100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill.

The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May.

Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.

However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.

Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way to give them the payments.

This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.

The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.

Do I have to spend the money on my energy bill?

The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy.

But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts so you could choose to spend it on something else, while some people may choose to receive the Â£100 as a credit on their council tax bill.

How is the government funding this payment?

The chancellor said the money for the Â£100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.

The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.

- Published28 October

item.title: Silicon Valley divorce lawyers see surge of CEO requests for prenups and partner NDAs after the Nvidia scandal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Relevant to business and leadership with insightful analysis of a high-profile case.

Silicon Valley divorce lawyers are seeing surge in outreach from CEOs, founders, and high-net-worth employees who are citing the Nvidia scandal as the reason for their calls.

The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affairs, and Nvidia’s board subsequently firing him from the company he founded, is a “precautionary tale for other CEOs,” said one lawyer who has been involved in the high-profile divorces of some of the tech industry’s most famous CEOs.

Although Huang’s board reinstated him on Monday in a controversial move, the roller coaster of events has pushed other CEOs to think about how their assets are connected, and potentially at risk, as a result of their personal relationships. In addition to pursuing prenuptial agreements, many are interested in drafting nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for their significant others, which is a new trend, says Monica Mazzei, a partner in Buchalter’s San Francisco family law office.

“It’s totally changed the landscape,” said Mazzei. “I’ve never seen this before. This was definitely big news in the family law space.”

Since the Nvidia scandal broke, three clients have contacted Mazzei with requests to draft NDAs for the significant others of CEOs. They specifically cited Huang in the outreach, said Mazzei, who specializes in representing high-net-worth clients. Most of the requests are coming from the company, not the CEO themselves, in an effort to protect the business.

“The company is probably telling the CEO, ‘Anyone you need to date needs to sign this because we don’t want you to end up in a Jensen Huang situation,’” Mazzei said.

Huang had at least three known affairs, two with internal Nvidia employees, and one extra controversial relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. Alice Huang is reportedly suspected by some intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy and of illegally providing Chinese companies access to advanced Nvidia chips. The allegations are that Alice Huang is a “honeypot” who lured Jensen Huang into a relationship to get access to proprietary information.

“Why honeypots work is because when you’re dating someone you’re not thinking about what they might overhear on a phone call, or see on papers lying out at home,” said Mazzei. “They’re just in your life, overhearing a lot.”

Demand for prenuptial agreements has also surged. Jensen and Lori Huang have been married for 41 years, and reportedly do not have a prenuptial agreement. Jensen Huang is one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of roughly $137 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. According to California law, Lori stands to come away with half of that in a potential divorce, along with shares in Nvidia.

It remains to be seen if Lori Huang will file for a divorce. If the couple were to decide to split up, Lori and Jensen Huang would most likely agree to a settlement prior to the divorce proceedings becoming public, says Mazzei. Once the terms are finalized, Mazzei reckons, the couple would then go public with the news, as Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott did.

Tech execs are the new celebs

Libby Leffler, founder and CEO of thisfirst.com, an online prenup service, says she’s seen more customers naming tech billionaires and founders as the inspiration for their agreements since the Nvidia scandal broke. Most of Leffler’s clients are founders and early employees at pre-IPO companies, especially in California and New York. Every time a public figure’s divorce or prenup makes headlines, Leffler’s inbound requests jump, but the naming of tech CEOs this time is different.

“People used to name-check celebs, but now they are name-checking tech CEOs,” Leffler tells Fortune. “What they really mean is that they want to feel as protected as they assume those people are.” The most referenced arrangement is Jeff Bezos’s rumored prenuptial agreement with Lauren Sánchez, who became his second wife in 2025.

“Your relationship and your cap table are more connected than people think, and founders are seeing that play out,” Leffler said.

Mazzei also noted a surge in prenup requests, specifically coming from Anthropic employees. When the company went public at a $1.5 trillion valuation on Nov. 19—a week after Huang’s ousting—it minted thousands of multimillionaires among the company’s relatively small staff of 5,300. The average fortune of its non-founding staff is roughly $44 million, although nearly 600 pocketed at least $100 million.

Mazzei could not link the Anthropic employees’ requests to Nvidia directly, although the Huangs’ lack of a prenup may have spooked them. In general, many of them are on the younger side, and Mazzei noted that among younger generations prenups are becoming more common.
