item.title: A walkable city of tomorrow is growing in suburban Utah
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant environmental development with useful vocabulary and context for an English learner.

Sarah Miller biked with her 5-year-old son on a hot afternoon this summer to a vibrant new park in Utah City, a community rising on 700 acres in the heart of Vineyard, one of Utah’s fastest-growing cities, and envisioned as its new downtown.

They rode along the Greenline, a wide promenade flanked by pickleball, tennis, and basketball courts that runs through the development, from the FrontRunner train station toward glittering Utah Lake. Miller said she moved with her kids a few ago to live by the lakeshore, and she’s enjoyed watching Utah City go up near her home.

Its first two swanky apartment complexes, called simply 120 and 220 Bend, were finished in February, though only a few balconies had patio furniture. Miller and her son had the park, with its array of slides and wooden play structures to explore, almost to themselves.

“It’s very quiet for now,” Miller said. “I imagine as it grows, more people will come in, and it will feel a bit more alive, but I think it’s beautiful.”

Utah City’s developer is building on a rare opportunity to create a transit-oriented, high-density community from scratch in the middle of one of the country’s fastest-growing metro areas — with strong support from former Vineyard city officials, new tools from the local government to help with financing, and investments from taxpayers. It currently has 1,400 units for rent.

The new community has spread across property that was once home to Geneva Steel, an industrial complex built during World War II that went defunct in the 2000s. Former Vineyard officials created tax incentives to clean up the site and agreed to allow the construction of thousands of housing units and high-rise buildings in hopes of luring developers. The Utah Transit Authority built a stop at the site in 2022 for FrontRunner, the commuter train that runs along the Wasatch Front, the state’s urban corridor.

Flagborough LLC, the primary developer of Utah City, says it’s setting an example of how Utah and other Western states can abandon suburban sprawl, with a downtown designed for pedestrians instead of cars and a solution to the smog that plagues the region every summer and winter. They promise that it will be the most ambitious transit-oriented community in the state, with thousands of housing units, limited only by the cost of constructing high-rises.

“The biggest benefit of this project, the greatest opportunity, is that the project’s so big,” said Nate Hutchinson, a partner in both The Flagship Companies, one of the largest housing developers in the state, and Flagborough. They expect to finish building Utah City in 15 to 20 years.

“We’ve been working with a lot of people who’ve done this really well all over the country,” said Pete Evans, a co-managing partner of Utah City and Flagship. “We think we have a pretty good formula on how to make it viable.”

But Utah City is facing heightened scrutiny from a new mayor of Vineyard and new City Council members who say they have a mandate from voters to roll back policies they consider too deferential to developers. They’re skeptical of the vision for Utah City and the leeway and incentives provided to its developer. “Maybe it can work, maybe it can’t,” said Jacob Wood, a Vineyard City Council member who took office in January. “It’s a gamble, but they shouldn’t be gambling with city money.”

David Lauret, another Vineyard City Council member who took office this year, questions whether too many public resources have been committed to Utah City. City Council members also complain about the project’s dense clusters of units for rent, which are partly funded using property tax incentives.

“The problem we have is many of the citizens feel they’re trying to use our money … toward building their business,” Lauret said. “It’s all rental facilities. We’re basically helping to hand them a business they’ll make money with in perpetuity.”

The city paid $4.5 million to Utah City developers in 2026 alone, and council members interviewed for this story said they’re reviewing what those payments covered.

Bella’s Market, a grocery store with sparkling floor-to-ceiling glass windows, opened in Utah City late last year across the street from the FrontRunner train station. Next door is the newly opened Fini Pizza, a slice shop recruited from New York City.

Utah City’s water-wise landscaping and green spaces have communal firepits and clusters of chairs under candy-striped sun umbrellas. At the end of the Greenline walkway lies the Utah City playground, topped by a spherical — and climbable — centerpiece that seemingly floats like a hot-air balloon. Taken together, the development has the feel of a vintage boardwalk or century-old World’s Fair promenade, minus the crowds.

These are welcome amenities for Vineyard, which has surged from a sleepy town of 139 in 2010 to a city of about 16,000 today.

Gently curving paseos beckon pedestrians to discover what’s ahead — usually a small plaza with more common spaces. In apartment buildings, board games, books, and vinyl records are neatly arranged in the lobbies.

“The community’s rad,” said Cameron Larsen, a 34-year-old father of four who moved into a three-bedroom apartment with his family in Utah City last February. “The units are pretty bougie.”

Larsen was about to start a new office job, and expected to take the FrontRunner for his commute. His wife, 29-year-old Aunica Larsen, walks to work at Bella’s Market. “This is literally my favorite place I’ve ever lived,” she said. “It’s all very vibey.”

The developers have thrown in all kinds of perks to lure residents, including ski passes to Sundance Mountain Resort and unlimited access to a nearby Peloton fitness center as well as a future swimming pool.

Strolling or cycling through it all, visitors and residents likely won’t think much about dodging cars, let alone traffic. That’s a big win, according to Jeff Speck, a lauded urban designer that Flagship tapped for the project.…

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, though the learning value is slightly reduced due to the focus on political dynamics rather than env

Climate activists around the country saw this month’s midterm elections as a win. From congressional seats to governors’ mansions to local offices, progressive candidates leveraged voters’ frustration with the rising cost of living, especially high power bills, to defeat fossil fuel-friendly challengers.

But voters in two communities — Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Kitsap County, Washington — also rejected an idea that some say can address both climate change and affordability: replacing for-profit utilities with publicly owned ones.

On average, public utilities in the country charge lower electric rates and offer more reliable service than for-profit providers. Advocates contend that by being accountable to communities, they could transition to cleaner forms of energy faster than their counterparts beholden to shareholders and bottom lines.

Despite being in different regions of the country, the two community efforts unfolded in eerily similar ways. In each, private utilities spent roughly $2 million on local opposition campaigns, even using identical terms, like “too costly” and “too risky.” In the end, both initiatives failed by single-digit margins, sharing the same fate as the vast majority of recent public power efforts around the country.

These results highlight the unique challenges of creating a new public power utility in the 21st century. A century ago, building a new public utility meant building a new grid. Today, it means buying out the poles and wires already owned by a for-profit utility, a process that more closely resembles a hostile takeover.

Kitsap County, Washington

Public power has been an important part of Washington’s history for almost as long as Washington has been a state. But the movement really took off in the 1930s, triggered by two major events. First, a citizen-led state ballot initiative gave every community the right to form its own public utility district, or PUD. These new public agencies, run by elected commissioners, were empowered to provide power, water, and eventually internet to their constituents without taking a profit. Soon after, Congress created the Bonneville Power Administration, a New Deal-era agency that sold hydropower from the Columbia River. The new agency was required to give public utilities first dibs on its cheap hydropower, causing dozens of power districts to pop up around the state in the following decades.

It was in this golden age that Kitsap County — a community on the small peninsula across the Puget Sound from Seattle — formed its own public utility district intended to provide electricity. But the outbreak of World War II a few years later delayed that effort for long enough that its authorization expired. Today, the utility district oversees water and internet infrastructure but allows a private utility called Puget Sound Energy to provide power.

By the 1950s, the red-scare movement took aim at public power. Private utility groups ran ads in national magazines. “It was ‘creeping communism,’ and had pictures of Russian dictators,” said Steve Johnson, the former executive director of the Washington Public Utility Association. Since then, public power has been in a dry spell, with most community efforts failing in Washington and across the U.S.

There was a notable exception in 2008, when Jefferson County — Kitsap’s rural neighbor to the west — passed a ballot initiative to create a new public utility that would take over power service from Puget Sound Energy. “I think that was a big wake-up call for the company, because there had not been a new PUD since the 1950s,” said Johnson. Today, Jefferson County runs entirely on carbon-free electricity from Bonneville Power, and typical bills there are roughly 19 percent lower than for Puget Sound Energy’s 1.24 million customers in surrounding areas.

Meanwhile, in neighboring Kitsap County, which today is home to about 280,000 people, Puget Sound Energy’s power rates continued to rise. Over the last five years, the average power bill has nearly doubled, and the company is proposing a series of increases totaling 32 percent by 2029. Puget Sound Energy told Grist that its rates reflect rising demand, infrastructure costs, and the challenge of meeting Washington’s clean electricity targets. State law requires utilities to be carbon neutral by 2030, leaving Puget Sound Energy, which still gets about half its energy from fossil fuels, scrambling to meet deadlines.

Earlier this year, as bills with new rates arrived in mailboxes, Kitsap utility commissioners started to hear from residents struggling to make ends meet. “Not being able to decide between feeding your kids and paying your electric bill — it’s not OK,” said commissioner Heather Pauley. This led the utility district to put forward a ballot initiative asking voters to give it the authority to take over power service from Puget Sound Energy.

The initiative’s design had, in one commissioner’s words, an “Achilles’ heel.” Voters would be approving the proposal without an official feasibility study. If the measure passed, the district would pay for an extensive study on the plan’s costs and benefits. Only if it penciled out would the commissioners move ahead with taking over the grid. While this was intended as a gesture of fiscal responsibility, it also left voters with few details to vote on.

This ended up being the opening for Puget Sound Energy’s opposition campaign: “Too Costly. Too Risky. No Plan,” their flyers and yard signs read. The campaign spent $2.3 million, making it one of the most expensive local ballot measure fights in state history.

Meanwhile, the public utility district was strictly prohibited from any form of advocacy. “Was there misinformation out there? Absolutely,” said Angela Bennink, the district’s general manager. “But we were limited in what we could do.”…

item.title: Nepal hoped for flood aid at COP31. It got nothing.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Good reporting on a significant environmental issue with useful vocabulary, though the learning value is limited by the focus on financial aspects rather than e

When almost 200 countries endorsed the Paris Agreement in 2015, they agreed to a massive transfer of money between the world’s largest carbon emitters and the poor countries on the front lines of climate change. The accord promised that developed countries would begin “mobilizing climate finance” in “a progression beyond previous efforts,” with a focus on “public and grant-based resources” as opposed to loans that poor countries would have to pay back. This money would help develop clean energy projects like solar and wind farms, as well as sea walls, water wells, and other projects that could help the Global South adapt to extreme weather. For countries already facing down climate disasters, it would pay to help them recover from the loss and damage caused by these events.

The reality has been a lot uglier. These promises were always voluntary, or at least impossible to enforce, and rich countries have failed to meet most of their obligations. They have provided most clean energy finance through loans, which have strained the budgets of many poor countries. They have failed to cut their own emissions fast enough to slow down global warming, which has increased the cost of adapting to a warmer world. They have failed to provide money for that adaptation, which has increased the scale of loss and damage. And they have failed to provide money for loss and damage, which has forced developing countries to spend their own money on recovery from extreme weather.

In recent years this financial failure has all but derailed the United Nations climate process, in which countries try to achieve global decisions based on universal consensus. Developing countries say they can’t ditch fossil fuels without much more money, while rich countries say they can’t go beyond their current commitment to provide $300 billion a year in climate finance by 2035.

It was against this backdrop that leaders from Nepal arrived at COP31, this year’s U.N. climate meeting, or “conference of the parties,” in Antalya, Turkey. Just three months ago, a glacial collapse in the Himalayas caused massive flooding in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi region, leaving more than 1,400 dead and another 5,000 missing. Initial scientific studies have concluded that global warming likely contributed to the weakening of the glacier and the melting of permafrost that triggered the catastrophic avalanche. The estimated cost of rebuilding exceeds $4.8 billion, or around 10 percent of the country’s gross domestic product, but the world has pledged only a few hundred million in aid. Nepal hoped that other countries would provide more relief money at COP31.

Two weeks later, Nepal left Antalya no better off than when it arrived. Not only did rich countries fail to provide any additional assistance to the ravaged country, they declined to deliver almost any new disaster aid. One European negotiator said even before the conference began that such an idea was “dead in the water.” Nepali negotiators also hoped to win global support for less expensive interventions, like glacial melt detection systems and a dedicated forum to research mountain climate risks. Yet these items also failed to secure consensus amid a collapse in talks at the summit, which was only the second in 20 years to conclude without a final overarching agreement.

Leaders and experts from Nepal and other mountain countries said the failure to deliver for Nepal reflects fundamental problems with the U.N. process.

“We left with empty hands,” said Dharam Uprety, a Nepali climate scientist who serves as the head of the country’s disaster response agency. “In the past, I used to be very optimistic, but I’m very pessimistic about the COPs. Without any adequate outcomes, it’s just a waste of money.”

The U.N. has a vehicle for dealing with catastrophes like the one in Nepal — the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, which rich nations agreed to establish in 2022 after years of pressure from developing countries to fulfill the promise of the Paris Agreement. This commitment to climate reparations was hailed as a breakthrough at the time, but it has taken years for the fund to establish bylaws and procedures for disbursing money. When the Nepal floods hit in August, the fund had just finished taking applications for its first-ever grants, and it was months away from actually sending out any checks.

The catastrophe in Nepal was an early test of the fund’s relevance. Even as the fund’s board considered this first round of applications, Nepal submitted an emergency request for recovery money, saying that it couldn’t wait for ordinary bureaucracy to take its course; a number of leaders from other developing countries endorsed this request. The board met for an “extraordinary meeting” in October and allocated Nepal $20 million, plus administrative costs, less than half a percent of the cost of rebuilding. Even this emergency funding will take months to arrive — before it can get money, Nepal still has to submit an application saying what it plans to spend the money on. It’s unclear if it will be able to get any more money from the fund down the road.

“If we can’t respond to the urgency, then [the process] is obviously not healthy,” said Manjeet Dhakal, a Nepali climate negotiator who advises the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a bloc of developing nations. “The scale of the resources — and also the way of doing business, if a country has to wait for two months to get resources — is not fit for purpose.”

Dhakal said that while emergency donations from Nepal’s neighboring countries helped with immediate rescues and debris clearance, the money from the U.N. fund will support reconstruction of destroyed buildings — although it will cover only a tiny fraction of the more than 7,000 ruined structures. Nepal’s own finances are so thin that it has turned to crowdfunding to help close the gap.…

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-24 09:15 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Britain’s ‘Rigged’ Fishing Industry Is Fueling Overfishing
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, though the learning value is slightly reduced by the focus on the fishing industry rather than broad

Along England’s southern coast lies a fishing community whose existence can be traced back almost a millennium. From its shingled shore, Hastings once housed the largest beach-launched fleet in Europe. But when retired fisherman Jerry Percy visited a few weeks ago, he could count the operational boats on his fingers.

“If you take the argument to the end game, then you’ll have nothing but a picture-postcard fleet bobbing about in little pretty harbors and bugger-all else,” said Percy, describing a “spiral of decline” across the U.K.’s small-boat fleet.

This hollowing out of coastal livelihoods is part of a “rigged system,” according to a new report by Oceana UK. Unequal government subsidies, outdated quota systems and catch limits that routinely ignore science have concentrated wealth in large corporate fleets at the expense of coastal communities and the marine ecosystems they rely on.

“The non-compliance, the discards, the very poor transparency and the quota inequality is all really adding up,” said Izzy Ross, Oceana UK’s habitats and fisheries campaign manager. “It’s not a fair playing field for those who want to do things right and want to do things more sustainably.”

Fishing vessels over 39 feet were found to have falsified logbooks, deployed illegal gear or dumped fish during 66 percent of at-sea inspections in English waters between April 2025 and March 2026, according to Freedom of Information data obtained from the Marine Management Organisation.

For vessels under 33 feet, these activities were documented just 10 percent of the time.

Operating “out of sight and out of mind” in rough seas where boarding is often impossible, larger vessels easily evade scrutiny, said Percy, who spent decades fishing the entire circumference of the U.K., and jokes he’s been both “poacher and gamekeeper.” Even when violations were documented, authorities merely issued “verbal advice” in almost 70 percent of cases.

Only 1 percent of infringements resulted in any financial penalty—totalling less than $37,000 across the entire fleet between April 2024 and March 2025.

“When you compare it to the amount of millions of pounds going out in fuel subsidies and some of the profits that these large [boats] are pulling in, that’s a very, very small amount,” said Ross. “It’s not even something they probably notice.”

Crews scrapped more than 100,000 metric tons of dead or dying fish, across 57 U.K. quota stocks, last year—equal to the weight of around 8,300 of London’s red double-decker buses. From spotted dogfish and silver smelt to haddock and whiting, crews often chuck lower-value catches to keep space for potentially more profitable products, or dump “choke species” with low quotas that would otherwise force boats back to port.

Ross warns the “disgusting level of discards” is pushing some populations toward total collapse. For Irish Sea plaice, a popular flatfish, over 80 percent caught between 2023 and 2025 was thrown back overboard, despite unsustainable fishing pressure for the species and a recommendation of no catches for 2027.

Because accurate discard data relies on occasional observers and voluntary disclosures, the 100,000-ton figure is likely an underestimate. When remote monitoring cameras were deployed on fishing boats in New Zealand in 2024, the true discard rate jumped 46 percent above original estimates.

Though the U.K. government recently announced the requirement of cameras and GPS monitoring for large pelagic boats—those that catch fish in the water column rather than from the seabed—from November 2028, the rules exclude bottom trawlers, which have the highest discard rates.

“It’s a step in the right direction, but it’s not far enough,” said Ross. “It’ll be 2028 before that’s implemented, and we’d like to see the government going further because it’s a really pressing issue. If we’re discarding another 100,000 tons next year and the year after, we need it to come sooner.”

A Marine Management Organisation spokesperson told Inside Climate News the agency “takes non-compliance with fisheries rules seriously and uses a risk-based, intelligence-led approach to target inspection and enforcement activity where the risk is greatest,” highlighting discards are not always illegal, and said it’s working with regulators to keep monitoring “operationally effective.”

While boats under 33 feet make up three-quarters of the fleet, they’re allocated just a few percent of the quota—part of what Oceana UK describes as the “systemic injustices” of British fisheries.

Nearly 90 percent of U.K. quota is still allocated based on what vessels caught between 1994 and 1996, turning a brief historical snapshot into a tradeable commodity controlled by a small handful of large companies.

“Our ocean is for everyone, and our fish stocks are a public resource. Yet successive governments have created a system that favours a handful of large companies, allowing them to profit at the expense of the ocean and local communities,” said Hugo Tagholm, executive director of Oceana UK in a press release.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Last year, the five largest quota-holding companies pocketed over $160 million in combined profits while drawing disproportionately from taxpayer-funded fuel subsidies. Traveling farthest offshore with the heaviest gear, vessels over 130 feet benefited from an estimated $300 million in British fuel subsidies between 2012 and 2022.

Across European waters, these “mega-industrial” trawlers burn the most fuel, scrape the seafloor with vast trawl nets and swipe the most marine life.

Percy, now senior advisor to the Low Impact Fishers of Europe organization, believes the small-boat fleet he’s spent decades advocating for is “finished” if current trends continue.…

Source: Inside Climate News | Published: 2026-11-24 17:03 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Climate Generation at COP31
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, though the learning value is limited by the focus on a specific generation rather than broader envir

The youth of this era, both Gen Z and Gen Alpha, are often described as the “climate generation,” in part because climate change is already shaping how this generation (which also happens to be my generation) lives and what our futures will look like. Researchers have linked climate change to shifts in where Bangladeshi children live and learn, girls dropping out of school in Kenya during droughts or floods and declining the mental health of students.

But we are also the generation that has learned to push back: taking to the streets, as millions did worldwide during the global climate strikes inspired by Greta Thunberg’ in 2019, and to the courts, where 27 students from the University of the South Pacific launched the campaign that ultimately led to the International Court of Justice’s 2025 climate opinion. At this year’s COP31, the United Nations’ 31st climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, the climate generation was back.

The draft texts: The cover decision serves as the closest thing to a final summary of the agreements reached by nearly 200 countries in Antalya to advance the goals of the Paris Agreement. The first draft was released on Nov. 16, a week into the proceedings, and called for countries to treat climate impacts on children “as a primary consideration in national planning.” On Nov. 19, a shorter second draft was released. A paragraph recognizing the “meaningful participation of children and youth” in climate decision-making survived. Language on how climate change harms children, direct mentions of gender and education, a $120 billion target for adaptation finance and a reference to fossil fuels were cut. When I compared the two drafts, what stood out the most was that agriculture, the sector that employs 44 percent of working youth ages 15 to 24 worldwide, appeared in neither.

A third draft, released on Sunday, restored much of what had been cut, including language on the “disproportionate impacts of climate change on children” and their access to health and education. But the European Union, small island states, the U.K., Norway, and others rejected the cover decision due to a lack of mention of fossil fuels and no final decision was adopted in the end; you can read more on the breakdown from my colleague Bob Berwyn. This year’s talks were the longest COP in history and the first major breakdownin negotiations since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009.

Before the summit, the food and agriculture working group of YOUNGO, the official youth constituency in U.N. climate talks, called for grant-based adaptation finance that young farmers could access directly. The Nov. 19 draft does mention grant-based adaptation finance, but it reserves the “direct access” language for national development banks, not young people.

The one finance decision that appears to have survived the summit is on the loss and damage fund. It calls for the board to “enhance engagement” with the youth and to “take into account their perspectives, as appropriate.”

Did you also spend your free time reading the draft decisions? Email me at [email protected] to share what you noticed in the texts.

Inside the venue: The climate generation also had a dedicated physical space in Antalya. The Children and Youth Pavilion is in its fifth consecutive year as the only fully youth-led space at the official climate summit, opened with Sally Higgins, the COP31 Presidency Youth Climate Champion, in attendance. Higgins’ responsibility is to connect the voices of the global youth to the COP presidency. At the U.N. Secretary-General’s youth roundtable, Jayanti Bam, UNICEF Nepal’s youth advocate for climate action, asked that leaders “protect children. Listen to children. And act for children.”

On Nov. 19, Higgins said in a video published to the UN Climate Change Facebook account that “farming practices are really under threat from climate change,” the same concern YOUNGO expressed.

Outside the venue: One of the most prominent voices in the climate generation finally returned to the COP proceedings this year. On Nov. 10, Greta Thunberg, now 23, arrived at the Antalya Expo Center. It was her first U.N. climate summit since the 2021 COP in Glasgow, where she dismissed global leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah.” She’s continued that thread. This year, she said that host governments use the summit to “whitewash themselves,” adding that the negotiations are full of lobbyists that are paid by industries profiting from fossil fuel dependence. Thunberg’s criticism of fossil fuel interests and lobbying proved prescient, as they contributed to the breakdown of the agreement.

Addis Ababa, Ethiopia will host the next COP next November. The climate generation, who came to Antalya asking for more support, now have a year to regroup and try again. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in a Facebook post describing their work in Turkey that “the activism of young people today is what gives [him] hope for the future.”

This Week on Earth

Last week, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, 62–33. The contentious permitting bill has the potential to lower energy costs for consumers, but as currently written, it weakens some environmental laws to speed up the permitting process.

Here are some stories that stood out to me outside the coverage of BAAJA:

Just in time for Thanksgiving, The Guardian and Climate Central reported that cranberry-growing regions now see an average of 14 more warm winter days than in 1970. In Wisconsin, which grows more than 60 percent of the U.S. cranberry supply, early thaws are melting the ice that protects the vines.…

Source: Inside Climate News | Published: 2026-11-24 13:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: As Wildfires Stress Montana’s Insurance Market, the State is Getting Harder to Call Home
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, though the learning value is limited by the focus on a specific state rather than broader environmen

Montana’s snow-capped mountains, vast forests and open valleys have long attracted people seeking a life close to nature. But that lifestyle is becoming increasingly difficult to afford, or even attain, as the state’s growing wildfire risk spikes homeowners insurance premiums and leaves some home buyers unable to purchase coverage at all.

As wildfire seasons grow longer and more destructive across the American West, insurers are fundamentally changing how they evaluate risk, said James Brown, Montana’s elected state auditor, who also serves as the state’s commissioner of securities and insurance. About 70 percent of the acreage burned by wildfires in Montana since 1888 has burned since 2000, according to the state Legislature. And nearly two-thirds of Montana homes are located within the Wildland-Urban Interface, or WUI, where residential development meets fire-prone forests and grasslands, leaving them vulnerable to wildfires.

“We’re receiving more complaints from homeowners about wildfire insurance than almost any other issue,” said Brown in an interview with Inside Climate News. “People are finding that either their premiums have increased significantly or their policies are not being renewed because companies are reassessing wildfire risk.”

The challenges facing Montana homeowners reflect a broader national trend. An August 2026 report by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners reported that inflation-adjusted homeowners insurance premiums increased between 18.3 percent and 43.3 percent across different U.S. regions from 2018 to 2024. During the same period, insurer-initiated policy nonrenewal rates rose between 96 percent and 216 percent, depending on the region.

Property insurance costs have risen fastest in regions exposed to climate-related hazards, according to the U.S. Treasury Department, and insurers are increasingly declining to renew policies in high-risk areas.

National Crisis Hits Home

Montana has not experienced the insurance market collapse seen in parts of California and Florida, where major insurers have sharply reduced the new business they take on, but the state’s market is still under great stress.

Data from the American Property Casualty Insurance Association show that homeowners insurance premiums in Montana have increased roughly 40 percent since 2019.

A September report by the Montana Legislature’s Economic Affairs Interim Committee highlighted growing concerns about homeowners’ insurance costs. Citing data from the Consumer Federation of America, the report found that average homeowners insurance premiums in Montana increased by 10 percent between 2021 and 2024. Rural homeowners experienced an 11 percent increase, compared with 5 percent in urban and suburban areas.

Rising insurance costs are adding to the financial pressures facing Montana homeowners, who are also dealing with rapidly increasing house prices. According to the Montana Department of Revenue, the statewide median residential home value increased by $67,000, or 22 percent, between Tax Year 2024 and 2025.

According to the Montana Environmental Information Center, the number of homes built in wildfire-prone areas doubled between 1990 and 2020. Researchers say that growth has placed more people and more expensive homes directly in the path of increasingly severe wildfires.

Mike Kent, president of the Bitterroot Board of Realtors, traced the trend to around 2018, when catastrophic wildfire seasons in California and Oregon began reshaping how insurers viewed risk across the West.

Some insurers may still offer replacement coverage, Kent said, but often at substantially higher prices, while others are not renewing policies.

Insurance Can Be a Deal Breaker

For many prospective buyers, insurance has become an unexpected obstacle in purchasing a home. Real estate agents across western Montana say clients are now requesting insurance quotes before finalizing purchase agreements, a practice that was uncommon only a few years ago.

“It’s no longer enough to find the perfect house,” Kent said. “Buyers first need to know whether they can insure it and whether they can afford that insurance.”

Today, real estate agents across western Montana say getting homeowners insurance, once one of the final steps before closing, has become one of the first things buyers ask about. In some cases, the answer determines whether a family can afford to purchase a home at all.

“It has changed dramatically,” said Missoula-based real estate agent Mandy Snook. “I’m advising clients that the insurance contingency is just as important as their inspection contingency.”

The advice reflects a rapidly changing marketplace.

Insurance contingencies allow buyers to withdraw from a purchase if they cannot obtain acceptable homeowners insurance.

“I’ve seen transactions fall apart because of insurance,” Snook said. “The wildfire risk pushed the premium so high that buyers simply couldn’t move forward.”

Scott Countryman, an agent with Goosehead Insurance in Kalispell, says many buyers are surprised by insurance quotes.

“When the insurance premium increases significantly, it changes the buyer’s monthly payment,” Countryman said. “Sometimes that’s enough to affect loan qualification.”

A family may have sufficient income to pay the asking price for a home, but once insurance costs are added, the monthly payment may exceed what the lender will approve.

Homeowners are facing another challenge as well—reduced competition among insurers as companies abandon areas threatened by climate-driven disasters.

Countryman remembers a time when homeowners routinely received quotes from several insurers.

“Five or six years ago, we might have had three or four companies competing for the same home,” he said. “Now there are situations where only one company is willing to write the policy.”

When Homeowners Lose Coverage…

item.title: COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and useful vocabulary, though the learning value is limited by the focus on a specific region rather than broader environme

COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya

The “Antalya pact” took up much of the two weeks of negotiating time in Turkey, only to be rejected during the closing plenary by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable countries.

Several countries expressed their regret during the plenary that significant work on advancing ocean-climate action would be lost.

The COP ran nearly 50 hours over time, but did not end with substantive outcomes on several key topics.

For the second year in a row, negotiations on agriculture and food security broke down and will now have to resume next year.

Food-systems advocates were, however, heartened by the explicit inclusion of “agroecology” in a decision within the “just transition work programme”.

Ocean-conservation groups noted an increased focus on ocean-climate links at this year’s COP, but said COP31 did not live up to its promise of being a “blue COP”.

There was also scant new funding for food systems and nature, with just a handful of small pledges to ocean initiatives and two newly announced contributions to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility.

Here, Carbon Brief analyses all of the key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at COP31 – both inside and out of the negotiating rooms.

(See Carbon Brief’s coverage of food, forests, oceans and nature at COP30, COP29, COP28, COP27 and COP26.)

Formal negotiations

Cover decision

The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious – closing plenary in Antalya.

Other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent.

However, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations.

Ultimately, parties did not find consensus on the text, particularly around the removal of any reference to fossil fuels and the lack of concrete climate-finance targets.

The cover text was one of the places in the negotiations where ocean advocates were hoping to see ocean-climate linkages highlighted.

Marine Lecerf, head of international policy at Ocean & Climate Platform, told a press huddle:

“What we’re really asking for right now is to make sure we can recognise ocean-based interlinkages…We’re not asking for a new mandate. We are asking for acceleration of the work that is already undertaken.”

The first draft of the cover decision, published on 16 November, was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion. It was accompanied by a short “presidency note” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text.

This lengthy first draft had 21 references to the ocean, including recognising the impacts of climate change, support for ocean-observing systems, encouraging parties to strengthen ocean-climate action and a multi-year plan for the “ocean and climate change dialogue”, which occurs annually at the Bonn intersessional meetings in June.

Regarding that draft, Steven Guilbeault, former environment minister of Canada, told Carbon Brief:

“I don’t see why the elements that are in the cover decision right now on oceans should be controversial or problematic to any nations. If you’re serious about fighting climate change, there’s nothing in this text regarding oceans that should be problematic for you.”

(Earth Negotiations Bulletin reported that Russia opposed mentions of the ocean in the cover text during the ocean ministerial consultation.)

The next iteration of the text, on 19 November, retained many of the ocean elements, albeit with less detail than the first draft. The second text also removed references to post-2028 ocean work and a proposed high-level ministerial ocean dialogue.

In the end, oceans had 19 mentions in the rejected Antalya pact.

During the final plenary, Fiji’s Dr Sivendra Michael – co-chair of the ocean and climate change dialogue – appealed to the COP31 president to “humbly consolidate” the consensus on ocean as a “standalone ocean decision” and “directly submit” ten paragraphs with no objections in text as a “way to preserve” work done.

Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s environment and climate change minister, said:

“The ocean-climate nexus is undeniable. We, the people of the Pacific, are deeply indebted, as the ocean is our home, our identity and it is what connects us. There is no climate action without ocean action. We hope this is not lost today and that parties will please consider keeping the ocean text alive.”

Other aspects of the natural world garnered significantly less attention in the cover text.

The final decision failed to mention the Brazil-led roadmap on deforestation, although it was “welcome[d]” in the initial draft. (See: Deforestation.)

Mentions of the “critical role” of forests in carbon storage, food security, biodiversity and community adaptation were also stripped from the text between the first and second iterations.

The final Antalya pact – that was rejected – did, however, retain wording on deforestation agreed by countries in the global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai.

The same draft also “recognises” the role of nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches as “essential climate solutions” – although many experts reject the former term and warn that its vagueness leaves it open to deliberate misuse.

The final draft cover decision “emphasised the importance” of nature, forests, the ocean and other ecosystems as “natural infrastructure for resilience”, while “recogni[sing] that they play a critical role as sinks and reservoirs of greenhouse gases”.…

Why it is here: original reporting, detailed recipe

It’s no exaggeration to say that xawaash is at the heart of Somali cuisine. It is Somali history on a plate—a culinary reminder of Somalia’s centuries of global trade, particularly along the Indian Ocean. Xawaash is what makes many Somali dishes taste distinctly Somali. While every household’s xawaash recipe is its own, typically seven core spices—cumin, coriander, black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and turmeric—are toasted until their fragrance blooms, then blended into an earthy golden-brown powder. Xawaash stores very well and for a long time in an airtight container, though it’s at its peak shortly after it’s made. If you use it often, you can double or triple the recipe for a big batch.

Like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar. It has a hint of heat thanks to the black pepper and optional jalapeño. Suqaar is cooked covered to keep the meat juicy and moist. Serve with the flatbread of your choice (canjeero, muufo, or sabaayad) for a light lunch or over plenty of rice for a more filling dinner.

- Yield 4 servings

Xawaash (Somali Spice Mix)

Preparation

- Xawaash (Somali Spice Mix) Step 1 Toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp. green cardamom pods, and 1½ tsp. whole cloves in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly so the spices don’t burn. The spices are toasted when they have a slightly darker color and become fragrant, 1–2 minutes. Transfer the toasted spices to a blender or spice grinder and blend until they become a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and mix in ¼ cup (30 g) ground turmeric until it’s fully incorporated and the spice mix is golden brown. Allow to cool completely, then store in an airtight container.

- Suqaar Digaag Step 2 In a medium bowl, combine the juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp. xawaash, 1 tsp. fine sea salt, ½ tsp. paprika, and ⅛ tsp. ground black pepper. Add 1 lb. (450 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-sized pieces, and mix everything together to coat the chicken. Set aside. Step 3 In a large skillet over medium-high heat, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil until loose. Add 1 large yellow onion, halved and sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes, or until the onion is softened. Add 6 garlic cloves, minced, and 1 medium jalapeño, halved, and stir for another minute, then add the chicken in a single layer. Allow it to cook undisturbed for 5 minutes, then turn the pieces over and cook for 3 minutes more, until fully cooked through. Step 4 Add the remaining 1½ tsp. xawaash, ¾ cup (12 g) coarsely chopped cilantro leaves, 1 medium red bell pepper, sliced, and 1 medium yellow bell pepper, sliced, and stir to combine. Cover the skillet and turn the heat down to medium-low; cook until the peppers have softened, 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again: Every holiday table needs a salad. This one was dreamed up for Hanukkah, my family’s second-favorite special occasion after Thanksgiving. Serve it with roast chicken or salmon and you have an objectively perfect meal. It’s bright, crunchy, and decked out with little “latkes.” Potato croutons have popped up in a few places over the years, like The Salad Lab’s own Hanukkah-inspired salad (great minds!), Daniel Humm’s salmon rösti salad from Made Nice, and Ore-Ida’s cutely named CrouTots. My take is as lazy as it gets: frozen tater tots, smashed. The result is ultra-crisp, like the tiniest potato pancake in the world. A salad spinner is a godsend for washing the lettuce and herbs. Any type of apple works (I like Honeycrisp or Fuji) and the fresh horseradish on top is optional. But if you can find it, get it!

- Yield 4–6 servings

Preparation

- Step 1 Preheat oven to 425°. Mix together ½ cup sour cream, 3 Tbsp. drained prepared horseradish, 1 Tbsp. distilled white vinegar, a big pinch of kosher salt, and 1 tsp. water in a small bowl, adding more water a little at a time if needed until dressing it drizzle-able. Taste and season with more salt if needed. Step 2 Bake 1 lb. frozen tater tots on a large rimmed baking sheet for half the time of package directions (about 10 minutes). Step 3 Meanwhile, place 1 small white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, in a small bowl; pour in cold water to cover and add a few ice cubes. Set onions aside. Step 4 Tear pull apart leaves from 1 lb. romaine lettuce (about ⅔ head) and/or Little Gem lettuce (4–5 heads) and tear large leaves in half. Place in a large bowl. Remove tough stems from 1 bunch dill and 1 bunch parsley; discard. Coarsely tear remaining leaves and tender stems. Add to lettuce. Step 5 Remove tater tots from oven and, using oven mitts for safety, lay another baking sheet directly on top; firmly press down on tots to flatten. (If you don’t have a second baking sheet, use a heatproof measuring cup or mug instead.) Return tater tots to oven and bake until deep golden brown and crisp, 10–20 minutes.(If your oven has a convection setting, now is a great time to use it.) Step 6 Drain reserved onion and pat dry. Thinly slice 2 large apples (about 1 lb.). Add both to bowl with lettuce and herbs. Step 7 Drizzle 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and add a big pinch of flaky sea salt. Toss to combine, then mound salad on a platter. Evenly scatter tater tots and ¾ cup pomegranate seeds over. Step 8 Serve salad with remaining dressing for drizzling over and peeled fresh horseradish (if using) for grating over.

This Restaurant Chain Was Just Named America’s Favorite

This beloved American fast-food chain is known for its ButterBurgers and frozen custard. Can you guess?

Pop the cheese curds, Wisconsin! Forbes just released its first-ever America’s Favorite Restaurants list, and the No. 1 spot didn’t go to Chick-fil-A, McDonald’s or any coastal cult favorite (lookin’ at you, In-N-Out). It went to Culver’s.

To build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights company HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

A Wisconsin Favorite Takes the Crown

The Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

We’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

Culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the company is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

The Best of the Rest

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

The biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

item.title: We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, historical context

We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

What is the spout on a gravy boat for?

According to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

Moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He says that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

How to Use a Gravy Boat

For gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

This is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

And if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

The Inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards Highlight the Vagaries of Daily Life

From architecture to brooding skies to happenstance, the images of the finalists of the inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards highlight the humor, friction, and tenderness of everyday moments. The competition is presented by AUSSIE STREET, an organization founded by street photographers to showcase work from across the nation, which builds upon a series of festivals presented between 2018 and 2023.

Co-founder Sam Ferris says that the outfit’s mission is to not only exhibit great photos but to tap into the dispersed network of those who make them. “Street photography can be a pretty solitary obsession,” he says in a statement. “But there’s a whole community of people out there doing exactly the same thing. Getting them together, seeing the work printed, and hearing the stories behind the photographs is a reminder that we’re part of something much bigger than our individual pursuits.”

The awards opened with a show of 25 finalists at Studio 551 in Newtown, New South Wales, and AUSSIE STREET awarded the top prize to Adam Oxley. “One of the things I love about street photography is that you don’t need an enormous budget to make a remarkable image,” Ferris adds. “You need curiosity, patience, persistence and a way of seeing. Some of the most extraordinary photographs happen in completely ordinary places.”

See more on AUSSIE STREET’s Instagram, where you can keep an eye out for updates about the 2027 edition.

item.title: Thelma Golden To Step Down From Role as Director of Studio Museum in Harlem
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, significant career milestone

Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her position in late 2027, the museum announced Tuesday.

The announcement coincides with Golden’s 20th anniversary in the role, which she assumed in 2006, and comes just one year after the museum reopened in a new, purpose-built building after a seven-year closure. The new $125 million building was designed by architect David Adjaye and provides 82,000 square feet across seven floors, including a 139-seat public lobby, a rooftop terrace, education spaces, a library, and a cafe. It received rave reviews upon its reopening.

Kathryn C. Chenault, chair of the museum’s board of trustees, said in a statement that the board has formed a search committee to identify Golden’s successor and has retained an international executive search firm to assist. Golden will remain in her post until a replacement is hired.

While Golden’s departure was not entirely expected, it is not unusual for museum directors to exit their positions after a major renovation or expansion. Lisa Phillips announced in September 2025 that she would leave her role as director of the New Museum after its reopening, and Janne Sirén, director of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, said in April that he would step down following the museum’s 2023 expansion.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to new projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of Directors, Trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences, and beloved Harlem neighbors; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us. Together, they are an expansive community I cherish that will continue to inspire and enable the next leader of the Studio Museum.”

Before becoming director of the Studio Museum, Golden worked there as a curatorial fellow. She then joined the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1988 as a curatorial assistant and held several curatorial positions there, co-organizing the 1993 Whitney Biennial and organizing the landmark 1994 exhibition “Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art.” In 2000, she returned to the Studio Museum as deputy director for exhibitions and programs under then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. When Sims stepped down in 2005, Golden was named as her successor.

Golden has been credited with raising the profile of the Studio Museum through numerous groundbreaking exhibitions, including 2001’s “Freestyle”. Organized with curator Christine Y. Kim, the show featured 28 emerging Black artists whose work the curators described as “post-Black.” Among the artists championed in that show were Mark Bradford, Rashid Johnson, and Julie Mehretu.

In 2023, Golden won the Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, which carries a $250,000 award and recognizes a person who has made a significant contribution to the arts.

Speaking to ARTnews in 2020, Golden described what the Studio Museum meant to her and other young Black creatives:

[At the Studio Museum], they begin their careers and are able to not only get real professional experience but to form a mission and get a vision of real museum work. I say this as someone whose career is the result of those early experiences at the Studio Museum. It cannot be overstated how significant it was for me, as a 19-year-old art history/African-American studies double major from Smith College, to encounter Dr. Mary Schmidt Campbell, art historian and director of the Studio Museum. I can’t tell you what it meant for me, after over a decade as a curator at the Whitney, to become chief curator at the Studio Museum and to work for Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims, a pioneer in the museum field.

item.title: Military History Museum in Dresden Agrees to Return Contested Nazi-Era Family Archive to Jehovah’s Witnesses
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, historical significance

Five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the New York Times. Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history published by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau.

At the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website notes, given that her brothers lost their lives due to their pacifism.

The parties came to an “amicable agreement” on November 19, which was formalized the following day by the Higher Regional Court of Cologne. The museum and the Jehovah’s Witnesses agreed to keep the details of the settlement private. A Kusserow relative told the New York Times it is “a great relief that at last we will have these precious documents back where Annemarie always wanted them.”

After an inaugural edition last year, the Bukhara Biennial will return to Uzbekistan in 2027, this time with “The Long Welcome” as a theme (after 2025’s theme of “Recipes for Broken Hearts”). As announced this past summer, the artistic director for the next edition—slated to open September 3 and run through November 21—is Kulapat Yantrasast, the revered architect behind museum projects for institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Louvre, Harvard Art Museums, and the Art Institute of Chicago (as well as others while he worked for Tadao Ando).

“At a time when the world needs dialogue and understanding more than ever, culture can bring people together and open space for a shared future,” Bukhara Biennial commissioner Gayane Umerova said in a press release announcing the theme, which will be organized around four parts: Local Hospitality, Co-Creation, Resilience and Biodiversity, and Living Heritage. “For centuries, Bukhara welcomed travelers, craftspeople and merchants from across the world, and that openness shaped its identity. Through the biennial, we want to carry this legacy forward through contemporary art, so that it becomes part of life in the city, creates opportunities for its residents and leaves a lasting cultural legacy.”

Yantrasast added: “The Long Welcome celebrates the spirit of hospitality that made Bukhara worth crossing continents to reach, and worth returning to again and again. When people welcome you into their city, you want to give something back. My hope is that an artist who returns to Bukhara years from now will find that something they made with people here has become part of everyday life.”

Along with news of the theme, the Bukhara Biennial announced its first slate of artists to exhibit work in the city, which will also host the 19th Annual Conference of UNESCO Creative Cities next year. Below, see the artists enlisted.

item.title: Iraq’s Museums Are Finally Opening Their Doors Again
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, cultural significance

In 2022, Iraq’s National Museum in Baghdad reopened after being closed for three years following political unrest. Then in 2024, the museum closed again, this time for renovations. Now, it’s scheduled to open on December 1.

The Art Newspaper reported that the museum will open with several new galleries, such as the Abbasid and Islamic galleries. There will also be specially curated wings.

The museum will display artifacts including winged bulls (lamassu) and stone carvings depicting legendary Assyrian monarchs, ancient clay tablets and historical prisms recording legal codes, calligraphic friezes, stone carvings, glassworks, and mosaics that have been recovered and restored. According to the newspaper Iraqi News, the museum’s doors are opening to domestic visitors, international tourists, and researchers from around the world.

The reopening of the museum has been a long time coming. In 2003, the National Museum was the subject of looting during the US-led invasion. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has said that reopening the museum in December, rather than January 2027, is a priority, and that he also has plans for “a new building that befits the historical and civilizational value of Iraq.”

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum, told the Art Newspaper that the reopening of the museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism.”

As Iraq rebuilds itself after years of political unrest, the museums’ opening is a big step for the country’s cultural sector.

The Abbasid Palace in Baghdad opened its doors on November 15, and Iraq’s first Jewish museum, the Shamash Museum, opened its doors on October 22. Many of Iraq’s museums are also close to its large-scale monuments that are part of the city’s charm, such as the Al-Shaheed Monument designed by Iraqi sculptor Ismail Fatah al-Turk, the Monument to the Unknown Soldier designed by Khaled al-Rahal and Marcello D’Olivo, and the Saving Iraqi Culture Monument designed by Mohammed Ghani Hikmat.

The EVA International biennial in Limerick, Ireland, will celebrate its 50th anniversary next year. Running from August 27 to October 27, it will be titled “Forms of Inheritance.”

The biennial also announced that Matt Packer will step down after 10 years as director in spring 2028.

EVA’s organizers said in a release that the upcoming theme will question “the values between the past and the future” during a time when “promises carried forward from the late twentieth century—integration, openness and shared progress—can no longer be taken as given.” The works on view will pull from EVA International’s history with a series of new artist commissions, as well as other commissions that focus on the wider historical narratives between Ireland and Europe.

The new works at the biennale will include a work by Lisa Freeman in response to Minerva Cuevas’s Story of the Celtic Tiger, which was made for the 2006 EVA International in 2006. Dina Mimi will exhibit a work that follows the cross-generational solidarity between Irish Republican and Palestinian prisoners, while Sam Keogh’s large-scale “cartoons” installation will be based on the The Hunt of the Unicorn tapestry. To mark the biennial’s semicentennial, the 2027 program will host events and publications such as “Still (the) Barbarians?” a publication of testimonies and critical reflections of the 2016 EVA International, which will be published in early 2027 with the John Hansard Gallery.

The biennial will also change the curatorial organization of its main exhibition in which a guest curator takes on the task. Instead, local curatorial partners will collaborate on the exhibition as a way to recognize “community of curatorial practice that sustains contemporary art in the region,” per a release. Askeaton Contemporary Arts, STARLING, Ormston House, and Féile na Gréine will develop the program together. Participating artists and venues will be announced next spring.

item.title: Dora Maar’s Paris Apartment Is For Sale, Picasso Wall Drawings and All
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, historical context

In this quiet, 17th-century Parisian apartment on rue de Savoie in the 6th arrondissement, strange-looking insects appear to be climbing up the middle of the living room wall near the chimney. But these 15 or so critters—spiders, ants, and cockroaches—are actually drawn and carefully protected by glass coverings.

That’s because they were made by none other than Pablo Picasso, once a regular visitor to this home, where his lover, the artist Dora Maar, lived from 1946 until she died in 1997. The abode, along with the Picasso drawings on the wall, is now for sale, listed for the lump sum of €2.85 million (about $3.1 million), reports Le Parisien. How’s that for a dinner party icebreaker?

Picasso used to call Maar “ma puce,” which literally means “my flea” and is used as an endearing term in French for “my sweetheart.” It is believed Picasso’s drawings were a playful pun on his nickname for Maar, per the apartment’s current owner, identified only as Ida. “They give it a history,” she added.

All the wall artworks have been officially recognized by the Picasso Administration, which manages the artist’s estate, and oversees a committee that catalogs his works.

Many may know Maar (1907–97) as the famous figure Picasso depicted in many paintings over the course of their seven-year relationship, including his “Weeping Woman” series, and another portrait of her from 1943 that sold for $37 million in 2025, quadrupling its estimate. Yet Maar herself has been belatedly recognized for her own paintings and photographs that contributed to the Surrealist movement’s heyday in Paris from the 1920s to the 1940s.

The 1,600-square-foot apartment’s well-lit rooms, large windows, and high ceilings do fit an artistic sensibility, said the owner. With two bedrooms, an office, kitchen, and the famous Picasso-drawn living room, the Maar’s former home also boasts 13th-century petrified wooden beams from a former mansion that was converted into the apartment building.

Future owners of Maar’s apartment will also be able to hop over to the Louvre and the Centre Pompidou, right across the Seine River. Then again, if the urge to see art by a modern master strikes them, they won’t even need to leave their living room.

item.title: Studio Gang completes women's leadership campus in Wisconsin
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: demonstrates original reporting and clear, well-structured English

Studio Gang completes women’s leadership campus in Wisconsin

Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women’s conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site’s oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex issues within their industries”.

“Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” said the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. “I wanted to build one that was.”

Studio Gang said key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

“We designed the Women’s Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive,” said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

“Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings’ carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site’s ecology and enhance its biodiversity.”

The campus contains three main buildings — the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.

White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to “reflect the tones and textures of the forest”, according to the studio.

The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.

A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

It also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building’s green roof contains a “coffee nook” and patios for seating.

Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.

Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.

Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.

Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate New York and a Denver hotel.

Photography courtesy Studio Gang
