item.title: Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: high learning value with original reporting and clear explanation

Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will “help shape the next chapter of African architecture”.

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a “linear prescription of urbanisation”.

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is currently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would “preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account,” Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

“The committee at MIT was a bit shocked, because they weren’t used to the idea of a thesis project existing in the real world,” Kpodo told Dezeen. “But I still thought of it as almost as a sort of sketch, just at 1:1 scale.”

“Doing that gives you something to test – people are going to interface with it; you can test out its failures and success very quickly.”

Growing up in Kumasi, Kpodo initially focused on visual art in school before pursuing a course in architecture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), and subsequently MIT.

At KNUST he was quickly exposed to narratives around both architectural success and Ghana’s own architectural history that left him seeking something more “homegrown”.

“We had a lecture from Francis Kéré in which he spoke about his Serpentine Pavilion, and how taking on commissions from big institutions or big clients can become critical for defining your practice,” said Kpodo.

I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come?

“At the time, I couldn’t imagine any of these commissions coming to those of us working in the South. I couldn’t see any architects who were operating on that scale, or even at a kind of global scale,” he continued.

“It almost had the opposite effect on me. I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come? I think it’s by being local that I can have something to offer to the world.”

Kpodo became interested in local architectural archives, initially those of the KNUST Development Office, but also the less formalised collections of images and drawings that he encountered online.

He soon helped establish Postbox Ghana, a research collective initiated by artist Manuela Nebuloni to create an alternative architectural archive using postcards and stamps from the 1950s to the 1980s, which often depicted examples of Tropical Modernism and state infrastructure constructed following Ghana’s independence.

However, Kpodo still felt that these archival materials did not speak to his own understanding of Ghanaian architecture, having grown up in a “not-so-well-to-do context” in Kumasi and only really encountering modernist architecture when first entering the KNUST campus.

“The whole archive that I was exposed to, whether it was in the Development Office or in the postcards, had a huge, significant gap in it,” he said. “I remember stories my dad would tell me about building practices and cultures that just didn’t make it into this archive or our training in architecture school.”

“As a newly independent country, Ghana wanted to break away from any kind of ethnographic notion of what the ‘Gold Coast’ – to use its colonial name – was. So those ‘traditional’ buildings and other forms of practices did not make it into the framework of thinking about what our future meant,” he continued.

“But even though these buildings are far removed from the city centres and from the archive, they were foundational in the sense that they enabled the cocoa industry, and brought in the money that built the institutions and structures that are enshrined in postcards.”

Kpodo began to photograph these vernacular buildings himself, many of them farm structures made using laterite, a type of local red earth that is formed into air and sun-dried blocks for construction

When I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’

Upon finding many of these buildings slated for demolition, Kpodo has more recently begun to purchase them, before carefully deconstructing their laterite structures to become the raw material for new structures on his land.

The idea was initially met locally with some confusion. “I remember one man said, ‘oh, are you going to extract gold from the walls?’ because laterite can contain gold,” he recalled.

“But when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’ And then some kids would even begin making their own proposals. For me, just creating that imagination is worth it.”…

item.title: "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique design concept with clear explanation and learning value

“Intensely physical patterns” cloak Gerhard Richter’s self-designed gallery in Doha

Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” said Richter.

“The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.

“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she said.

“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.

“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”

Inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that “what matters is I know why we did things”.

Photography by Iwan Baan

item.title: Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: freshness and diversity in design week coverage

Dezeen reports from New York’s new November design week

A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen’s US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

While BDNY and high-end showcase Salon Art + Design have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers Ross Lovegrove, Karim Rashid and Rem D Koolhaas for a talk moderated by New York-based design writer Camille Okhio.

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows.

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.

This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

Among these was the Brussels-founded design fair Collectible. For its third New York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a defunct movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities related to WSA.

While the unfinished theatre fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, chaotic, with one worker being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head.

Collectible called it an “isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor’s equipment”.

“The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously,” a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.

“Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately.”

Despite some chaos, including recently laid cement, there were strong showings. Philadelphia-based Dudd Haus showed a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by Jordan Maurice and a paravent made with telephone cords by Overt Cove.

Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by Upstate New York gallery Freaks, and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by Iitem studio.

The fair’s scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators Alex Tieghi-Walker and Lynette Nylander designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki for Objekt Gallery and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by Small Things Studio for Salon 21.

At Collectible, Montreal design collective Ensemble showcased its members’ work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

This was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to Yabu Pushelberg’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including new lamps by Zebulon Perron, sculptural glass lamps by Alex Joncas, metal works by Jérémy Paguet, leather lamps by Jeta Studio and brass-lined mirrors by Jeremy Le Chatelier.

It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.

At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based Zarolat’s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and Polybion, while New York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, Bossa Furniture, showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

BDNY was, as usual, where most of the actual commerce took place during the week. While the interior designers and architects descended on the sample-forward showing, a few brands showed stand-out collections, including Sancal’s showing of Júlia Esqué’s playfully fringed armchairs and Santa & Cole’s modern, fun lighting.

Later in the week, LA-based Basic Space, run by the organisers behind Design Miami, returned to SoHo. With artistic direction by Alexander May, the stark, white-cube approach differed from the in-situ, multi-room afair that characterised the first New York Basic Space in 2025.

The fair featured a focus on big names and multiple co-curators competing for attention on the promotional materials and in the execution.

Standout pieces included the live-edge wood furniture with small metal connective elements by Brooklyn-based designer Gregory Beson, as well as Daniel Swarilov’s metal credenzas, in a section curated by Marquel Williams.

Paris-based Harry Nuriev created a metallic take on first-class airline seats as a standalone installation. Another booth featured an oversized sofa by NFL player Stefon Diggs’ luxury furniture brand Si Vis Pacem, illustrating the fair’s mix of design with celebrity culture.

Finally, Mexico City-based creative studio Fábrica, run by artist Darryl Richardson and partner Maryah Ananda, held its La Sala showcase in a loft near Penn Station.…

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: demonstrates studio ethos with clear explanation and learning value

Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa

This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

“We believe it is important not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.

“Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I quickly lose interest when things are planned in advance.”

“That said, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work,” added Escobedo.

“We try to approach them with a sense of joy.”

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

“It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point…” said Escobedo.

“More seriously, I’d love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople.”

“I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially those that have little place in architectural history and attract few expectations,” added Kuma. “Designing a toilet pavilion for the Expo, a building type that nobody expects to become architecture, is one example.”

Along with the variety in projects, both architects agreed that the wide range of daily activities is what they most enjoy about being an architect.

“The variety, the diversity,” said Escobedo, when asked about her favourite part about being an architect.

“One day you’re on a construction site with incredible Japanese carpenters, the next you’re discussing a detail with your favourite thermal engineer, the following week you’re taking part in a conversation with colleagues you admire, before finding yourself struggling to install the plumbing and tiles in a shower because you had the brilliant idea of taking on a self-build project.”

Kuma also added that he enjoys the intensity of working on site.

“The construction site,” he said. “Nothing is more stressful or demanding, with all the struggles involving people and money. Yet every time I see a building taking shape, I feel glad I chose architecture. There is something addictive about it.”

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa, as described by the duo:

Nakano House, Tokyo, Japan, 2026

“The client’s childhood home, a traditional Japanese house, has an engawa gallery open to the garden. The new residence occupies the top two floors of a building owned by the client. She, along with her two sons and their families, will move into three apartments located on the sixth and seventh floors.

“At the centre of each apartment, we inserted a hut-like volume that gathers the quieter rooms: a small living room and the bedrooms. In the space carved out around it emerges an intermediate zone – an engawa that serves both as a place to stay and as a passage.

“Balcony, engawa, and hut thus form three spatial layers that resonate with the childhood home. The structure consists of Y-shaped modules made of lightweight steel sections and bracing cables, typically used in shelving systems.

“These modules are arranged two by two in mirrored pairs along a regular grid, with occasional inversions. From these new dwellings, one can look down across the street at the engawa of the childhood home. This project does not seek to nostalgically replicate that memory-laden place, but rather to build a new home nourished by the memories of the old one.”

One Water, Osaka, Japan, 2025

“One water is a bathing and rest pavilion for the Osaka World Expo 2025. Toilets are at first glance a pragmatic facility, dedicated to human physiology. But they are also intimately linked to contemporary issues such as the use of natural resources and gender.

“One water uses the path of rainfall on the accessible roof and its subsequent accumulation to create encounters between water and the public, and contribute to the supply of the toilets.

“The design of the pavilion allows for the reuse of materials and structural components, and makes no gender distinction in the toilets, because, after all, ‘we are all fish in one water’.”

House by the temple, Saitama Prefecture, Japan, 2024

“The house is opposite the entrance of a temple that is surrounded by a park of ancient trees and a wall, as if it belongs to another world. Reflecting this closed composition, we designed the house as an everyday world for a family.

“The main building is located at the back of the plot and has a quarter-circle plan to reduce its own shadow. The street facade is a single-storey hut, which creates a continuity between the open space of the park and the garden of the house.

“On the ground floor, the park is the backdrop to the house. On the first floor, each room offers distant views of the temple, like an observatory.”

Yamada House, Fukuoka, Japan, 2020

“A daily public space in a residential area. We create a plaza in a small residential area where human life is still at human scale.

“The house is like the background that forms the square. The composition consists of various couples: the smooth black mortar of the outer wall and the rough crushed black basalt ground, the emerald entrance hut and the crape myrtle tree with white flowers, the interior spaces and the outside square.”

Water Flower Courtyard, Montpellier, France, 2019…

item.title: London Museum brings "back a bit of London's heritage" with Smithfield Market opening
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and clear explanation of heritage project

London Museum brings “back a bit of London’s heritage” with Smithfield Market opening

Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.

According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum’s relocation from the Barbican Estate’s former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market, which is expected to open in 2028.

“There’s an opportunity to represent London as it is now and in the future, and really take city museums to another level,” said London Museum’s New Museum Project director Alec Shaw.

“We’re bringing back a bit of London’s heritage – one building that has not been seen or encountered for at least 30 years, and the other one an amazing architectural gem that hasn’t been fully appreciated and will now be,” he told Dezeen.

The main entrance to the London Museum is marked by a covered street, West Poultry Avenue, which doubles as the Real Time gallery that stretches between the General Market and Poultry Market.

Entering the transformed Victorian market, visitors pass a museum shop and an auditorium before entering Our Time – an expansive gallery illuminated from above by an oculus.

Shops that once wrapped the perimeter of the market trading floor were removed to open up the space, but the restoration was designed to retain hints of the building fabric’s history.

“You can see pockets in the brickwork walls where joists of the first floor and little plaster columns were originally located,” said Julian Harrap Architects partner Lyall Thow.

“There was a second floor, represented by a darkened band where we didn’t overly clean the brickwork, and fireplaces in the upper offices were taken out, restored, and put back where they would have been originally.”

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects overhauled 42 individual shops that formerly encircled the General Market into 12 multi-storey units.

Six units were kept to contain a restaurant, galleries and learning spaces, while the other six were left for the museum to invite partner institutions to occupy.

“What the ‘museum of tomorrow’ will be is not just a single institute, but a coral reef of small institutes that can plug in – Dezeen could have an office here, a leather upholsterer might have a craft workshop here, restaurants and pop-ups…” said Khan.

“This living ecosystem, which is reflective of the city, is possible because of this market building we’ve moved into,” he continued.

“What we’ve done is make openings, windows, and cuts through the floor and ceiling, which allow that energy to emanate out of the city and for the city’s energy to emanate inwards,” added Khan. “At the centre of it all is this enormous public space, the General Market ground floor, where anything can happen.”

A staircase takes visitors down to London’s Roman street level, to the museum’s permanent Past Time exhibition, which displays precious artefacts.

The restored brickwork walls in the subterranean space are interrupted by a six-metre window, revealing passing Thameslink trains.

A series of underground vaults that were discovered during the museum’s construction will open to visitors in spring 2027.

“This museum epitomises the idea of the primordial reflex in us to dig to find various treasures,” said Stanton Williams co-founder Paul Williams.

The architects aimed to make the qualities of the existing spaces work to the museum’s advantage, displaying delicate objects in the underground gallery and maintaining the communal feel of the market space on ground level.

“Decisions based on the building – like precious objects should be kept underground because it’s got a greater thermal inertia – loosen the straitjacket around the museum having to act like a museum in other spaces,” said Khan.

“It means some other spaces can be more market-like and have a more public-facing potential that a normal museum wouldn’t be able to do,” he continued. “The building has enabled the museum to become a different kind of museum.”

Unisex toilets were designed in a Victorian style, with decorative tiles depicting wildflowers that grew in London’s bombed-out sites.

Elsewhere in the museum is a 24-hour cafe where original interior tiles and a timber staircase were restored.

Shaw hopes the London Museum will be an inviting place that residents and tourists want to return to time and again.

“We want to be super welcoming – we don’t want to be intimidating as a museum,” said Shaw. “Some of the other museums are quite imposing buildings.”

“We want to be a destination, not just a museum, but a place for people to keep coming back to.”

Other museums recently completed in London include V&A East by O’Donnell + Tuomey and the V&A East Storehouse by Diller Scofidio + Renfro, which was given a Dezeen Award for its wayfinding design.

Photography by Hufton + Crow

item.title: Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique design concept with clear explanation and learning value

Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry

Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

“This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee said. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.

“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee said of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.

Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

Photography courtesy of Burberry

item.title: Raúl Sánchez Architects transforms laundry into light-filled Barcelona home
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and clear explanation of architectural transformation

Raúl Sánchez Architects transforms laundry into light-filled Barcelona home

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.

Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for new solutions to add more light.

“Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight,” studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a “modern translation of the old wells” that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house’s upper level.

The 40-square-metre lower level houses an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area, a bathroom and a small study.

This can be partitioned off from the living space using folding doors made from wood and rice paper, inspired by the clients’ time living in Japan.

In the kitchen, Sánchez said he added a mirror-clad island to “introduce a sense of fragility without disrupting the open feel of the space”.

The upper level, meanwhile, houses the home’s bedrooms and a bathroom. The two floors are connected by the Klein-blue lightwell, which has oculi on all four sides to help distribute the illumination from its skylight throughout the space.

Sánchez wanted to “bring that picturesque atmosphere of Aiguafreda Street into the house, making it part of its surroundings by reclaiming that well – now translated into a lightwell that also helps regulate the home’s temperature.”

This was one of many tailor-made solutions to turn the former laundry house into a home.

“There were many challenges, both technical – access to the mezzanine level, the new staircase, the structural reinforcements – and functional, like fitting the program into just 80 square metres,” Sánchez said.

His studio also worked with materials that would complement the existing ones, using terracotta tiles on the ground floor to extend the traditional exterior clay paving and adding colored glazed tiles to the washbasins and bathroom walls.

“Ultimately, the goal is always to create a cohesive, overarching project that addresses all these challenges and offers something extra – something almost hard to put into words, but that translates into simply feeling good in the space,” Sánchez concluded.

Rául Sánchez Architects is currently working on the final phase of the project, the design of its orchard and garden, which will begin at the start of 2027.

The studio also recently designed a concrete home with a sunken courtyard in Cala Tamarit.

Project credits:

Architecture team: Nerea Moya, Marta Gámiz, Flavia

Structure consultant: Diagonal Estructuras

Engineering consultant: Mares Engyniers

Photography by José Hevia

item.title: Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).

In 2027, Australian author Helen Garner will be feted with the Hadada, a prize that recognizes a writer’s lifelong literary contributions. I am here as an independent body to hype this choice.

Garner—a novelist, journalist, and diarist—writes big-hearted heroines who are often on the edge of a crisis. Her other fans include Lauren Groff, Lily King, Rumaan Alam, and Ben Lerner, but we are legion. Why, you ask?

In a recent piece for The Guardian, Emma Brockes also praised Garner’s “ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth.” And it’s true—that earthiness is what makes her work indelible. But it’s also just the tip of an iceberg.

Here are three of Garner’s best known books (and why you should make like the Parisians and pick them up, stat).

Monkey Grip, Garner’s 1977 debut, sent a shockwave through Australia. This novel chronicles a woman’s doomed-from-the-jump situationship with a heroin addict who charms her intermittently as they orbit a communal living situation.

A little like Susie Boyt’s sleeper hit, Loved and Missed, this book beautifully captures the recurring heartbreak involved in loving an addict. But it’s never saccharine, or sanctimonious.

Following a bohemian Melbourne milieu that echoes the author’s own set at the time, Garner’s non-judgmental portrait of freewheeling radicals brought out the moralizers on publication. Nora, our heroine, ruffled feathers for depicting ambivalent parenthood administered with a very loose latchkey. All adults in this book are libidinally motivated. Drugs and sex are world-structuring forces.

But what’s most exciting is how naked the prose is about all of that want. In Garner’s matter-of-fact voice, Nora’s thirst for the grifting Javo is rendered tender, abject, holy, and pathetic by turns. She feels like a real and vulnerable person with a mighty human flaw. The best kind of protagonist.

My favorite of Garner’s novels is The Children’s Bach. Another tale of domestic upheaval ignited by a charismatic chaos agent, this book traces the happily partnered Athena Fox’s infatuation with a blast from the past. Against reason, she leaves her partner and two small children for… a rock star.

What follows is a little predictable, but as with Monkey Grip the pleasure is in experiencing that slow road to ruin. (Or is it ecstasy?)

The third person POV serves this book, which manages to texturize everyone affected by Athena’s choices. She feels like a modern Nora, in the Ibsen sense.

The Spare Room is a cool, slim, spiky book. I find this Garner still gnaws at me. Following two semi-estranged old friends who fall back together when one seeks harbor following a terminal diagnosis, this novel depicts the unpleasant side of caretaking and the indignity of illness.

This book asks some truly itchy questions. Such as, what do you do when your patient is delusional—and/or, you want them out of your house?

As in the other novels, our protagonist chafes against conventionality and obligatory mutual obligation. And her extreme honesty hits you like a glass of cold water. As always, there’s a nakedness to a Garner subject. She doesn’t flinch from depicting those ugly emotions or unwanted thoughts.

In a review for the Times, Daphne Merkin once compared Garner to other “laconic and wayward,” ladies who specialize in the “art of artlessness, like Jean Rhys, Jane Bowles and Paula Fox.”

I agree with wayward, but I think that artful eye is in a class all its own. Do yourself a favor and join the Helen hive. Today.

Source: Literary Hub | Published: 2026-11-24 20:53 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Filmmaker Ava DuVernay challenges the stories America tells about itself in '14th'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Filmmaker Ava DuVernay challenges the stories America tells about itself in '14th'

A decade after examining the 13th Amendment and its connection to mass incarceration, DuVernay has a new documentary about the 14th Amendment and the struggle over citizenship and equal rights.

TONYA MOSLEY, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Tonya Mosley. Who gets to belong in America? It's a question the country confronted after the Civil War when some 4 million enslaved people gained their freedom. In 1868, the 14th Amendment established birthright citizenship and guaranteed due process and equal protection under the law. But those promises were contested almost from the beginning.

In her new documentary, "14th," my guest today, filmmaker Ava DuVernay, traces the struggle over these rights from the extraordinary possibilities of Reconstruction and the backlash that followed to the present-day battles over citizenship, equality and presidential power.

DuVernay has built a body of work that challenges the stories America tells about itself, often connecting personal experiences to larger questions of race, history and power. Her films include "Selma," about the Civil Rights Movement, "Origin," an exploration of caste, and the Oscar-nominated documentary "13th" about race and mass incarceration. She also created the acclaimed television dramas "When They See Us" about the wrongful convictions of the Central Park Five and "Queen Sugar" about a Black family in Louisiana. DuVernay began making "14th" during Donald Trump's campaign for a second term and has said making the documentary became a way to channel her own fear and anger about the direction of this country.

Ava DuVernay, welcome back to Fresh Air.

AVA DUVERNAY: Thank you. It's always so wonderful to sit with you, although somewhat intimidating because you have the best voice on radio. So my kind of scratchy voice here is no comparison, but I'll do my best to keep up.

MOSLEY: Oh, I appreciate it...

DUVERNAY: (Laughter).

MOSLEY: ...So much. Thank you for the compliment.

DUVERNAY: It's true.

MOSLEY: But, you know, starting - I mean, knowing that you started this to channel your fear and anxiety, I'm just wondering how you're feeling now post-midterms.

DUVERNAY: Gosh. Well, it's pretty recent. And I feel good about the information and ideas that we're sharing in "14th." I'm hopeful that by people watching the film and interacting with the film, challenging the film, thinking about the film and what's in it, that there'll be some guidance from history on how to move forward. But without some kind of grounding and common language, a common vocabulary and understanding as to where we are now, I fear that this moment will slip away.

And I feel like we're in a time of celebration. But, you know, the vote should just be the beginning. And a big part of what we talk about in "14th" is the fact that we've been trained not to do anything much in between the votes as citizens. And this is really what we all need to look at and step up to right now.

MOSLEY: One of your subjects calls the 14th Amendment the workhorse of the Constitution. Can you say more about that? Why? What would Americans lose without it?

DUVERNAY: Well, I love this part of the documentary because we have a montage of all of our different experts - over 50 historians, scholars, politicians, even a contractor, librarians, podcasters - talking about the 14th Amendment and how to describe it in one line. Stacey Abrams calls it the everything bagel. And it is so much of what we hold dear as Americans.

First, I am an American because I was born here or because I am naturalized, right? That's just a base-level understanding. The next is, I am equal to the person next to me because I am American. These are just basic tenets. These are the things that we believe as Americans, that we abide by, right? The next is, I am protected by my citizenship, right? If I am arrested, am I - if I am accused of something, there is a process that is due to me - is a way to think about that, right? That we have certain rights in our voting mechanisms, that we can depend on Congress to advocate for us.

These are just some key facts of our citizenship that most people consider to be a given. But it's not a given because it's at risk. And not only is it at risk. It's under direct attack. And that's what the film steps through piece by piece, to show how this has really been a sinister strategy that's been unfolding on many levels - political, economic, social, cultural. And it's raging at a even higher level and a more expedited velocity than it ever has been.

MOSLEY: Experts in the film call the 14th Amendment a constitutional reset after the Civil War because they needed something that makes sure that equality was embedded into the law of the land. Can you lay out exactly what that means?

DUVERNAY: Yes. I mean, the Constitution before the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendment didn't have the word equal in it as it related to human beings.

MOSLEY: Right.

DUVERNAY: Before the Reconstruction Amendments, as they're known, Black people were considered three-fifths of a human being.

MOSLEY: Yeah.

DUVERNAY: And the catalyst for the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendment were the rights of African American people after the Civil War. These 4 million people had to be dealt with. So 13th said they are no longer property.

MOSLEY: Yeah.

DUVERNAY: OK? They are full human beings. They're not three-fifths of a human being anymore. 14th Amendment said, OK. Oh. Saying that they're free weren't - wasn't enough. They are citizens. OK, everybody? OK. We're going to come back on the 15th. They can vote. OK? Let's just keep getting more and more clear. So this was all around the impetus for the rights that so many people enjoy, right? The rights that have been gained because of the 14th Amendment for women, for Asian Americans, for, you know, people with disabilities, for children.…

Source: NPR Culture | Published: 2026-11-24 15:44 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Here’s the shortlist for the first-ever Children’s Booker Prize.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Here’s the shortlist for the first-ever Children’s Booker Prize.

Today, the Booker Prize Foundation announced the “Great Eight” shortlist of titles for inaugural Children’s Booker Prize, which will be awarded annually beginning in 2027. The Children’s Booker is the latest off-shoot of the prestigious Booker Prize (most recently awarded to M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything) and celebrates fiction for eight- to 12-year-olds, written in or translated into English and published in the UK or Ireland. The winner will take home £50,000 and the Booker Foundation will be donating at least 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books to children across the United Kingdom and Ireland.

“Any of these books stands comparison with any adult book, whatever the category, on its own terms,” said Frank Cottrell-Boyce, Chair of the Children’s Booker Prize 2027 judges, in the shortlist announcement. He, along with fellow judges Sanchita Basu De Sarkar and Lolly Adefope, narrowed down the shortlist from 89 submissions and will be joined for the final decision by four young people: Ibrahim (12), Lainey (12), Luna (8), and Myla (11).

Here’s the shortlist:

Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts, The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen

Catherine Bruton, Tadpole Summer

Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano, War

Iqbal Hussain, The Night I Borrowed Time

Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, The Teller of Tall Tales

Mikey Please, The Rambler’s Curse

Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor, Séamus Almost Famous

Shaun Tan, Hometown

The winner will be announced in a ceremony on February 2, 2027.

Drew Broussard

Drew Broussard is the bookstores editor-at-large for Literary Hub and the host of The Lit Hub Podcast. His writing has appeared around the internet and in friends' mailboxes. After a decade working at The Public Theater, he decamped to the woods of upstate New York, where he now lives. He is the manager of Rough Draft Bar & Books in Kingston, NY.

In 'GTA VI,' every stolen car is a music discovery machine

Each time a 'Grand Theft Auto VI' player enters a new vehicle, the in-game radio opens a rabbit hole for curious listeners

If you've ever wondered what it might feel like to lead cops on a high-speed chase through downtown Miami as Young Thug croons, "Hustlers don't stop, they keep going," Grand Theft Auto VI has you covered. The massive open-world action game, which turns a one-to-one recreation of Florida's central hotspot — dubbed Vice City, Leonida — into the playpen for a Bonnie and Clyde-style outlaw campaign, is largely powered by music. There are currently more than 800 songs in the game, all of which have been spun off into bespoke radio stations representing the vibrant music culture of the place it simulates. Early into my playthrough, Kevin Lyttle's 2003 soca hit "Turn Me On" blared out of a speedboat's onboard radio as I pulled up to a yacht party, creating a unique thrill as the familiar suddenly became new again.

The most anticipated video game sequel of all time, and now among the most successful entertainment properties ever, GTA VI follows military vet Jason Duval and new parolee Lucia Caminos as they repair their broken relationship, cutting their teeth in a high-stakes criminal megalopolis with hopes of regaining custody of their son. Players split time between the two characters, playing linear missions that advance the story, triggering side quests that spiral into all corners of a vast map, or testing the limits of the open world by doing, well, whatever they want. Where similar games allow the user to "fast travel," or teleport, to important areas, GTA values the scenic route, the atmosphere that linear travel creates. And since hijacking rides is a core mechanic, that atmosphere is always changing: Each time you pull the door shut on a new exotic whip, helicopter or airboat, that vehicle's radio kicks on one of more than 20 stations spanning pop, rock, hip-hop, jazz, dance and classical. As reggaeton artist Rauw Alejandro noted of his playing experience in an interview with Billboard, "Sometimes, I wasn't even doing the missions — I was just vibing, discovering new things, listening to the music on the radio."

The need to spend lots of time driving around in cars makes the user a captive audience, and as such, the radio is a pipeline — to old songs, newer songs, new-to-you songs and even a few new-to-everyone songs. A previously unreleased D'Angelo track can be found on the Gilles Peterson-hosted station Worldwide FM. When Jason picks Lucia up from prison, "Crazy for You," a new song by Lana Del Rey, plays as they start their desperado journey together. Premieres from Burna Boy, Kali Uchis & Helado Negro, Zara Larsson and Cardi B are scattered across the stations. Beyond the exclusives, one of which pairs SZA with King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, are relatively recent songs given new life by the narrative. Two versions of Carly Rae Jepsen's cult classic "Run Away with Me" soundtrack key scenes in the early game, a jet ski excursion turned supercar race to the nightclub NINE1NINE — and when Jason and Lucia get there, Tove Lo and SG Lewis' dance sleeper "Heat" is blaring. Deeper in are songs that will be familiar to many but are transformed by context. The couple's first string of robberies together has a sync so perfect I dare not spoil it.

The gameplay of GTA VI opens the door to a unique kind of sonic immersion, one that straddles classic radio functionality and the unique surreality that only video game storytelling allows. On one hand, the radio experience exposes players to a distinctly old-world curation on a scale that maybe isn't possible anywhere else, given the size of the player base. On the other, it treats most in-game playback like needle drops in a movie: highly subjective, there to make the player feel as much as possible like the star.

There are just enough songs that each playthrough will be slightly different for every player, but the sensations are comparable. When I went to dump a car that belonged to Jason's co-worker Donnie, a volatile, coke-addled drug mule fed to pigs by rival swamp gang the Kingfishers, the V-Rock station was blasting "Nothin' but a Good Time" by Poison, which felt like high irony. Donnie was a screw-up whose incompetence led directly to his demise, and as I sank his red '85 Blista in the marsh, the song's cries in pursuit of a more exciting life rang out like an unlikely funeral dirge. Echoing the game's broader attention to detail, the radio serves as an entry point into the inner lives of the characters who populate its world, and a window into its broader attempt to render a dynamic culture.

Of course, at least some of the charm is that these are, overtly, not real radio stations, and that the surrounding culture is a trick mirror. The hosts are often celebrities of distinct pedigree playing off their public perceptions — "Weird Al" Yankovic and Brigitte Nielsen, Robyn and model Alex Consani, Buddy Guy and Keith Richards, Bad Bunny and RaiNao. The ads that pop up between songs are absurd and satirical. In a talk-radio segment, the Brazilian singer Anitta plays "Dr. Nita," a quack giving sex advice. The hold the radio exerts on you as a player is tied up in the game's blown-out otherworldliness.…

Eighty-one-year-old Bob Windrem spent half his life at NBC News. As a senior investigative producer, he drew on CIA sources to feed Tom Brokaw early info on the September 11 terrorist attacks. He filed stories about the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and cartel violence in Mexico, and went undercover in Johannesburg to help reveal Israel’s role in South Africa’s missile development program. Today, he’s perhaps best known as “Net Income,” the name under which he’s chronicled the Brooklyn Nets for more than two decades. James Herbert’s profile is an entertaining look at the journalistic chops of an octogenarian NBA blogger who kept his hard-news edge, and the most interesting guy lurking just outside the locker room.

Before he’d written a word for NetsDaily, Windrem was the main character on the NJ.com forum. Many posters hated how he defended the front office’s decision to let Kenyon Martin walk in 2004. The personal attacks he receives now can be a bit much, but Windrem either throws a jab back or rolls his eyes. “I’m a big boy. I’ve been yelled at by members of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard and the White House press secretary and TV anchors,” he said. He can handle a few mean tweets.

PEN Writes US Emerges as Free Speech Group “For Writers, by Writers”

Big names in literature are attached to an aspiring PEN Center that launched this week. Omar El Akkad, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Carmen Maria Machado, Sarah McNally, and Percival Everett are among the heavyweights listed as founding members of PEN Writes Us. More than 100 writers, artists, translators, and more are attached to the free speech group.

Pulitzer Prize-winning author and founding member M. Gessen said in a press release announcing the launch:

“I have watched, in more than one country, how the space for speech closes: not all at once, but one exception at a time – one category of speech declared too dangerous, one publisher persuaded to stay quiet. A PEN center’s job is to refuse the exceptions. The United States needs a center that will defend protected speech without carve-outs for whatever is politically inconvenient this year.”

A former PEN America president is among the founding members. Author Dinaw Mengestu resigned as president after the organization released a report about cultural boycotts and the “rising isolation and exclusion” of Israeli and Jewish writers.

PEN Writes US is “dedicated to defending free expression, supporting writers and artists at risk, and championing reading, translation and literature.” The group will seek to join more than 140 PEN centers at the PEN International Congress in September 2027.

item.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition, and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?

The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.

GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

GPUs vs. CPUs

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

From pretty pictures to AI data centers

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

AI takes off

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

AI ‘arms race’

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.…

item.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.

That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.

Gaps in climate science grow

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars.

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.

Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.

What this means for supply chains

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.

And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.

What it means for consumers

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.

Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year.…

item.title: Why neutrality is worth chasing, even if no one gets there
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

This content is locked.

Critics say neutrality is impossible, but Jimmy Wales, founder of Wikipedia and author of The Seven Rules of Trust, argues that this is no reason to stop trying. In this conversation with Jonny Thomson, he explains why a fight over a single word, from "Gdańsk" to "security fence," is often what an encyclopedia should explain. He also says no one can fully see the biases built into AI models, and that people were cruel to each other online long before algorithms. The two also discuss why Wales won't put money into Wikipedia editing and where editorial judgment ends and censorship begins. They close with his optimistic view of the next 20 years.

Jimmy Wales: One of the things that I really do believe in is that people tend to overestimate the short run and underestimate the long run. So when some of the top AI people say things like 80% of all white-collar jobs will be gone in three years, I'm like, no, they won't. Nothing moves that fast. That isn't how it's going to happen. And I remember as a survivor of the dot-com era when people were like, yeah, brick-and-mortar stores, they're done. Five years, they're all going to close. It's like, no, they're not.

Jonny Thomson: Hello and welcome to today's Mini Philosophy conversation, today with Jimmy Wales, the founder of Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia that anybody can edit, which now draws around 11 billion page views a month in English alone. Born in Huntsville, Alabama, and now based in London, he's the author of The Seven Rules of Trust, on how Wikipedia earned it.

Jonny Thomson: I get attacked from both sides. People accuse me of being either a Christian apologist or an atheist. They accuse me of being left wing, right wing. Is that a good sign, to be accused of being both?

Jimmy Wales: I think you have to dig in. That's always my view. Whenever we get any kind of criticism, one of the things I advise people in the community is, let's not get defensive. Because the minute you get defensive, you're not listening anymore. And you can listen and you can say, OK, how can we improve? What have we got? Have we actually got anything? And then sometimes you go, you know what? Actually, we're fine. But sometimes you're like, you know what? Actually, there is a kernel of something here that we could do better, particularly around neutrality, because it's quite easy.

It's quite easy. You know, there's an old expression: if you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, what water? Because it's just around them. And there's a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world that we just float in. We've never necessarily examined them because it's sort of obvious. And then when somebody comes in to challenge that, well, sometimes it's because they're crazy. They have actually no rationale whatsoever, and then, okay, you can safely get through that. But in other cases, it's like, oh, I never thought of it that way. I never even considered that, and that's super interesting, particularly around, I would say, a lot of historical things.

One of my favorite examples is who invented the airplane, which for every English speaker in the world, as far as I'm aware, is a very simple answer: the Wright brothers. You learned it when you were six years old. Everybody knows that. It's not even a historically contested fact at all, except it is. And it's actually kind of interesting. In other places, apparently in French-speaking places, people learn about this Brazilian who was living in France at the time. And when you dig into it, what's actually interesting is – so the Wright brothers were the first. They flew further than they would have without power. So it was in that sense the first powered flight, because they went quite far. They never figured out how to go up, which is actually kind of important.

Jonny Thomson: So more of a glider then, wasn't it? Like a powered glider that would go for longer.

Jimmy Wales: Yeah. And it was very, very close to getting the shape just right so you could then go up as well. But the going-up part is quite important. So it's actually a more interesting story than the simple one you learned when you were six years old. But if somebody comes to you and says, what? Are you crazy? The Wright brothers? They didn't invent the airplane. Your first reaction is probably like, oh, are you mad? Everybody knows that, you know? But then, oh, slow down a minute. Maybe there's something more here to the story that's actually interesting.

Jonny Thomson: And it's not just – I mean, obviously a lot of people care about the truth, being right, getting the facts in order. But it's also a matter of pride for a lot of people, isn't it? I remember my first book, Mini Philosophy, sold very well in Poland. And it was fact-checked by the Germans. Out of all of the countries, the Germans fact-checked it. And the most feedback, the most pushback I got was from the Poles, because I had wrongly claimed that the British broke the Enigma code. And actually, it was a group of Poles who had broken the Enigma code, but they had then brought a lot of their work over to Bletchley Park in the UK. So, massive pushback, understandably, because it's a big part of Polish pride.

Jimmy Wales: If you haven't studied that specifically as a time in history – I hope the Wikipedia article's got the whole story and so on and so forth – then you know, oh, it's Bletchley. That's all we really know. It's all you need to know on a day-to-day basis. And yeah, it's quite easy.…

Source: Big Think | Published: 2026-11-24 18:48 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: How to make a lovable city
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

Everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.

The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.

Sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.

Sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.

Anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte showed, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.

Create enclosed spaces

The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.

While the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.

The picture above shows the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.

Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.

London’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.

An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.

Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above shows Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.…
