item.title: The Wall Street Journal joins a growing list of publishers disallowing bots by default
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

As part of the shift, the company revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

“As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” said Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”

The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent company, News Corp.

“We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” said Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”

Robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents shows that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

Many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the company’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

“One of the most important issues for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson said in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”

More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

People Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the company made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

Many of these publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

Despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The company started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

Known Agents currently tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

“Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” said King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”

King acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

“It’s been such a manual process,” said King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”

Slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the company’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

“We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, said. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”…

Source: Nieman Lab | Published: 2026-11-24 19:27 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Confident kids, cautious elders: What we get wrong (and right) about who really understands social media algorithms
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug.

The scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages, which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there.

But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up.

In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in New Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range.

Surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias.

The self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat.

In other words, the generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

To capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know.

Then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency.

Exposure to social media differs sharply by age. About 95% of 18- to 29-year-olds use YouTube and about 63% use TikTok, according to Pew Research; among adults 65 and older, those figures drop to 64% and 12%. For younger users, algorithmic feeds are part of the daily routine, and that routine produces a comfortable sense of “I know how this works,” whether or not it’s true. Older adults, with less exposure, don’t get the same fluency cues, and default to more conservative self-assessments.

My data are consistent with this explanation. The number of platforms people used daily accounted for a meaningful share of the link between age and overconfidence: The more platforms someone used, the further their self-rated understanding outran their demonstrated awareness. Because this is a survey taken at one point in time, it can’t prove that heavy use causes overconfidence, but the pattern fits the fluency account well.

This miscalibration isn’t just a matter of bruised egos or modest grandparents. It shows up in how people evaluate the news and information in their feeds.

Younger adults who overestimated their algorithmic understanding were more likely to see the content in their feeds as reliable and trustworthy, and more likely to believe they were being exposed to a diverse range of viewpoints. Older adults who underestimated their understanding showed the opposite pattern: more skepticism about the reliability of what they saw, and a sense that their feeds were narrower than they might actually be.

Other research points in the same direction for younger audiences. A Stanford study found that two-thirds of U.S. high school students couldn’t tell a news article from sponsored content, a reminder that growing up inside algorithmic feeds is no guarantee of being able to evaluate them.

But the older adults’ pattern isn’t a healthy one either. Blanket distrust is as poor a guide to information as blanket confidence. It can lead people to dismiss accurate reporting along with misinformation, or to disengage from platforms entirely rather than learning to use them critically.

So what can be done?

First, algorithmic literacy needs to teach calibration, not just content. Most digital literacy efforts focus on pouring in more information about how algorithms work. My findings suggest that’s only half the job. The other half is helping people accurately judge what they don’t know.

Second, interventions should look different for different audiences. For younger, overconfident users, that might mean exercises designed to puncture false certainty: quick self-assessments that reveal the gap between what someone assumes and what they can actually explain, or interactive demonstrations of common misconceptions about how feeds are built. For older, underconfident users, the goal isn’t to manufacture confidence. It’s to help them recognize the caution they already bring to online information as a genuine strength, and to pair it with the skills to tell trustworthy sources from untrustworthy ones, so that skepticism becomes discernment rather than disengagement.…

Source: Nieman Lab | Published: 2026-11-24 15:06 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: 10 Old-Fashioned Words for Being Lazy
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

In 16th-century English, at the height of the English Reformation, an abbey-lubber was a derogatory term for a monk or clergyman who lived a life of blissful idleness and self-indulgence. The first part of the word understandably refers to a place of worship, but lubberâthe same tag youâll hear in a landlubberâis an old English word for a silly, clumsy person.Â

Based on an abbey-lubber, though, in the later 1500s describing someone as âabbey-lubber-likeâ meant that they were habitually lazy according to the Oxford English Dictionary. Nor is that the only obscure and old-fashioned word for being lazy thatâs long fallen by the linguistic wayside.Â

CAW-MAGGINGÂ

To caw is to gawp or to stare foolishly or empty-headed, while to mag is to chatter incessantly or pointlessly. Put the two together, and youâve the adjective caw-magging, according to the English Dialect Dictionary, which is to be habitually idle or lazy.Â Â

CLUMPSTÂ

If youâre clumpsed, then youâre numb with coldâor, more figuratively, slow-witted, dumbfounded, or somehow rendered unable to move or speak. Derived from that, to be clumpst is to be lazy in 19th century Yorkshire dialect.Â

DRAW-LATCHINGÂ

In medieval times, a draw-latch was a thief who would let himself into peopleâs homes by âdrawingâ up the âlatchâ of their door by some kind of nefarious means. Confusion with the old verb latch, which once meant to slacken a horseâs reinsâand therefore to dawdle or walk slowlyâultimately led to the word being reinterpreted in the 1500s as a nickname for someone who lags behind. And that makes the adjective draw-latching another word meaning idling, acting lazily, or falling behind the others.Â Â

GERT AND DAISYÂ

Gert and Daisy were characters played on British radio in the early 1900s by comic actresses and sisters Elsie and Doris Waters. The duoâs popularity led to their names falling into use in English rhyming slang: Gert and Daisy is a 1960s way of saying someone is lazy.Â

ILLABORIOUSÂ

Just as illogical is the opposite of logical and illegal the opposite of legal, illaborious is a seldom-used and long-obsolete opposite of laboriousâor, in other words, an early 17th century word meaning workshy or sluggish.Â

KIPPER-KAPERÂ

Kipper-kaper is a Scots adjective meaning lazy or sluggish, recorded in the early 1900s, which is intended to sound like the clomping of a horseâs hooves. The connection between the two is, according to the Dictionary of the Scots Language, that kipper-kaper describes someone who is âeasy-going, as of a tired or lazy horse.âÂ

LAZY AS LUDLAMâS DOGÂ

In English folklore, Ludlam was the name of a supposed witch who dwelt in a cave near the town of Farnham in Surrey, around 30 miles south of London. A host of bizarre and often quite quirky stories emerged around her, including a joke that her familiar, a large dog, was so lazy that it would lean against the cave wall to barkâbut if anyone approached the cave, it was so lazy that it wouldnât even bark at all. âAs lazy as Ludlamâs dog,â ultimately, became a popular simile for laziness in 18th century English.

SCOWBANKINGÂ

Scowbanker is an 18th-century word for a loafer, while the related adjective scowbanking has been recorded in both Scots and northern English since the early 1800s to mean lazy, oafish, or idling. Quite where the word comes from is a complete mystery, but given that a scow is a large flat-bottomed boat, this may be one of a number of bizarre English words that come from maritime slang.Â

SICK OF THE IDLESÂ

First recorded as far back as 1639, if you were âsick of the idlesâ in 17th and 18th century parlance then you were âexceedingly lazyâ or âidle without the will to work,â according to one definition. You could also be âsick of the Lombard fever,â if you were habitually lazy (a play on the old dialect word lomber, meaning to idle around or drag something heavy), or in an even more extended version, âsick of the idle crick and the belly-work in the heelââa made-up medical complaint used as a jokey excuse for acting lazy in 17th-century English.Â

SLOTTERYÂ

To slotter is to spill or slop something messily, or to make something foul or dirty. From there, perhaps in allusion to someone wearing soiled clothing or not making an effort in their appearance, the same word came to be used to mean to be slothful or indolentâand derived from there, the adjective slottery means lazy.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-24 19:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Think you know everything about the history of Thanksgiving? These 21 facts will prove you wrong
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

Think you know everything about the history of Thanksgiving? These 21 facts will prove you wrong

From tales of pumpkin-pie panics to the story of the president who turned his dinner into a pet, Jonny Wilkes uncovers the surprising history behind Thanksgiving: America’s turkey-tastic holiday

1. There are only two accounts of the first Thanksgiving

The story of the first Thanksgiving has been highly mythologised in American history. In 1621, the so-called Pilgrims who travelled on the Mayflower and formed the settlement of Plymouth, in Massachusetts, came together with the local indigenous peoples, the Wampanoag, for a feast to celebrate a good harvest and the growing friendship of settler and Native American in the New World. That is the version long told in schools.

In truth, the Pilgrims threw themselves a harvest festival and around 90 of the Wampanoag showed up. Without their help, especially a man named Squanto, the European settlers would have likely perished in their brutal first winter. The only sources for the three-day feast are sparse mentions in writings by two of the Pilgrims, Edward Winslow and William Bradford. Neither actually used the word ‘thanksgiving’, however, and since they gave few details of what happened, the mythologising took over.

2. They may not have eaten turkey at the first Thanksgiving

For many Americans, no modern Thanksgiving meal is complete without a turkey as the centrepiece of the table. It’s unclear, however, whether this tradition began in 1621.

The Pilgrims cooked up a selection of fowl – which may have included turkey, but could just as easily been duck and goose – while the Wampanoag killed a number of deer, meaning venison was on the menu. They might have had seafood, too, including eels, clams, mussels and lobster.

Yes, William Bradford mentioned a “great store of wild Turkies” in the region, but the bird did not become a staple of the Thanksgiving meal until the 19th century.

3. The first Thanksgiving may have happened earlier than 1621

While the 1621 feast became the foundation for the Thanksgiving holiday, perhaps Americans should celebrate a different year. Other acts of thanksgiving, based in the tradition of Christian harvest festivals, took place earlier in the short-lived Popham Colony in Maine and Jamestown in Virginia, both founded in 1607.

Two years before the Pilgrims and Wampanoag, the Berkeley Hundred settlement, also in Virginia, held a celebration and decreed that the same day should be “perpetually kept holy as a day of thanksgiving to Almighty God”. The true first Thanksgiving, however, was not English, but Spanish. On 8 September 1565, in what is now St Augustine, Florida, hundreds of Spaniards held a religious ceremony and shared a meal with the local people to mark their safe arrival.

4. Americans eat around 46 million turkeys every year

A major reason why turkey became the meat of choice for Thanksgiving is that the birds are both abundant and large (meaning a lot of meat), and it’s a good thing, too. There’s a reason the holiday is also referred to as Turkey Day.

With apologies to the non-meat eaters out there, it is estimated that around 46 million birds are killed for the holiday every year in the US alone, according to the Department of Agriculture. That’s one turkey for every seven or eight Americans.

5. The fastest time to carve a turkey is under four minutes

Without wanting to dismay all the Americans who take immense pride in serving up the meal every Thanksgiving, the Guinness World Record for the fastest time to carve a turkey is currently held by a British person.

The UK does eat its fair share of turkeys at Christmas, after all. In 2009, Paul Kelly, a turkey farmer in Essex, managed the feat in just three minutes and 19.47 seconds.

6. The author of Mary Had a Little Lamb is known as the ‘Mother of Thanksgiving’

Sarah Josepha Hale was a writer, the first American woman to be editor of a magazine and, in 1830, she published the nursery rhyme, Mary Had a Little Lamb (originally titled Mary’s Lamb).

One of her biggest passions, though, would always be Thanksgiving. Born in 1788 in New England, she grew up with the local celebrations and customs that took place every year, and wanted Thanksgiving to become a national holiday. For years, she embarked on this campaign, writing editorials for her magazine, Godey’s Lady’s Book, which had a peak circulation of 150,000, as well as countless letters to presidents asking for their help.

Finally getting somewhere with Abraham Lincoln, she is now heralded as the ‘Mother of Thanksgiving’.

7. In 1705, a town postponed Thanksgiving because of pumpkin pie

Until Sarah Josepha Hale’s campaign, it was up to each town and state to determine how to mark Thanksgiving, with most of the events taking place only in the US northeast. For the people of Colchester, Connecticut, the celebrations had to include pumpkin pie. The dessert had become a symbol of the bounty of the New World.

In 1705, however, they faced a problem: bad weather prevented supplies from reaching them, including the molasses that they needed to make their pies. Rather than have a Thanksgiving without them, the townsfolk elected to postpone the festivities for a week until the molasses could be delivered.

8. Thomas Jefferson was opposed to Thanksgiving (sort of)

In 1789, George Washington issued a presidential proclamation naming Thursday 26 November as a “day of public thanksgiving and prayer”. This did not make the holiday official, as each president had to issue their own proclamations every year. While John Adams followed Washington’s example, the third president, Thomas Jefferson, did not.…

Source: HistoryExtra | Published: 2026-11-24 14:35 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person in History to Win in Two Different Sciences
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth exploration of Marie Curie's achievements and impact, with historical context and clear, well-structured English.

For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes.

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “Floating University” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the Sorbonne, the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site Famous Scientists, “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the French Academy of Sciences. It would take another 51 years before the first woman, Marguerite Perey, a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influential scientists and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Incidentally, in the following year, the Curies’ daughter Irène Joliot-Curie and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Since then, only seven other women have claimed that honor, and only five women, including Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics, out of 230 winners total.

There may be nothing yet like gender parity in the sciences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women scientists running women-owned companies, women-founded research institutes and academic departments, and, like the famous Curies, making major contributions to chemistry. Perhaps not long from now, many of those exceptional scientists will be as well-known and widely celebrated as Marie Curie.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

Related Content:

Marie Curie’s Research Papers Are Still Radioactive a Century Later

Josh Jones is a writer and musician based in Durham, NC.

item.title: 25 Films Inspired by Edgar Allan Poe Online: The Fall of the House of Usher, The Tell-Tale Heart, and More
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging and informative listicle with a focus on films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, offering a mix of analysis and historical context.

Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane.”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story, which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films, you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman. Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe, a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature, the directorial debut of Jules Dassin, an animated short narrated by James Mason, a British psychological thriller, and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans. And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

item.title: Pochettino leads Man Utd fury at Yoro red card ruling
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Pochettino leads Man Utd fury at Yoro red card ruling

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has questioned the competence of video assistant referee officials after defender Leny Yoro had his red card overturned by the Football Association.

Yoro was sent off eight minutes into United's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday after bringing down Aleksander Isak just outside the United penalty area.

United sources say they have conclusive proof it was impossible for Isak to reach the ball after he took a heavy touch, that it would have run on to goalkeeper Senne Lammens and Yoro should not have been punished for denying a goalscoring opportunity.

Pochettino said he had some sympathy with referee Sam Barrott but he is livid at how the situation played out.

"I am very disappointed," the Argentine said. "This type of thing can never happen.

"We can accept the referee can make a mistake. But if we have VAR, what were they doing? What were they doing? Are we going to repeat the game? Are we going to have the possibility to play 11 by 11? No.

"We have an unbelievable car, but we need to be at the level to drive [it]. We accept that the technology is there but what are they doing?"

United are furious at both the nature of the audio of the incident, and referees' chief Howard Webb defending referee Barrott's decision and the VAR John Brooks' reinforcing it on the Mic'd Up programme, which was shown on Sky Sports.

They intend to take the matter up with both the Premier League and ProRef.

It is the second time this season United been on the wrong end of a major VAR error.

Webb apologised to United after Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby at Old Trafford on 13 September was allowed to stand even though a clearly offside Enzo Fernandez was interfering with play.

There has been no apology from Webb on this occasion.

Instead, he has doubled down on the call, saying: "I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball."

United sources claim this interpretation is wrong.

The club are unhappy at the speed the on-field decision was confirmed. It is thought United used data around Isak's top speed and his chances of reaching the ball in their defence of Yoro to the FA. They claim this could have been done "within minutes" of the incident occurring.

This is not the only bone of contention at Old Trafford around the incident.

Pochettino also pointed out Liverpool forward Bradley Barcola was too close to the United wall from the resulting free-kick and Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal should have been disallowed.

"No-one talked about [the fact] that the goal wasn't legal," said Pochettino. "Barcola was touching our wall. It must be disallowed.

"We need to defend my players and my club, and that is to denounce it and to say, the decision wasn't good. And now, the three points, where are the three points?"

Webb defends Yoro red card

What referee's chief Webb said about the incident on the Mic'd Up programme.

"There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

"That was the referee's call made on the field, and then the VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn't.

"That if there was any doubt, then it was doubt.

"It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. and

"I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.

"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable. Certainly not clearly wrong."

We're not fragile, we are strong - Pochettino

United's fury over Yoro and the way the situation has been handled cannot completely obscure the fact they lost 4-0 in Pochettino's first game in charge.

It extended a terrible start to the season that has seen the Red Devils win on just three occasions - and only once in the Premier League, against newly-promoted Ipswich in August.

The club are 19th in the Premier League and facing up to the possibility of being relegated for the first time since 1973-74.

Yet Pochettino is adamant there is no fragility about his new squad.

"The situation is fragile in [terms of] the environment, or the people want it to look like we're fragile. But I don't say that we are fragile. I think we are strong.

"We have great mentality and a great mindset.

"There are many things we need to improve. It's normal to be in a different position, and everyone can use different words to describe the situation.

"But we are a strong team. They showed that last season, capable of finishing third. I think we are going to turn around the situation and start to perform in the level like before Bruno [Fernandes] said, deserve to be at this club."

Contract talks 'irrelevant' - Fernandes

Skipper Bruno Fernandes revealed at the weekend talks over a new United contract were on hold.

The 32-year-old's present deal expires in the summer, although the club have an option to extend it by 12 months.

Speaking alongside Pochettino at a media conference before his first meeting with Sporting since he left to join United in a Â£47m deal in January 2020, Fernandes said his sole focus at present is to drag United out of the mire.

"For us to start winning games, then we can start speaking about contract," he said.

"It's not important now. It's irrelevant. Obviously, I know it's my future and I probably shouldn't look into that way because I haven't got much left in my contract, but I'm not really worried about that.

"I'm more worried about getting results, trying to bring the club back in a position that we can be proud of, and we're not there at the moment."

Follow Manchester United on BBC Sounds…

Source: BBC Sport | Published: 2026-11-24 22:05 UTC

item.title: No two off-seasons are the same
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

How restless do you feel when you have no racing to watch? Imagine how unsettled athletes are during the off-season, when they can’t do what they most want — race.

Rest days were already difficult, let alone stringing 28 of them end-to-end. Being active and outdoors for many hours of the day racing is their default state of being. Then again, the off-season is a fleeting chance to live a relatively normal life from which a new structure develops. As with anything challenging, pros could do worse than to move forward with a vision, rather than looking back on the season finished. And that vision should produce a formula that they feel works for their recovery. With the entire professional peloton — bar the cyclocrossers — calling time on the season after the Tour of Guangxi, the Veneto Classic, or the Chrono des Nations, we can see how an array of ways riders are approaching their off-seasons. And in each scenario, the psychology of a rider’s season will influence their holidays.

The early enders

Sometimes a season finishes abruptly and without choice, no matter how successful it was. Maybe it’s a crash, like Tadej Pogačar’s at La Vuelta à España. Maybe it’s falling ill with the now seemingly seasonal COVID that rolls in at the turn of the weather. Perhaps it’s an acquired injury akin to the knee niggle that just can’t be shaken because the body is crying out for rest. An early exit can allow for full physical recovery, but the winter is particularly long when structured training restarts before October is out. In another (common) scenario, the stinging urge to get back into training overpowers all logic. In so doing, it teases the entire spectator landscape – and sometimes team management – with an impending, miraculous return, but curtailing time off runs the risk of further compounding setbacks.

The long campaigners

The next archetype has raced what feels like the entire racing season and has been winning from the start of the campaign right until the end, when weariness is laid bare, impossible to cover up. Someone like Isaac Del Toro, who was clearly tiring when he began to complain of a knee niggle after the World Championships. It seemed as if he mustered the remaining power from all corners of his body as his muscles slowly wound down from the efforts and rewards of the long season. After 60 racing days around the world, at just 22 years old, tiredness cannot be masked, no matter how much one wills it to be hidden.

Did we do a good job with this story?

Source: Escape Collective | Published: 2026-11-24 21:58 UTC

Tuesday 24 November 2026 21:57, UK

Arsenal were punished for failing to take their chances for the second game in a row as Maximilian Beier clinched a 1-1 draw for Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League.

Viktor Gyokeres gave Arsenal an early lead with a stunning strike from distance but the game followed a similar pattern to Saturday's 2-2 draw with Newcastle as they were unable to capitalise on a one-sided first half before conceding after the break.

Dortmund's leveller came when Beier slotted a clinical finish past Kepa Arrizabalaga, standing in for the injured David Raya, following a rampaging run from defender Joane Gadou.

- Match stats | How the teams lined up | As it happened

Arsenal racked up 30 shots and had a string of chances to win it in the closing stages, hitting the woodwork through Jurrien Timber's deflected cut-back and again through Declan Rice's low shot.

Gyokeres also spurned opportunities, firing over from close range from Martin Odegaard's pass shortly before half-time, then heading awkwardly wide from a few yards out when it looked easier to score from another Odegaard ball.

Arsenal remain unbeaten in the Champions League but the draw causes them to drop two places in the league phase table to fifth before they resume their Premier League campaign at home to Manchester City, live on Sky Sports on Sunday.

item.description:

Sheffield United vs Southampton; EFL Championship

Sheffield United vs Southampton. EFL Championship.

Bramall LaneAttendance24,519.

Sheffield United 1-1 Southampton: Sydie Peck strikes again to earn point for Blades

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Sheffield United and Southampton at Bramall Lane on Tuesday night; Sydie Peck scores again as the Blades hit back to earn a point and cancel out Lewis Dobbins opener.

Tuesday 24 November 2026 22:03, UK

Sydie Peck equalised in the 90th minute as Sheffield United came from behind to secure a 1-1 Championship draw with Southampton at Bramall Lane.

Lewis Dobbin had given the visitors an early lead but the Blades stepped up a gear after the break and finally found a way past Saints goalkeeper Daniel Peretz through Peck.

The equaliser saw the Blades move within a point of the top eight and remain two behind their sixth-placed opponents.

United have lost just once in their last seven games while Southampton have only suffered one defeat in their last nine outings.

Southampton struck in the 10th minute when Dobbin cut inside from the left wing and fired into the far corner of Michael Cooper's net.

Shortly after, Dobbin tested Cooper with a shot from 25 yards as the Saints pushed for a second.

United's solitary first-half effort on goal came from Romelle Donovan, whose angled shot was comfortably dealt with by Daniel Peretz.

United were lacklustre in the opening period as they missed loanee Ben Brereton-Diaz, who scored twice at the weekend but was unable to face his parent club.

In a bid to strengthen his side's firepower, manager Chris Wilder introduced Patrick Bamford at the start of the second half with Tom Cannon making way.

It did not take long for Bamford to have his first chance, putting a close-range header over after Peck's corner had been headed towards goal by Mark McGuinness.

Peretz had to keep out a near-post header from Jordan Ayew as the hosts looked to capitalise on their improved second-half performance.

The Southampton keeper was also called into action to thwart Harrison Burrows, Tahith Chong and Peck. The pick of his saves was when he flung himself to his right to keep out Chong's shot while Peck was disappointed to head straight at Peretz.

Southampton's resistance was finally broken in the final minute of the game when Ayew wriggled past his marker on the right byline and pulled the ball back to Peck, who slotted beyond Peretz for his fifth goal in four games.

Substitute Samuel Edozie spurned a great chance to score a winner for Southampton in added time. He was put through on goal by Finn Azaz and looked certain to score but Cooper stuck out a leg to divert the ball wide.

A Southampton winner would have been very harsh on the Blades who deserved at least a point from the game after dominating the second period.

Middlesbrough vs Swansea City; EFL Championship

Middlesbrough vs Swansea City. EFL Championship.

Riverside StadiumAttendance26,960.

Middlesbrough 2

- M Peart-Harris (9th minute)

- W Lankshear (54th minute)

Swansea City 1

- J Opoku (22nd minute)

Will Lankshear was back among the goals as Middlesbrough cemented their position at the top of the Championship with a 2-1 win over Swansea City.

Lankshear had missed the final two games prior to the international break because of a hamstring injury, and was only afforded a late substitute appearance in Saturday's win over Bristol City.

Having been restored to the starting line-up at the Riverside, the Championship's leading scorer claimed his 14th league goal of the season to reestablish his side's lead in the second half after Joseph Opoku's driven finish had cancelled out Myles Peart-Harris' opener.

Lankshear's winner came nine minutes into the second half, but the England Under-21 international was also heavily involved in the slick passing move that led to Boro opening the scoring in the ninth minute.

Lankshear's first-time pass released Neto Borges into the left of the area and when he squared across the face of the box, Peart-Harris slotted home a first-time strike of his own to claim his first goal since joining Middlesbrough in the summer.

Boro's lead lasted 13 minutes, with Swansea levelling when Lankshear was at fault at the opposite end of the field.

The striker bundled over Elijah Just on the edge of the area to concede a free-kick. Ben Cabango's goalbound header was nodded off the line by Ashley Phillips, but the ball broke to Opoku, who drilled home an excellent low finish from the edge of the area.

Boro went close to regaining their lead when Riley McGree fired a first-time strike just wide from a corner, and threatened again just before the interval when Peart-Harris volleyed over at the back post after David Strelec flicked Borges' cross into his path.

Swansea remained a threat though, and six minutes into the second half Adilson Malanda played Eom Ji-sung onside as Opoku's through ball unpicked the Boro defence, only for goalkeeper Radek Vitek to burst from his line to keep out the midfielder's shot with his foot.

It was a crucial save as just three minutes later Boro were scoring their second goal at the other end. Callum Brittain's pass sent Peart-Harris breaking away down the right, and when he squared the ball across the face of goal Lankshear was left with the easy task of tapping home.

Sebastian Berhalter should have added a third goal with 18 minutes remaining, but after coming off the bench the American midfielder dragged a shot wide from the right of the area.

His fellow replacement, Max Arfsten, also wasted a good late opportunity, drilling a low strike straight at goalkeeper Lawrence Vigouroux.

item.title: Skift Global Forum East: Five Decisions in the Room
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: strong, worth their time

One of the most enduring narratives in travel over the past decade has been built around a clear set of assumptions: Global aviation will flow through Gulf hubs, international travelers will discover and then visit the Middle East repeatedly, and major events and attractions will reap the rewards of that demand well into the next decade and beyond.

War across the Middle East over the past 9 months has called all of those assumptions into question. Airspace disruptions have rerouted traffic, leading to suspended service for some airlines. Demand has significantly weakened, and hotels have leaned more heavily on domestic, regional, and short-haul travelers.

The historically ambitious growth vision for Gulf tourism is facing an existential crisis. Every Middle East destination and travel executive that operates in the region has a decision to make: How much of 2026 is a temporary disruption, and how much do our long-term travel strategies need to be rewritten now?

Skift Global Forum East:

Grand Hyatt Abu Dhabi, December 8–9, 2026

Standard Pass – AED 2,920

Complimentary registration available (subject to approval) for senior leaders – email events@skift.com

How Will Gulf Aviation Hubs Win Back Traffic?

The Gulf’s aviation strategy depends on being one of the easiest places in the world to connect, and Gulf carriers are still planning for substantial long-term growth. New aircraft, larger airports, and expanded networks assume the region will retain its central role in global connectivity.

However, recent airspace closures and airline suspensions gave travelers and competing hubs a reason to find alternatives. Some of that traffic will return as operations normalize. It’s much harder to predict how much actually does. The decision is how to win back displaced traffic while planning for a future in which geopolitical disruption may remain part of the operating environment.

Emblematic of the air traffic disruption around the Gulf, Turkish Airlines cut Middle East capacity 26% year over year in the third quarter of 2026 while increasing East Asian capacity 18%. [1]

The Decisions Being Made Right Now

- Where should we position ourselves as air traffic volume returns?

- Where have competing hubs gained passengers that may be harder to win back?

- Which new markets can reduce dependence on traditional connecting flows?

- How much geopolitical disruption should now be built into fleet and network planning?

What to Discuss in the Room

- How Gulf airline CEOs distinguish temporarily displaced traffic from longer-term changes in demand.

- What commercial and network leaders see in the markets recovering fastest.

- How hub carriers rebuild traveler confidence while continuing to expand.

- Where aviation leaders see the Gulf hub model gaining or losing ground.

Are Gulf Hotels Building Enough Midscale to Meet Demand?

The Gulf has spent years building a hospitality proposition around luxury. The next phase of growth will also depend on domestic, regional, Asian, business, religious, and event-driven travelers with a wider range of budgets and trip types.

Development has continued through the disruption. The decision is whether the mix of rooms being built still matches the travelers expected to arrive, without overreacting to a difficult 2026 or leaving the region short of the mid-market supply needed for 2030 and beyond.

The Middle East had a record total hotel construction pipeline of 771 projects at the close of the third quarter 2026, up 17% year over year. Luxury, upper-upscale, and upscale projects account for 78% of that total. [2]

The Decisions Being Made Right Now

- How much more midscale supply will the region need before major events in 2030 and 2034?

- Which markets remain deep enough to support continued luxury development?

- Should projects already in the pipeline change their positioning before they open?

- Where do short-term rentals and flexible accommodation fit into future demand?

What to Discuss in the Room

- How regional and global hotel operators are adapting development plans for a broader traveler mix.

- Where hotel growth leaders see the biggest gaps between planned supply and future demand.

- How accommodation platforms and operators are responding to demand beyond traditional hotels.

- Which segments hospitality investors and developers believe can absorb the next wave of supply.

How Much Should the Gulf Bet on Asian Demand?

Asia has become centrally important to the Gulf’s growth story. India is already one of the region’s largest source markets. Coupled with Europe’s decline, China’s resurgence is even more critical. Gulf airlines, hotels, and destinations are adapting connectivity, products, and marketing around both.

The opportunity comes with constraints. India’s aviation market remains capacity-constrained, while Chinese demand can be interrupted quickly by safety concerns and airline suspensions. The decision is how much Gulf operators should invest now in Asian-market product, air access, and distribution before near-term demand becomes more predictable.

India’s outbound travel market is projected to reach $55.4 billion by 2034, while Chinese is one of the top source markets for the UAE, representing 5% of inbound volume. [3] [4]

The Decisions Being Made Right Now

- How much investment should shift toward India, China, and other Asian markets?

- Which hospitality products need to change to compete for those travelers?

- Where is insufficient air access limiting otherwise strong demand?

- Which Asian markets offer the best balance of volume, spending, and resilience?

What to Discuss in the Room

- What South Asian hotel leaders are learning as India’s outbound market expands.

- What Indian travel platforms see in the traveler segments and destinations gaining share.

- How regional and Asian booking platforms are identifying the Gulf’s next growth markets.

- What Gulf destinations and operators need to change to turn Asian demand into repeat business.…

item.title: AirAsia’s Q3 Shows Why Fernandes Pushed the Comeback to 2028
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: average

AirAsia’s Q3 Shows Why Fernandes Pushed the Comeback to 2028

AirAsia has shown it can charge more. It hasn't shown it can make money at its new, smaller size. Until the $1 billion debt financing lands, the balance sheet, not demand, decides when the comeback starts.

AirAsia Group posted a smaller third-quarter loss on Monday as higher fares made up for most of the jump in fuel costs, but the results show why Tony Fernandes pushed the comeback to 2028: a smaller AirAsia costs more to run, and it is still losing money.

AirAsia Group, the listed company that now houses all of AirAsia’s airlines, posted a loss attributable to shareholders of RM175 million ($43 million), according to its third-quarter results. That’s about a third of its second-quarter loss. Most of the improvement came from charging more, helped by jet fuel easing from its second-quarter peak. Planes stayed nearly as full as fares rose sharply, and that won back much of what the jet fuel spike had taken earlier in the year.

Including minority interests, the loss after tax was RM381.3 million ($93 million). Revenue fell 11% from a year earlier to RM4.66 billion, and 8% from the second quarter.

“Our third quarter performance suggests that the worst is behind us,” CEO Bo Lingam said in a statement. AirAsia is a smaller airline than it was a year ago, and a smaller low-cost airline is an expensive one to run. It still spends more to fly each seat than it earns from it, and its equity cushion is thin, with shareholders’ equity of RM362 million. The refinancing it needs to steady the balance sheet, which AirAsia targeted for this quarter and as recently as last week expected by December or January, is now due to conclude in the fourth quarter or early 2027.

The results came the same day Thai Airways reported its own third-quarter loss on fuel costs. If jet fuel eases as AirAsia expects in 2027, higher fares could start turning into profit across the region. For AirAsia, the question is whether that comes fast enough.

Pricing Did the Work

AirAsia consolidated its Malaysian, Thai, Indonesian, Philippine and Cambodian airlines with AirAsia X in January. This was the first quarter in which the merged group had almost no seats left that were sold before the fuel shock, which let it reprice. Average fares rose by almost a quarter from a year earlier, while the share of filled seats barely moved.

The group suspended 76 routes in the third quarter, mostly fuel-heavy international flights to India, China and Australia, and kept most of its flying close to home, where demand held up best. The retreat has cost it ground. Malaysia Airlines this month overtook the AirAsia group as the largest operator between Malaysia and India for the first time since 2021, though Fernandes has dismissed suggestions that rivals could take the lead for internal Malaysia flights.

Smaller Is Not Cheaper

AirAsia cut what it spends on staff, airport charges and leases, but its remaining fixed costs were spread over far fewer seats, so the cost of flying each one rose. Higher fares more than covered the extra fuel bill. The rise in other costs per passenger then took back part of that gain.

Not every market pulled its weight. Malaysia and Cambodia were profitable at the operating level, Indonesia and the Philippines lost less than a year earlier, and Thailand had a weak quarter. Currency losses added to the damage further down the income statement.

Fuel is squeezing AirAsia’s regional rivals too. Cebu Pacific’s management said this month it has pretty much no chance of making money this year, and Thai Airways’ finance chief warned that if current oil prices become the new normal then its third-quarter loss could be a guide to performance in the fourth.

Balance Sheet Dictates the Pace

AirAsia is handing back older, more expensive aircraft: 25 of them this year and most of them early. And it says it may return more in 2027. That move cuts lease bills but leaves less room to grow, six months after the group placed a record order for 150 Airbus A220s. Many of the planes it keeps aren’t flying either. About 31% of the 234 aircraft in the group’s main fleet were out of service at the end of September, mostly for scheduled maintenance, with engine problems among the other causes.

That trade-off worries some analysts. Handing back jets now could slow AirAsia’s eventual comeback, analysts told Skift this month, because new narrowbody delivery slots are scarce until around 2033.

The pressure point is funding. AirAsia ended June with far less cash than it owed within the year. It is working on up to $1 billion in debt financing and says talks with creditors are progressing.

The strain has been visible for months. In September, Endau Analytics’ Shukor Yusof questioned the airline’s financial resilience, citing its balance sheet and reports of delayed rental payments. Fernandes insisted that no aircraft had been grounded over nonpayment, and he has denied reports of a government-backed contingency plan. Malaysia’s transport and finance ministries remain in talks with the airline.

Wanted: Strong Year End

For now, management is betting on the year-end peak. It plans to add back capacity in the fourth quarter, restore some routes and keep pushing fares higher — and says forward bookings are running in line with last year, at elevated yields. The Q3 presentation called 2026 and 2027 a “reset” and 2028 the “rebuild,” when new fuel-efficient jets begin arriving. It gave no passenger targets for 2027.

Fernandes has been somewhat blunter. In a LinkedIn post last week, he called 2027 “a period of consolidation” and warned of “more painful decisions” on costs, without repeating his September target of 80 million passengers next year. Expansion elsewhere is on hold too: the group’s Bahrain hub is now targeted for March 2027, should conditions in the Gulf allow.…

Source: Skift | Published: 2026-11-24 11:12 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Princeton Ph.D. Student Remains in ICE Custody
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: essential reporting on a significant issue

Matthew Hoen/NurPhoto/Getty Images

A Chinese-born Ph.D. student remains in custody after she was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Ronald Reagan Washington National airport last week, according to the AP.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student in Princeton University’s Brody Lab, was returning to New Jersey after presenting at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting in Washington, multiple news outlets have reported.

She is being held at ICE’s Caroline Detention Center in Virginia. “Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings,” the Department of Homeland Security told the AP.

Xie immigrated to the U.S. from China with her family in 2016, when she was 14 years old. She graduated in 2020 from the Bronx High School of Science and in 2024 from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Her attorney, Kerry Doyle, told the AP that Xie has had an asylum application pending for years and has the right to live, work and study in the U.S.

But in a statement to The New York Times, a DHS spokesperson contradicted those claims. “Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, but chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of Sept. 15, 2016,” the department said in an email.

“Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States,” it added. “To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States.”

Princeton confirmed to The New York Times that it has arranged for Xie to receive legal counsel.

“Eva is a gentle, kind, caring person who is contributing enormously to the United States,” Xie’s adviser and head of the Brody lab, Carlos Brody, told NBC News. “She belongs back home in Princeton, doing the science that she loves, and helping our country excel and grow.”

Xie is the latest noncitizen student to be detained by ICE as it steps up immigration enforcement at airports. On Oct. 30, ICE detained Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez, a 23-year-old business administration student and asylum seeker from Colombia studying at the University of California, Berkeley, at San Francisco International Airport. She was released on Nov. 10 after a federal judge ordered ICE to release her, according to Berkeleyside.
