item.title: Loan Limits Unlikely to Reduce Defaults, New Data Shows
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful analysis of student loan policy

Republican lawmakers say dramatic loan limits for graduate students are designed to rein in a mounting student debt crisis. But new data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia indicates that those limits might not be entirely effective at curbing borrower default.

Roughly 60 percent of borrowers who defaulted on their loans from 2011 to 2016 took out less than the new loan limits, according to the study, which was conducted by combining enrollment records, credit history reports and program-level earnings data. Meanwhile, students who borrowed the most above the cap and pursued high-paying careers, such as medicine, law and dentistry, “rarely defaulted.”

So, if borrowing follows similar trends moving forward, the new federal caps won’t directly hinder the most at-risk students from borrowing more than they can repay. What the caps will do, researchers argue, is limit college access.

The caps, which took effect July 1, allow graduate students to take out $50,000 a year if they are in a professional degree program and $20,500 a year for anything else; any cost above those limits must be paid out of pocket or using private loans. But nearly four in 10 students who borrowed above the limits either have a subprime credit score or no credit score at all, a prior report from the Philadelphia Fed shows. So, unless those borrowers can find a co-signer with a better credit score, they may not be able to finance their degree at all—even if it’s one with a high return on investment.

Based on their cumulative findings, the bank’s researchers argue that “loan size alone is a coarse signal of repayment risk,” and that the current loan limits will cut off from loans certain groups of students who would be able to repay them. Moving forward, they add, the government should consider factoring in other student outcome data points, like a student’s expected salary after graduation. Doing so could help rein in the debt crisis without blocking students with low credit scores from being able to afford high return-on-investment degrees.

Jordan Matsudaira, a visiting scholar at the Philadelphia Fed and co-author of the report, described the current loan limits as “a ham-fisted way of addressing the real problems in the federal loan program.”

“It’s not the amount that matters. It’s the amount relative to your ability to repay it. And that latter piece varies A LOT across different types of borrowers,” Matsudaira said in an email to Inside Higher Ed.

For instance, in degree programs where the median salary postgraduation was above $156,000, only about 4 percent of borrowers with a low credit score defaulted. Meanwhile, in careers that pay less than $60,000, nearly 12 percent of borrowers defaulted. Even among borrowers with prime credit scores in the lower-earning programs, the default rate was higher than those who earned $156,000, at 5 percent.

But as the federal policy stands, student outcomes aren’t factored in.

“The point of the loan program is to allow students to pursue valuable training opportunities that their families can’t pay for out of pocket,” Matsudaira said. Still, “I fear the current limits will mainly serve to cut off access to high-value programs for low-income students, and will do little to reduce default among federal borrowers or reduce taxpayer exposure to unpaid debts.”

Matsudaira hopes this latest round of data will encourage not only lawmakers to start considering future earnings, but also private lenders.

“This report shows that even for borrowers with no or low credit, those in programs with good labor market outcomes often have very good loan outcomes—sometimes better than the average borrowers with good credit,” he said. “If private lenders continue to overlook measures of program quality in their underwriting, then many students who should be getting loans to attend graduate school might not be able to.”

The report does note that default rates could climb, as the data used in Monday’s report was pulled from a time when students had access to more repayment options and lower interest rates through federal loans. Now, many borrowers are forced to turn to private lenders and federal loans now come with fewer repayment options with higher monthly dues.

Without the previous “protections” and “accommodations,” researchers say, default rates could rise across the board—even among students in careers with a high return on investment.

“We expect the patterns we see in loan default would be similar, but perhaps with higher levels, in a world of private loans that lack those protections,” Matsudaira said. Still, “it is hard to know since private loans have been such a small share of education loans over the past several decades.”

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-24 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.insidehighered.com/news/government/student-aid-policy/2026/11/24/loan-limits-unlikely-reduce-defaults-new-data-shows

item.title: What’s Really Fueling Higher Ed’s AI ‘Witch Hunt’?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: important discussion on AI in education

Four years after AI tools capable of generating human-sounding writing began infiltrating higher education, a majority of faculty are using them in some capacity.

Yet there’s no consensus on what distinguishes acceptable AI-assisted writing from academic dishonesty, fueling fears of anti-AI bias and discouraging many faculty from disclosing their AI use. At the same time, keeping quiet carries its own risks: Faculty and administrators who have admitted to writing with AI only after their work was flagged by students, peers or editors have been attacked for laziness, dishonesty or intellectual shortcomings.

The tension has put some academics in a difficult position.

In August, Zvezdelina Stankova, a math professor at the University of California, Berkeley, insisted she’d used AI only to help edit an opinion piece on her students’ math deficiencies after the student newspaper ran it through the AI detector Pangram, which said the article was 33 percent AI-generated. Stankova defended the essay as “the result of several hundred person-hours of intensive human work, of which about 80 hours are my own.”

In September, Nicholas Polson, a statistician at the University of Chicago, faced a barrage of criticism about the quality of his work after he admitted to using a large language model to help author or co-author hundreds of papers this year without clearly disclosing his AI use. The preprint platform SSRN removed his articles, but Polson maintained that LLMs have only enhanced his pursuit of original ideas, speculating that the outrage from his peers is motivated by “envy and a desire to poach my process.”

And last month, Dartmouth College Provost Santiago Schnell resigned in the wake of revelations by Semafor and the Dartmouth student newspaper that an AI detector flagged some of his published writings as AI-generated. Although he hadn’t disclosed his LLM use ahead of publication, Schnell later admitted to using an LLM to help write, though he maintained that it didn’t “substitute” his “research, intellectual judgment or authorship.” Nonetheless, faculty and students called for his firing, and he stepped down the day after an internal review committee said he undermined the college’s “culture of integrity, honesty, and respect.”

‘Shame-and-Blame Witch Hunt’

Schnell’s headline-grabbing resignation was not a desirable or productive outcome, according to Reed Albergotti, the Semafor editor who first reported that Pangram flagged an editorial Schnell wrote for The Washington Post as AI-generated.

“My hope was that the reporting would lead to some smart questions, not a shame-and-blame witch hunt that would result in a resignation,” he wrote in an editorial lamenting Schnell’s resignation. “Years from now, we’ll look back on this time with regret and wonder why we were so outraged by people using a new tool that was so obviously useful.”

A contingent of experts on AI, higher education and ethics have already been thinking about that very question: Why is academia in such a panic about whether—and how—scholars are deploying AI in their essays and research papers? Although the answer remains far from definitive, many say the backlash is rooted in fear and anxiety about how AI is fundamentally changing work, academic incentive structures and human relationships.

“We think of writing as a window into someone’s mind and soul,” said Tawnya Means, a former academic administrator and consultant on AI in higher education. “So, for some people, using AI to help generate writing feels like a step too far. They want to know that if you’ve written something, it’s because it’s what you really think.” While many academics are using it as “an iterative thinking partner” in ways that don’t “feel so inauthentic,” she said, not disclosing it can make readers feel “deceived,” and lead them to assume the author circumvented the process of developing their own ideas.

In addition, faculty who use AI to help write papers are disrupting the decades-old practice of holding up published writing as the primary metric of academic success.

“Up until AI, writing took a tremendous amount of work. I suspect part of the anger toward AI is that it seems to do that work very quickly and easily,” James Cochran, an assistant professor of English and director of the writing center at Hartwick College, told Inside Higher Ed. “If we use scholarly output as a sign of a scholar’s expertise and worth, but find out that AI was involved in the process, it casts doubt on that person’s expertise—even if they just used AI to fix their commas.”

One problem is that AI detectors aren’t able to reliably pinpoint the extent to which a person used AI to help write—or to distinguish between their voice and the machine’s. While some faculty members cite that as a major concern about AI, their discontent may also stem from the way AI “challenges the myth that writing is this isolated, solitary act,” Cochran said.

“Even before AI, every writer had other people—editors, colleagues, friends, enemies—read their work,” he added. Regardless of that reality, “it’s easier to evaluate people or assess people and their writing if we think of it as produced by just them.”

The threat AI-assisted writing poses to academic power structures is also driving some of the targeted AI-shaming campaigns, said Patrick R. Dempsey, associate dean of learning design and technology at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University and author of What Education Becomes: Teaching and Learning in a Post-AI World.

“There’s a paradoxical fear that AI gives everyone an ability to write at least decently well,” he told Inside Higher Ed. And now that generative AI has undermined proficient writing as a gatekeeper of academic success, someone has to pay—and those who are publicly outed make easy targets. “There’s this need for a scapegoat—an ‘other’ outside the club,” Dempsey said. “Otherwise, there is no club worth being a part of.”…

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-24 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://www.insidehighered.com/news/faculty/2026/11/24/whats-really-fueling-higher-eds-ai-witch-hunt

item.title: Courts Deal Blows to Trump’s Key International Ed Policies
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: significant policy change affecting international students

Vipin Kumar/Hindustan Times/Getty Images

Since President Trump re-entered office, his second term has been characterized by a campaign to limit the number of international students in the country and make sure that those students leave once they complete their studies.

The crackdown began in spring 2025 with terminations of international students’ statuses in SEVIS, the online database that catalogs international students in the U.S. Those terminations were eventually reversed in court, but since then the administration has escalated its attacks, attempting to formally change the rules that govern international students.

Courts have repeatedly blocked those changes, including a rule that would have limited how long international students could study in the U.S. without an extension. But despite such wins, some advocates for international students say the fight is not yet over.

“The recent policy shifts, coupled with midterm election results … all of this combined leaves room for optimism,” said Anthony C. Ogden, founder and managing director at Gateway International Group, an international higher education firm. “But it’s not yet time to stop holding our breath, either.”

Inside Higher Ed has been tracking these developments from the beginning. Here’s a breakdown of some of the key changes and where they stand as of late November.

Visa Limits

Status: Blocked

It’s been over a year since the Department of Homeland Security first proposed ending duration of status, the long-standing policy allowing international students to stay in the United States until they finished their studies. The new rule, which also included limitations on international students’ ability to change their courses of study, would have only allowed them to stay in the country for four years unless they got an extension.

DHS said the goal of the change was to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. indefinitely, which the department said could lead to overstays and national security risks.

The rule was met with massive outcry from students and institutions, many of whom noted that almost all Ph.D. programs, as well as a handful of undergraduate programs, are designed to take longer than four years. Critics also took issue with a lack of information about the extension criteria, which left students essentially in the dark about whether they would be able to stay and complete their studies. Critics also noted that international students are also closely tracked by the federal government, characterizing the rule change as a solution in search of a problem.

Several higher ed groups and other associations sued in August to block the rule. They argued that DHS violated the Administrative Procedure Act—the statute that governs how federal agencies make rules—in a number of ways, including by failing to complete a thorough cost-benefit analysis of the rule’s impact. A federal judge blocked the rule just before it was slated to go into effect in mid-September. It was ultimately tossed out entirely last week, though the administration is appealing.

“At a time when uncertainty continues to affect our field, this decision is a powerful reminder that our collective voice matters and that standing firm in defense of educational opportunity can make a meaningful difference for institutions, students, and this nation,” said Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, in a news release. “International students and scholars deserve to have a level of predictability in pursuit of their dreams and it is in our nation’s best interest to provide it. Their contributions, combined with domestic talent, make our country stronger.”

Zachary New, an immigration attorney who has worked on several cases related to the Trump administration’s international student policies, called the decision a massive relief for his clients, and perhaps the most impactful decision by the courts on the fate of international students.

“The duration-of-status change has the potential to be a watershed moment in how international students were accessing the education system in the United States,” he said. “It [was] a really significant rule that would [have made it] very, very difficult for a lot of people to stay in status and very difficult for a lot of schools to retain talent or to recruit talent. So it was really a massive, massive change, and the fact that it is not in effect is— Words can’t say how big it is.”

Student Internships

Status: Blocked

Over the summer, the Student and Exchange Visitor Program severely limited curricular practical training, which authorizes international students to participate in internships. The agency’s guidance prohibited students from participating in internships unless one was required to graduate. The abrupt change shocked students and institutions; it prevented many students from continuing with internships they had already been offered in the fall of 2026, according to social media reports.

Although SEVP framed the memos as simply reinforcing existing norms of the program, international education experts argued that the guidelines marked a significant departure from how the program has operated.

Several higher education organizations challenged those changes in October, arguing that a memo was not the appropriate forum for making such drastic changes. A month and a half later, a judge temporarily blocked the guidelines while the litigation continues.

As a result, many institutions that had previously paused CPT due to the guidance resumed processing applications, according to public updates and articles in student-run publications. However, some institutions said they will continue operating under the August memos.

Work Authorization Fees

Status: Under Review

The next fight will likely center on optional practical training, which allows students on an F-1 visa to temporarily work in the U.S. after they graduate.…

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-24 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Why it is here: report on a specific incident with educational implications

John E. Moore III/Getty Images

Texas Tech University System board chair Cody Campbell allegedly pressured a university tenant to hire his oil and gas company to do consulting work and place him on its board, The Texas Tribune reported.

Campbell reportedly pitched consulting services from his firm, Double Eagle Energy Holdings, to executives at Fermi America, a company that plans to build the world’s largest data center. Fermi currently has a 99-year lease on nearly 5,000 acres owned by Texas Tech outside of Amarillo, Tex. Campbell reportedly sought to insert himself in the project and sought $150 million in stock options for his firm as well as partial ownership rights in a proposed natural gas pipeline for the data center, among other perks, according to a draft contract reviewed by the news outlet.

Former Fermi CEO and chairman Toby Neugebauer alleged that Texas Tech officials demanded his removal after he rejected Campbell’s offer and threatened to terminate its lease if he wasn’t pushed out of the company. Neugebauer was fired by Fermi’s board in April. SEC filings confirm Texas Tech raised concerns about him, specifically his behavior at a conference where he confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, which prompted critical media coverage.

Campbell told The Texas Tribune that Neugebauer’s allegations are “ridiculous and untrue.” Fermi officials also denied the claims.

The allegations come amid a bitter legal battle between Neugebauer and the company he co-founded with former Texas Gov. Rick Perry and others. The judge presiding over the case announced last week that he plans to dismiss the lawsuit challenging Neugebauer’s removal, The Texas Lawbook reported. Neugebauer also filed a separate lawsuit against Campbell on Nov. 9, alleging he used his “public office for personal enrichment.” That lawsuit remains active.

item.title: 5 Findings on Gen Z’s Changing Priorities
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting insights into Gen Z's priorities

Hispanolistic/E+/Getty Images

The evolving priorities, challenges and expectations of Gen Z are shaping how they navigate college and prepare to enter the workforce.

Recent research shows signs of improvement in college students’ mental health, even as artificial intelligence takes on a growing role in young people’s personal and academic lives. Other findings highlight how economic concerns are shaping their political engagement and how early career exploration may help students build confidence in their futures.

Here are five findings from recent Inside Higher Ed Student Success coverage that shed light on how colleges and universities can better understand and support the current generation of students.

- Student mental health is showing signs of improvement.

More than four in 10 American college students are flourishing—the highest share to report positive mental health in a decade, according to new survey data from the Healthy Minds Network. Meanwhile, rates of depression and anxiety have declined slightly as the stigma around discussing mental health wanes, though significant challenges remain.

The findings come from the 2025–26 Healthy Minds Study, led by researchers at Boston University; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Michigan; and Wayne State University. The study includes responses from 67,477 students at 107 colleges and universities; 77 percent were between the ages of 18 and 25.

Among respondents, 43 percent were identified as flourishing, up from 38 percent the previous academic year. Meanwhile, 34 percent reported symptoms of depression, down from 37 percent, and 30 percent reported symptoms of anxiety, down from 32 percent. However, rates of suicidal ideation and self-harm remained largely unchanged, as did the share of those reporting symptoms of disordered eating (28 percent).

Still, the overall trend is encouraging, experts said.

“Just because someone is not reporting depressive symptoms does not necessarily mean that they are functioning at the highest level they can,” said Justin Heinze, a health and psychology professor at the University of Michigan and a co-author of the study. “So to have decreases in loneliness, increases in flourishing, to see decreases in perceived stigma—that’s all moving in a positive direction.”

- Young people see AI as a safer source of emotional support.

Artificial intelligence has become increasingly intertwined with young people’s personal lives, including during their college years, when many are developing their identities and building meaningful relationships. But as AI becomes a source of emotional support and companionship, new research from The Rithm Project suggests that young people don’t necessarily have to trust the technology to turn to it for advice—they just need to perceive it as less risky than confiding in another person.

Earlier this year, the organization released research based on a survey of nearly 2,400 young people ages 13 to 24—including more than 500 young adults ages 18 to 24—examining how their AI use intersects with their social lives, emotional well-being and relationships.

In November, The Rithm Project released new research that builds on those findings through interviews with 29 young people from the original study—including 19 who are either currently enrolled in college or have completed a bachelor’s or associate degree. The interviews focused on two groups identified in the initial survey: those who turn to AI for personal and emotional support and those who interact with AI characters and personas.

Alison Lee, head of research and development at The Rithm Project, said one of the most notable findings was how young people weighed the perceived risks of confiding in AI against those of opening up to another person.

“What they were saying was ‘When I turn to AI, I know it’s hallucinating, I know that it’s glazing me, I know that it’s engaging in all these problematic behaviors,’” Lee said. “‘But those feel way more manageable as a risk than when I turn to a human.’

“Turning to a human is scary, it’s vulnerable, and you’re afraid of their judgment and emotional reactivity,” she added. “But big emotional events are a hallmark of the human experience … so it makes a lot of sense for young people to search for a place where those big emotions have a safe place to land and where they can make meaning of it.”

- AI is changing college, but long-standing challenges remain.

The college experience is evolving as new technologies reshape how students learn, complete coursework and seek academic support. While AI helps some students navigate their education more efficiently, it has also introduced new concerns about academic integrity and the quality of learning.

According to Inside Higher Ed’s 2026–27 Student Voice survey of 5,034 undergraduates from 310 mostly public two- and four-year institutions, 34 percent of students say generative or agentic AI helps them complete coursework and study more efficiently, while 33 percent say it helps them feel more confident understanding and tackling difficult concepts. However, 25 percent say they have changed how they write to avoid being falsely flagged by AI detectors.

Despite these technological shifts, long-standing challenges continue to affect students’ academic success and persistence. Mental health is the most commonly cited barrier, reported by 41 percent of students, followed by financial pressure at 37 percent. More than six in 10 students have also gone without at least one essential—such as food, housing or transportation—in the past year for financial reasons.

Looking ahead, 54 percent of students want their institutions to prioritize job pipelines and internships to better prepare them for the labor market. At the same time, 80 percent somewhat or strongly agree that their college is preparing them to succeed in today’s job market, even as many report stress about life after graduation.…

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-24 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.insidehighered.com/news/student-success/college-experience/2026/11/24/5-findings-gen-zs-changing-priorities

item.title: New, Full-Time Enrollees in Science, Health Grad Programs Dropped 10% Last Year
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: statistical overview of graduate enrollment trends

WUT789/iStock/Getty Images

First-time, full-time enrollment in U.S. science, engineering and health graduate programs declined about 10 percent from 2024 to 2025, according to survey results published last week by the National Science Foundation.

The total number of grad students in these fields dropped from roughly 818,100 to 796,300. The overall number of students specifically seeking master’s degrees dropped 5 percent, to 481,200.

But overall enrollment for doctoral students increased 1 percent, to 315,100, despite the significant drop in new, full-time doctoral enrollees. That’s the highest number of Ph.D. students in these fields ever reported to the survey, according to NSF’s National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics.

NSF did note precipitous drops in new enrollment by international students holding temporary visas. The Trump administration has targeted these students through deportations, visa restrictions and other avenues that have been challenged in court.

“From 2024 to 2025, 19,903 fewer temporary visa holders began full-time master’s degree programs (decrease of 32.5%) and 3,841 fewer temporary visa holders began full-time doctoral programs (down 16.2%)” in science, engineering and health, NSF reported.

The survey collected data from 635 colleges and universities that award research-based master’s or doctoral degrees in these fields. The National Institutes of Health assisted NSF with the survey.

Institutions may have hope for a rebound in new international student enrollments. Separate data from Common App shows that the number of first-year international students applying to college through the Common App is up 9 percent this year, compared to the same point in the application cycle last year.

item.title: Book Explores ‘New American Frontier’ of Training for Tech Jobs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: exploration of tech job training

Inside Higher Ed | Harvard Education Press

The American workforce is changing rapidly, and given this moment of “immense technological change,” Rachel Lipson argues, the fear and anxiety around disruption are pretty reasonable.

“There’s a good reason why people are concerned,” said Lipson, a research fellow at the Harvard University Kennedy School. However, state and college leaders “can’t just sit around hand-wringing.”

In her new book, The New American Frontier: Job Training for the Next Technological Age (Harvard Education Press), Lipson explores how community colleges can work with businesses to train workers for emerging jobs in industries such as electric vehicle manufacturing, semiconductors, cloud computing and quantum technologies.

It’s the book she said she wished she could have read when she started her job at the Department of Commerce as a senior policy adviser in the CHIPS program office, helping revitalize the U.S. semiconductor manufacturing industry.

The book, which Lipson said was written with college leaders and policymakers in mind, explains emerging industries, why they matter and what kinds of workers they need. It also highlights several instances in which community colleges have successfully expanded existing programs to meet the evolving workforce needs in their regions.

“These are not your grandfather’s factory jobs,” she writes. “The next-generation technician in a data center or semiconductor clean room will look very different from an assembly line worker whose day was defined by repetition.”

Lipson argues that working on the technological “frontier” will give colleges and policymakers an opportunity to “reimagine how we do workforce development overall.”

In an interview with Inside Higher Ed, Lipson discussed her new book, how she thinks four-year institutions can learn from community colleges and how institutions can overcome barriers to work with emerging technology companies. This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Q: What is the role of community colleges in “the new American frontier”? How is it different from the role they’ve historically played?

A: In some ways, the community colleges are the star of the book in that they’re the key educational institutions that are positioned to be the ones to respond to this next technological frontier. They are in every part of the country, they’re accessible, they’re much more in the business of not being afraid to train someone for a job.

I feel like a lot of higher ed has seen that as a dirty word. You know, “We are educating individuals and we don’t want to be told by a company what it is that they need for someone to actually know on day one,” whereas at least for some community colleges, that’s much more in their DNA to do that.

The set of jobs that are featured in the book are very hands-on. They often require access to state-of-the-art equipment and instructors who have worked in the industry. Community colleges—not all, but I’d say the best ones—that’s what they’ve been in the business of doing.

You’ll see a lot in the book of this concept I talked about in my prior work, too, noncredit as incubator. You have this arm—whether you want to call it noncredit or continuing education—that you’ve had as part of your institution that’s always worked directly with businesses on training new workers or upskilling their incumbent workforce. That is a great tool because those programs can often be more flexible. And importantly, for the types of technologies that are featured in the book, they have these really tight connections with employers and they’re grounded in the local economy.

One of the chapters is on the quantum industry in Colorado; the companies featured there, in a lot of cases, were founded by people who have Ph.D.s in physics who came out of big research institutions in that region that specialize in optics and photonics. These companies historically were really research heavy, so they had a lot of people with Ph.D.s, but now they have real products that are coming to market. They’re at that commercialization scale. And it’s become clear it’s no longer a good idea to have someone who has a Ph.D. in physics being the one who’s responsible for all the soldering of wires.

There’s a lot of reasons for that. But these companies tried hiring folks with bachelor’s in physics, but those candidates have never been in a lab—everything they have done was theory first. Even in a Ph.D. program, you don’t get out into the lab doing stuff with your hands until the later years of your program. But if you go and visit the community college, what you would see is actually on day one of the program, you start in the lab, you’re working with machines and everything you learn is by doing.

I think the rest of U.S. higher ed can learn a lot from community colleges right now, because at the pace with which technology is moving, learning in environments that look closer to the workplace is going to be what we need. Community colleges have done a really good job of making that a core part of their philosophy.

Q: Why is it so hard for colleges and workforce training programs to meaningfully work with employers? What does the best version of this look like?

A: I think it’s important to acknowledge that there are a lot of frictions and I don’t like when people say, “It’s natural that colleges and companies are going to work together and everything is magical.”…

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-24 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant political event with useful vocabulary and context.

Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends

An attempt by Reform UK to remove the Senedd's Presiding Officer has failed, following a passionate speech to the Welsh Parliament by Huw Irranca-Davies.

Members of the Senedd (MSs) rejected Reform's motion by 55 votes to 29.

Earlier the party ended a two-week boycott of most proceedings in the chamber after one of them, Joe Martin, was banned from speaking and told to apologise for remarks about immigration.

Irranca-Davies, whose title is Llywydd, said his duty was to "apply the rules fairly and impartially".

Reform's Llyr Powell said: "If you had a problem with what Joe Martin said, debate him, don't shut him down."

A source close to Irranca-Davies had "wholly refuted" Reform's accusations he had changed his mind during negotiations about Martin returning to the debating chamber.

Irranca-Davies had ruled that a claim by Martin - that white people were being "replaced" - broke the rules because it was "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Responding to Reform's attempt to remove him on Tuesday evening, the presiding office gave a long and passionate speech in defence of his role, which prompted a standing ovation from the other Cardiff Bay parties.

"The duty of the chair is not to please, it is not to flatter, not to avoid controversy, it is to apply the rules fairly and impartially, irrespective of pressure, of popularity or of political consequence," he said.

"Parliamentary privilege has never meant that anything goes, it has never meant speech without standards, it has never meant rights without responsibilities.

"Without rules, eventually it is only the loudest voices that are heard. "Without rules intimidation begins to replace persuasion, without rules scrutiny deteriorates into shouting."

After losing the vote, which Reform had no realistic prospect of winning, its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said it was "now clear that the establishment parties are content to see a Member of this Senedd silenced".

"We will continue to fight for the rights of elected members to represent their constituents as they see fit," she said.

At the start of the afternoon session, without announcing an end to their protest, Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon. Martin was not among them.

Jenner began her contribution by asking Senedd members: "Did you miss us?"

"It's been a little bit duller without us in here," she added.

In an answer to a question from her, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said "it's good of her to turn up today", and later accused her party of "chucking their toys out of the pram".

Reform is the biggest opposition group in the Senedd, but its members have stayed away from plenary sessions - full meetings in the debating chamber - since 11 November.

The party said it had left its seats empty during debates and questions to Welsh government ministers because it was standing up for free speech.

The boycott began after Irranca-Davies told Martin his comments had broken the Senedd's rules, and he would not be called to speak until he apologised.

Shortly after its members had returned to the Senedd chamber, the party sent journalists a statement from Jenner.

She said the party "thought we were approaching a sensible resolution" in talks with the Llywydd that would allow Martin "to return to the chamber without apologising for the speech he made in the Senedd".

"It has become clear this morning that the Llywydd has not been negotiating in good faith and has changed his mind at the eleventh hour," Jenner said.

"He has admitted to us that his decisions on this matter have been influenced by the feelings of outside organisations.

"It is now for him to explain to the people of Wales which organisations they are and what that means for Welsh democracy.

"We now have no choice but to escalate this situation."

The Senedd's authorities strongly denied Reform's "completely inaccurate" claims and said the Llywydd's position had remained the same since he ruled against Martin.

A source close to Irranca-Davies said he was "always clear" during four meetings with Reform that Martin needed to apologise.

Irranca-Davies, who chairs Senedd plenary sessions, left the chamber during First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon.

A spokesperson for the Llywydd said he met Jenner "entirely in good faith and had hoped to continue these confidential discussions constructively".

"It is unfortunate that they have chosen this course of action," the spokesperson added.

"While the Llywydd is disappointed, he respects the democratic process.

"Just as members elected him to this role, it is right that they have the opportunity to decide whether he continue to have their confidence."

Source: BBC Politics | Published: 2026-11-24 20:26 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

In Wake of Democrats’ Midterm Victory, Majority of Americans Approve of the Party’s Policies and Plans

Americans are greeting this month’s wave of Democratic election victories with generally positive feelings. Across several issues facing the country, more Americans say Democratic congressional leaders will have the better approach than say President Donald Trump will – by double-digit margins.

Democrats’ Optimism About the Party’s Future Rebounds as GOP Optimism Drops to Decade Low

Following big victories in this year’s midterm elections, 85% of Democrats say they are optimistic about their party’s future, rebounding from a decade low in 2024. Among Republicans, 57% say they are optimistic about the GOP’s future, down from 86% two years ago.

Two-Thirds of Americans Disapprove of Trump’s Handling of the Russia-Ukraine War

Around four-in-ten Americans say President Donald Trump is favoring Russia too much in its war with Ukraine. Just 7% say he is favoring Ukraine too much, while 21% say he is striking the right balance. There continues to be a wide partisan gap on whether the U.S. has a responsibility to help Ukraine defend itself.

How Americans View Federal Agencies

On balance, Americans view eight of 12 federal agencies we asked about more favorably than unfavorably. The National Park Service, National Weather Service and U.S. Postal Service are regarded especially positively.

item.title: Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed examination of a policy issue with concrete details and useful vocabulary.

Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs

The main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended.

The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition.

The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year.

The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system".

Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings.

The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million.

The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs.

It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report.

- Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit

He told MPs the current assessment process was "dehumanising" and focused on "what somebody cannot do", rather than "supporting independence".

The government has committed to a recommendation that people receiving end-of-life care or with "serious, well-evidenced conditions" would receive payments without a full assessment.

It has also agreed to reduce "unnecessary" reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve.

Under the report's proposals, cash payments would remain alongside better support to signpost people into education or employment, although claimants could choose to exchange part of their payment for practical services instead.

In the longer-term, the report recommends changes to the assessment process that look at someone's real-life additional costs and individual needs, focusing on "how people can live the life they want to live, rather than what they cannot do".

It proposes "improved" questions to understand the extra costs people face, although claimants would not be asked to calculate their costs or provide receipts.

'Rebalancing'

Currently eligibility for Pip is based on how difficult people find carrying out everyday tasks, with two levels of payment available.

But the review suggests future payment options could include bands more closely linked to extra costs.

The report says its approach is likely to lead to a "rebalancing" of payments, indicating that some claimants could lose out under a new system, either receiving less than they do currently or not qualifying for payments at all.

"Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support," it says.

"Conversely, this benefit is not appropriate for those who do not incur any additional costs associated with being disabled."

The review also calls for an increase in face-to-face assessments, which has been show to reduce eligibility.

The remit of the review was not to produce savings, and it does not set out whether the reforms would reduce the overall welfare bill.

Spending on Pip is set to be about Â£32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to Â£41.5bn by the end of the decade.

It comes after a separate review by former minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets).

The government welcomed Milburn's report, which included a recommendation to move under-25s off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.

This has lead to concerns about a two-tier system, where some people with the same conditions could get different levels of payments depending on their age.

The government has said it will consider the Timms review alongside Milburn's recommendations, with its final proposals set out early next year.

Sir Stephen said this would include detailing the overall costs of changes to the system.

- At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report

'Months of uncertainty'

Eduin Latimer, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said the review's recommendations had "the potential to better tailor Pip to claimants' needs".

But he said this would also create challenges, "most importantly in defining what disability-related costs are included, and finding a fair way of measuring them".

Latimer said making it easier to apply for Pip in its current form would "likely increase the number of claimants - and hence spending".

He added: "If the government wants to make Pip easier to apply for while also keeping spending in line with current projections, they would likely have to tighten eligibility criteria or reduce award amounts."

Disability charities have largely welcomed the review's recommendations of fast-tracked support and fewer reassessments.

However, they have said any changes should not leave disabled people financially worse off.

The Liberal Democrats said younger disabled people would now face "months of uncertainty" whilst the government considers the separate reviews from Timms and Milburn, and urged ministers to say quickly what they intend to do.…

item.title: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important news on security and business implications with clear reporting.

Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage

The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.

An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.

Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.

In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.

Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.

The joint alert, external between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.

It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".

When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation".

Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.

The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic".

"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.

Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".

Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

- Published1 day ago

item.title: Can AI Research Tools Help Code Data About Restrictions on Religion?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Exploration of a research topic with technical detail and useful vocabulary.

Every year, Pew Research Center releases a report measuring how governments and societies around the world restrict the free exercise of religion.

The study involves a demanding process of manually coding data from a set of publicly available sources, including national constitutions and publications from the U.S. government, the United Nations and nongovernmental organizations like Human Rights Watch.

We ran two experiments to see whether artificial intelligence could make this process easier for human coders to complete.

The problem

Typically, a team of five trained coders spends about four months combing through the source documents used for the study. Their goal is to answer more than 30 questions from the project’s codebook about laws, policies or events that may have restricted freedom of religious belief or practice in each country in a given year.

For example, the codebook questions ask whether the country has a constitution that provides for religious freedom; whether there were policies at any level of government (national, provincial or local) that restricted religious worship or conversion in a particular year; whether there was government harassment of religious groups; and whether religious groups faced harassment by nongovernmental actors such as mobs, organizations or individuals.

Two coders independently review each law, policy or event (or “case”) for a country and reconcile any disagreements. Next, the findings are combined into annual scores for each country, for each geographic region and for the world as a whole. We then use these scores to produce a Government Restrictions Index, or GRI, and a Social Hostilities Index, or SHI. (For more details, read the most recent study’s summary of results and methodology.)

There are two distinct steps for coding each question from the project codebook. First, coders search the source documents for all relevant information about a case. Second, they use that information to decide how the case should be categorized and counted, according to the question’s rubric.

Most of the time coders spend on each case is dedicated to combing through the source documents, so we were curious whether AI could speed up that process. Specifically, we wanted to try “source-grounded” AI tools, which can answer questions using specific documents and cite where each piece of information used in its answer came from.

What we tried

We ran two workflow experiments, each designed around a different commercially available AI research tool: Google’s NotebookLM and LexisNexis’ Nexis+ AI (updated versions of these products are now called Gemini Notebook and Nexis+ with Protégé). To assess reliability and consistency, we compared the results with data that had already been hand-coded in prior studies. Our main interest was whether the AI tools could make the coding process faster without degrading quality.

Each workflow experiment addressed a different question:

- NotebookLM: Can it help us identify relevant information from our regular source materials? Typically, we code each case from a standardized set of sources. For the experiment, we loaded the set of sources for each country into NotebookLM, which lets users chat with an AI model about uploaded documents. Then we asked it to find and summarize the key information from those sources.

- Nexis+ AI: Can it help us find relevant documents we don’t yet have? Sometimes we can get additional details about a case if we evaluate sources beyond our standard set. But finding these extra sources adds even more time to the process. To see whether AI could help when coding without any predefined list of sources, we entered codebook questions into Nexis+ AI, which can search a database of licensed news articles and summarize what it finds.

We conducted our tests with NotebookLM between December 2024 and February 2025. We asked the tool to review our standard sources from 2021, which our human coders had previously scoured to produce a report. In the first part of the experiment, we had it retrieve and summarize the relevant source materials for every codebook question for five countries that have varying levels of religious restrictions: Germany, Iceland, Jamaica, Nigeria and Singapore. Then we had the tool do the same for specific types of questions in a few additional countries: incident counts for Canada, China, India, Saudi Arabia and Turkmenistan; and questions about government processes and religious favoritism for Indonesia, Serbia and Syria.

We conducted our tests with Nexis+ AI between July and August 2025. In this experiment, we used previously coded data from 2020 and 2022 and worked with a subset of the codebook questions (rather than the entire codebook) for eight countries: Canada, Egypt, Germany, Jamaica, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, Singapore and South Korea. In this test, we used two thematic questions on COVID-19 and religious restrictions that we coded for 2020. (These questions were supplemental to our standard codebook only for that coding year. They were coded by humans using our standard sources and supplemental news sources. For more information on how we previously coded these supplemental questions, refer to the 2020 methodology.) The 2022 data we used was a subset of questions from our standard codebook and had been coded using our standard sources.

In both tests, we compared each tool’s summary with the results of human coding. Our coders also verified every citation the tools produced.

What we learned

Here are the key takeaways from our experiments:

The tools didn’t make things up. But they also didn’t find everything we wanted them to find.

Neither tool produced answers that we couldn’t verify in the cited sources, and NotebookLM was good at pulling together accounts of the same incident, from multiple sources, into an accurate summary.…

Source: Pew Research Center | Published: 2026-11-24 16:57 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Making the Most of South Korea’s Semiconductor Boom
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of an economic issue with useful context and vocabulary.

South Korea has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Its semiconductor industry is growing rapidly, lifting exports, corporate profits, and national income. But this success makes for an acute vulnerability: the stronger South Korea’s leading industry becomes, the more dependent the economy is on a single global technology cycle.

The semiconductor industry is growing at a rapid pace. In the first 10 months of 2026, South Korea’s merchandise exports surged by more than 60 percent year on year, reaching $930 billion, with semiconductors accounting for nearly 43 percent of the total. Stronger chip demand and rising export prices have helped push economic growth well above expectations. The International Monetary Fund raised its 2026 growth forecast for South Korea from 1.9 percent in January to 3.3 percent last month, and to 3.9 percent last week.

This is more than an ordinary semiconductor upturn. Massive investments in AI data centers have fueled demand for advanced high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, where South Korean manufacturers hold a strong competitive position. Expectations of continued progress on AI adoption suggest that demand for computing power and memory could continue expanding for years.

But the benefits of South Korea’s semiconductor boom are unevenly distributed. Chip manufacturing requires enormous capital investment but generates relatively few new jobs. Higher profits and wages are concentrated among leading firms and skilled workers in a single industry, leaving small businesses, service providers, and lower-skill workers behind. Although increased spending by semiconductor employees and suppliers can support local consumption, the gap between the chip industry and the rest of the economy remains substantial.

Moreover, South Korea’s dependence on semiconductors increases its vulnerability to global shocks – in particular, anything resembling a bubble collapse in the AI sector. The technology’s transformative potential does not guarantee that the current investment boom will continue uninterrupted. The Economist estimated that AI would need to generate $3 trillion in annual revenue by 2030 to justify the planned investments in data centers and computing infrastructure.

Political and regulatory pressures in the United States could make a downturn more likely. In the recent midterm elections, U.S. voters overwhelmingly backed more restrictions and even outright moratoria on data centers, over concerns about data centers’ electricity consumption, water use, and effects on local communities.

Higher financing costs, disappointing revenues, tighter regulations, or delays in infrastructure construction could slow AI investment in the United States, weakening demand for South Korean semiconductors at a time when chipmakers are expanding capacity. Shortages would quickly turn into oversupply and falling prices. The Bank of Korea estimates that a slowdown in U.S. investment in 2027 could cause South Korean semiconductor exports to fall by up to $100 billion below earlier projections, reducing South Korea’s GDP growth by approximately 0.4 percentage points. Falling corporate earnings could depress stock prices, weaken business investment, and reduce corporate tax revenues.

An AI bust could also threaten global financial stability. With tech firms increasingly reliant on private credit and entangled in complex circular-financing arrangements, a downturn could have far-reaching financial consequences. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s latest Financial Stability Report identified AI as the most frequently cited financial stability risk among surveyed market participants.

Trade tensions are another challenge. South Korea’s merchandise trade surplus reached nearly $295 billion in the first ten months of 2026, more than five times the level recorded a year earlier. That includes a $102 billion surplus with the United States. Already, U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has used tariffs to wrest concessions from countries running surpluses with the United States, including South Korea. The possibility of another round of U.S. demands cannot be dismissed.

South Korea also risks being collateral damage in the China-U.S. rivalry. South Korea’s semiconductor industry sits at the intersection of U.S. technology, Taiwanese advanced manufacturing, and Chinese electronics production. Samsung and SK Hynix operate manufacturing facilities in China, which is a major destination for Korean chip exports.

But Washington has long sought to restrict China’s access to advanced technologies. The recent scandal involving Nvidia’s ousted-then-reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, has added momentum to efforts to tighten export controls. New U.S. restrictions have already forced Samsung and TSMC to suspend some chip shipments to Chinese customers. Further restrictions could disrupt not only South Korean chip sales to China, but also the maintenance and upgrading of factories there.

In the longer term, such restrictions will motivate China to develop its own advanced chip sector. Already, Chinese memory producers are expanding their capacity and investing in more sophisticated chips. Though South Korea’s firms retain a considerable technological advantage today, particularly in advanced memory, China might gradually catch up, thanks to its large domestic market and substantial government support. As a result, South Korea could face heightened competition in conventional memory and, eventually, higher-value products.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-24 16:21 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Kidnapping Emerges as a Growing Tool of Militant Pressure in Pakistan
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Insightful piece on a security issue with relevant details and vocabulary.

Three young men were abducted at gunpoint in Pakistan’s southwestern province of Balochistan on November 16, after armed men riding motorcycles intercepted them near the Kotera River in Jhal Magsi district. Police identified the victims as Riaz Ahmed, Iltazai Lashari, and Tariq Lashari. While both the police and security forces launched a search operation, the men’s whereabouts remained unknown as of this writing. No group has claimed responsibility for the abduction, and authorities have not publicly identified the perpetrators.

The incident draws attention to a dimension of Pakistan’s security crisis that receives less scrutiny than suicide bombings, improvised explosive device attacks, and armed assaults: the use of kidnapping to intimidate, gain resources, and exert pressure.

There is a wider pattern of abductions across Balochistan, where a decades-long separatist insurgency has contributed to persistent insecurity. Government officials, security personnel, workers, and civilians have all been targeted in reported kidnappings carried out along major highways and in remote districts.

Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province by area, borders Afghanistan and Iran and is rich in natural resources, including minerals. Its strategic location, mining industry, and major transport corridors make it economically significant. It is also the center of a long-running separatist insurgency involving armed organizations seeking greater political autonomy and control over the province’s resources.

According to data from the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based security research organization, 88 people were abducted in incidents linked to militant violence across Pakistan in October 2026, up 22 percent from 72 in September. This was the highest monthly total recorded in the preceding year. Balochistan accounted for 70 of these abductions, nearly 80 percent of the national total.

Kidnappings increased even as conventional militant violence declined. Pakistan recorded 143 militant attacks in October, compared with 226 in September, a decrease of 37 percent. Deaths resulting from these attacks fell by 57 percent, from 260 to 111, while injuries dropped by 71 percent, according to the same PICSS assessment. The divergence suggests that kidnapping warrants attention as a separate dimension of insecurity. In assessments focused primarily on attacks and casualties, armed abductions can easily be overlooked.

On October 16, armed men intercepted the vehicle of Asad Ullah Kakar, commissioner of Rakhshan division, while he was travelling from Quetta to Kharan along the Noshki-Kharan highway. The attackers abducted the senior government official and his driver, although the latter was released. No group publicly claimed responsibility in the initial reporting.

In a similar case, Kharan Deputy Commissioner Munir Ahmed Soomro was seized along with his companions on September 20. He was released on October 3 after nearly two weeks in captivity, following negotiations involving local tribal elders and the kidnappers, according to officials. His release highlighted the role of informal tribal mediation in securing the freedom of abductees, particularly in areas where conventional law enforcement has struggled to resolve such cases.

Security personnel have also been targeted for kidnapping. On October 16, armed men intercepted a passenger van carrying 20 personnel of the Levies Force, a paramilitary group. The recruits were undergoing police training in Balochistan’s Kalat district and were travelling home for the weekend when they were abducted. The attackers released the driver and three other passengers but took the recruits to an undisclosed location. All 20 were recovered safely on October 20. No group claimed responsibility.

Two days later, armed men abducted 18 laborers and the son of a marble factory owner from a mining facility in Naal, Khuzdar district. One worker was shot and injured while attempting to escape. The attackers also took vehicles and equipment from the premises. Again, no group claimed responsibility for the incident.

Since so many of these crimes remain unattributed, it’s unclear how many abductions are being carried out by organized militant organizations and how many involve criminal networks exploiting weak security in remote areas. There is evidence pointing to both at times, although responsibility remains unestablished in several prominent cases.

In September, Pakistani security forces recovered 23 abducted people during an operation near Kalat. According to the military, armed men had established an unauthorized checkpoint along the N-25 highway, stopping vehicles to abduct passengers for ransom, extort money and seize vehicles. Five militants were killed during the operation.

The military pinned the abductions on Fitna-al-Hindustan, a designation used by Pakistani authorities for Baloch separatist militants, including the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) and associated groups. The BLA is an armed separatist organization seeking independence for Balochistan and has claimed responsibility for attacks against Pakistani security forces and infrastructure. The Kalat operation provided a documented example of militant hostage-taking, extortion, and the seizure of commercial vehicles.

However, not every disappearance or kidnapping in Balochistan can be attributed to separatist groups. There are also simple abductions for ransom by criminals seeking to take advantage of instability. Then there is the longstanding problem of enforced disappearances. Families have accused state security agencies of detaining relatives without disclosing their whereabouts, allegations that authorities have disputed. These cases are distinct from militant hostage-taking and should not be conflated.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-24 15:53 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Fiji Declares Nationwide Disaster Amid El Nino Drought
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: News report on a natural disaster with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Fiji has declared a nationwide state of disaster as a worsening El Nino-driven drought pushes water shortages across the Pacific island nation to crisis levels, threatening communities, agricultural production, and access to essential supplies.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka announced the declaration on November 18 after the Cabinet approved the measure following recommendations from the National Disaster Risk Management Council. The government has allocated 20 million Fijian dollars from existing ministerial funds to strengthen emergency water supplies and support affected households, farmers, and livestock owners.

According to the government, more than 2 million liters of emergency water have been delivered to affected maritime communities over the past month, while the Water Authority of Fiji continues supplying mainland communities.

The declaration, made under Section 91 of Fiji’s National Disaster Risk Management Act, enables the government to intensify its response and coordinate assistance nationwide. It can remain in force for up to 30 days.

The declaration reflects the severity of the drought. Fiji’s Meteorological and Hydrological Services reported that all monitoring stations recorded less than half their usual October rainfall. Twenty-six of the 27 stations experienced well-below-normal conditions, with Nadi, Yasawa, Viwa, and Rotuma recording their lowest October rainfall totals on record.

The agency’s November outlook also forecast below-normal rainfall through April 2027, raising concerns about the sustainability of water supplies and agricultural production. Fiji’s wet season typically runs from November to April, with about three-quarters of its annual rainfall coming in that period.

The drought is associated with El Nino, a climate phenomenon involving unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific that alters atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s November 12 assessment indicated that a strong to very strong El Nino was likely to persist through early 2027.

Beyond the immediate humanitarian consequences, the crisis raises questions about the capacity of Pacific Island governments to manage increasingly disruptive climate conditions. For Fiji, the challenge is not simply delivering emergency water but reducing the country’s vulnerability to recurring periods of extreme rainfall variability.

Fiji’s National Climate Change Policy 2018-2030 and National Adaptation Plan identify climate resilience, sustainable development, and coordinated adaptation as national priorities. The country’s National Adaptation Plan includes 160 adaptation measures designed to bolster five areas: food and nutrition security, health, human settlements, infrastructure, and biodiversity and the natural environment. It includes “a specific call for integrated water resource management.”

However, the current drought highlights the importance of translating these commitments into practical infrastructure and community-level protection. Investment in rainwater harvesting, water storage facilities, groundwater monitoring, improved distribution networks, and climate-resilient agriculture could help reduce dependence on emergency deliveries when rainfall declines.

However, financing these adaptation measures remains challenging. Fiji’s National Climate Finance Strategy identified water and sanitation, agriculture, health, and disaster risk management among the sectors requiring urgent investment. The current emergency illustrates the difficulty of balancing immediate disaster expenditure with longer-term resilience projects, particularly for small island developing states with limited fiscal resources. Fiji is responding to the national disaster by shifting funds from other projects.

Fiji and other small island developing states have repeatedly called for greater access to climate finance, arguing that countries with relatively small contributions to global emissions face disproportionate climate-related risks. The drought reinforces the importance of ensuring that international adaptation commitments translate into accessible funding for practical projects, rather than remaining diplomatic pledges.

Water shortages can undermine food production, increase household costs, and place additional pressure on public health systems. For remote maritime communities, where access to infrastructure and essential services is already limited, prolonged drought can deepen existing inequalities.

Neighboring Pacific countries face similar exposure to climate variability, making regional cooperation increasingly important. Sharing meteorological information, strengthening early-warning systems, and coordinating disaster preparedness could improve the ability of Pacific governments to respond to climate-related emergencies.

The immediate priority for Fiji will be securing safe drinking water and protecting vulnerable communities. But with forecasts indicating that dry conditions could continue into 2027, the disaster declaration also presents a broader test of the country’s ability to move from emergency relief toward sustained climate resilience.
